items.availability_note: Oily fish, egg yolk and UV-exposed mushrooms all supply measurable vitamin D, and fortified milk, spreads, juices and cereals add small amounts, so this is a genuine dietary nutrient rather than a manufactured one. The catch is scale: the richest ordinary foods deliver a few hundred IU per portion, while typical supplement doses run 1,000 to 4,000 IU/day and treatment doses go far higher.

items.dose_gap: A 1,000 IU (25 µg) daily capsule needs about 150 g of cooked sockeye salmon or 155 g of grilled herring every single day. A 4,000 IU (100 µg) capsule needs roughly 600 g of sockeye salmon, 620 g of grilled herring, 46 large egg yolks, or about 1 kg of UV-treated portabella mushrooms daily. A 50,000 IU (1,250 µg) weekly loading dose, standard for correcting deficiency, has no food equivalent at all: it is about 7.8 kg of grilled herring. Real intakes are nowhere near this. UK NDNS figures cited by SACN put mean vitamin D intake from food at 2.8 µg/day in adults aged 19 to 65 and 3.3 µg/day in over-65s, which is 28% and 33% of the 10 µg RNI, and mean intakes have stayed below the RNI in every age group. Above roughly 50 degrees north, cutaneous synthesis is effectively zero from October to March, so there is no sunlight to make up the shortfall in winter. SACN's own conclusion was that the 10 µg RNI is difficult to achieve from natural food sources, which is why year-round or autumn/winter supplementation is advised for the whole UK population. Anyone with a diagnosed deficiency will not eat their way out of it at a northern latitude.
items.form_caveat: Mushroom vitamin D is D2 (ergocalciferol), a different molecule from the D3 in fish, egg yolk and almost all supplements, and D3 raises serum 25(OH)D more effectively than D2, with the gap widest for intermittent bolus dosing (Tripkovic et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012;95:1357-64, PMID 22552031, DOI 10.3945/ajcn.111.031070). UV mushroom content is also wildly variable and usually unlabelled: USDA measured UV-treated portabella at 3.4 µg/100 g from one producer and 25.6 µg/100 g from another, and maitake from 0.1 to 56.1 µg/100 g depending on the growing method, while untreated white mushrooms sit at 0.1 µg/100 g. Buying ordinary mushrooms because 'mushrooms have vitamin D' gets you essentially nothing. Cod liver oil is nominally a food but behaves as a supplement and carries 18,000 µg retinol per 100 g (CoFID 17-488), so a tablespoon delivers about 8,160 IU of preformed vitamin A alongside the D3, which rules it out in pregnancy. Oily fish delivers D3 inside a fat matrix with EPA/DHA, protein, iodine and selenium; a capsule delivers D3 alone.
items.bioavailability: Vitamin D from both food and capsules is fat-soluble and absorbed better with a meal containing fat, which oily fish and egg yolk supply themselves. The form matters more than the source: D2 from mushrooms is less effective per microgram than D3 (PMID 22552031). Egg yolk additionally contains 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (0.36 µg/100 g, CoFID 12-939), an already-hydroxylated metabolite that supplements normally do not provide. Total vitamin D figures in composition tables often bundle 25-OH-D3 with cholecalciferol, so a headline 'vitamin D' number for eggs or canned salmon is not strictly comparable to the D3 in a capsule.

items.supplement: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d
items.availability_note: Alpha-tocopherol is abundant in ordinary foods: seed oils, sunflower seeds, almonds, hazelnuts and wheatgerm all supply meaningful amounts, and a normal diet covers the 15 mg/day RDA without effort. What food cannot do is reach 400 IU, which is 268 mg of RRR-alpha-tocopherol (natural form) or 180 mg of all-rac-alpha-tocopherol (synthetic), roughly 12 to 18 times the RDA.

items.dose_gap: 400 IU of natural vitamin E is 268 mg of RRR-alpha-tocopherol. Reaching that from food, every day, means about 720 g of sunflower seeds (roughly 4,200 kcal), or 1.05 kg of almonds, or 201 g of wheatgerm oil (about 15 tablespoons of neat oil), or 550 g of sunflower oil. If the capsule is synthetic all-rac (180 mg for 400 IU), it is still 484 g of sunflower seeds or 10 tablespoons of wheatgerm oil daily. No dietary pattern gets there: habitual intakes cluster around 5 to 20 mg/day, so 400 IU sits one to two orders of magnitude above anything eating produces. This is a pharmacological dose with no dietary analogue, and it cannot be reached by eating.
items.form_caveat: Most 400 IU capsules contain all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate, a synthetic mixture of eight stereoisomers of which only one eighth is the RRR form that human alpha-tocopherol transfer protein preferentially retains. Food contains only RRR. That difference is precisely why the label conversions differ (1 IU = 0.67 mg natural versus 0.45 mg synthetic). Food also never delivers alpha-tocopherol in isolation: sunflower oil carries 48.7 mg alpha with 5.1 mg gamma per 100 g, while rapeseed oil carries 18.4 mg alpha with 38.0 mg gamma (CoFID 17-045, 17-041), and nuts add tocotrienols. High-dose alpha-tocopherol actively removes part of what food supplies: 400 IU/day of RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate cut serum gamma-tocopherol by a median 58% and reduced detectable delta-tocopherol in a randomised placebo-controlled trial of 184 adults (Huang et al., J Nutr 2003;133:3137-40, PMID 14519797). A 400 IU capsule is therefore not a concentrated version of a handful of sunflower seeds; it changes the balance of vitamin E forms in blood in a direction food never does.
items.bioavailability: Alpha-tocopherol needs dietary fat and bile for absorption, which nuts and oils supply intrinsically, so food forms are absorbed efficiently in ordinary meals. Fractional absorption falls as the single dose rises, and hepatic alpha-TTP selectively retains only the 2R stereoisomers, so the 2S half of a synthetic all-rac dose is largely excreted. The practical consequence is that the useful fraction of a 400 IU synthetic capsule is well below its stated IU, and the plasma alpha-tocopherol achieved does not scale linearly with dose, while the displacement of gamma- and delta-tocopherol documented by Huang et al. (PMID 14519797) does.

items.supplement: Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU
items.availability_note: Liver is far more concentrated in preformed retinol than the supplement: 10,000 IU is 3,000 µg retinol, and every common liver measured in the UK tables contains 10,500 to 25,200 µg per 100 g. This is the one item in this set where the food beats the pill, which is exactly why liver carries a public-health warning rather than a recommendation.

items.dose_gap: There is no gap to close. Twelve grams of fried calf liver supplies the full 3,000 µg (10,000 IU) of a high-dose retinol capsule, and a normal 100 g portion of any liver delivers 3.5 to 8.4 times that dose in a single sitting. A 40 g serving of liver pate is functionally a 10,000 IU tablet. A tablespoon of cod liver oil is 8,160 IU. Anyone eating liver weekly is already taking supraphysiological preformed vitamin A intermittently, and adding a 10,000 IU supplement on top compounds a load the body stores rather than clears. For context, the US tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A is 3,000 µg/day, which is the supplement dose itself, and the UK RNI is 700 µg for men and 600 µg for women.
items.form_caveat: The retinol in liver is the same molecule as the retinyl palmitate or acetate in capsules, absorbed by the same route and stored in the liver in the same way, so the usual reassurance that 'food forms are safer' does not apply here. Pregnancy is the sharp edge: UK advice is that people who are pregnant or who might become pregnant should avoid liver and liver products including pate, and should avoid supplements containing vitamin A including fish liver oils, because excess retinol is teratogenic (NHS pregnancy vitamins guidance; UK Committee on Toxicity statement on vitamin A in the maternal diet, TOX-2021-57). Cod liver oil is the common trap because it is bought for omega-3 or vitamin D and delivers 60,000 IU of retinol per 100 g. Outside pregnancy, chronic preformed retinol above the 3,000 µg/day UL is associated with reduced bone mineral density and fracture risk, which is why UK advice is to eat liver no more than once a week rather than to eat more of it. Beta-carotene-rich foods are the safe substitute precisely because their conversion is regulated (see the beta-carotene entry).
items.bioavailability: Retinyl esters from liver and from supplements are absorbed at high efficiency and, critically, absorption is not down-regulated when stores are full, so intake accumulates in hepatic stellate cells over weeks and months. This is the opposite of carotenoid absorption, which is feedback-limited through retinoic-acid induction of the intestinal transcription factor ISX and consequent repression of SR-B1 and BCO1 (reviewed in Nutrients 2019;11(4):838, DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). Cooking concentrates liver retinol rather than destroying it: CoFID shows raw lamb liver at 17,300 µg/100 g rising to 19,700 µg/100 g fried, and raw ox liver at 14,200 rising to 17,300 stewed, through water loss (codes 18-413, 18-494, 18-415, 18-416).

items.availability_note: Carrots, sweet potato and dark leafy greens are dense, ordinary sources: raw old carrot carries 9,149 µg beta-carotene per 100 g and boiled sweet potato 5,560 µg. By mass, the 20 to 30 mg doses used in the intervention trials are within reach of a few large portions, which makes this the one case where the food and the supplement look superficially comparable and behave completely differently.

items.dose_gap: By raw mass the trial doses are reachable: 20 mg/day is about 219 g of raw carrot (roughly three and a half medium carrots) or 360 g of boiled sweet potato, and 30 mg/day is about 312 g of carrot. By absorbed dose it is a different story. The Dietary Reference Intake conversion factors treat 12 µg of food beta-carotene as equivalent to 1 µg retinol activity, against 2 µg for supplemental beta-carotene in oil, implying the supplement form is about six times more available (Institute of Medicine, DRIs for Vitamin A and related micronutrients, 2001, DOI 10.17226/10026). Matching the absorbed exposure of a 20 mg capsule therefore takes on the order of 120 mg of food beta-carotene, roughly 1.3 kg of raw carrots every day, which nobody eats and which the gut would not absorb anyway. So the honest answer is that food matches the label number and does not match the plasma exposure that produced the trial results.
items.form_caveat: This is the clearest food-versus-extract case in the set. Supplement beta-carotene is synthetic all-trans-beta-carotene or algal/fungal beta-carotene, formulated in oil or water-dispersible beadlets specifically to defeat the poor bioavailability of the food form, so it is engineered to do what a carrot cannot. Food never delivers beta-carotene alone: the same carrot supplies 5,230 µg/100 g of alpha-carotene (CoFID 13-496), and dark greens supply lutein with far less beta-carotene. Dietary carotenoids carry none of the supplement harm for three reasons. First, uptake and cleavage are feedback-regulated: absorbed beta-carotene raises intracellular retinoic acid, which induces ISX, which represses SR-B1 and BCO1 in the enterocyte, so absorption falls as vitamin A status rises (Nutrients 2019;11(4):838, DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). A capsule of purified beta-carotene in oil pushes plasma concentrations well past anything food produces. Second, the harm signals came from isolated high doses in high-risk groups: 20 mg/day raised lung cancer incidence by 18% in male smokers (ATBC, N Engl J Med 1994;330:1029-35, PMID 8127329, DOI 10.1056/nejm199404143301501) and 30 mg/day plus 25,000 IU retinyl palmitate produced 28% more lung cancers, RR 1.36, in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (CARET, J Natl Cancer Inst 1996;88:1550, PMID 8901853, DOI 10.1093/jnci/88.21.1550). CARET cannot even be attributed to beta-carotene alone, since it co-administered a large preformed retinol dose. Third, overloading on carrots produces carotenodermia, a harmless orange discolouration of the skin, rather than hypervitaminosis A, because the conversion step is regulated. 'Eat carrots' and 'take 20 mg of beta-carotene' are not the same intervention.
items.bioavailability: Beta-carotene in raw carrot and raw spinach is locked in chromoplasts behind intact plant cell walls, so absorption from raw vegetables is low; chopping, pureeing, cooking and eating with fat all raise it, and cooking does not destroy it (CoFID shows boiled old carrot at 9,616 µg/100 g against 9,149 raw, codes 13-497 and 13-496, reflecting water loss and retention). The formal expression of this is the 12:1 food versus 2:1 supplement-in-oil conversion factor (IOM 2001, DOI 10.17226/10026). Conversion efficiency also varies substantially between individuals through BCO1 genotype and vitamin A status, which is why plasma responses to the same carrot intake differ several-fold between people (DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). Spinach deserves a specific caution: it is the textbook carotenoid green, but baby spinach carries only 1,559 µg/100 g raw, well under a fifth of carrot, and its oxalate load makes it a poor recommendation for people managing kidney stones.

items.availability_note: Both menaquinones occur in ordinary food, but in completely separate places: MK-7 is concentrated in natto at 939 µg/100 g, while MK-4 is spread thinly through chicken, egg yolk, full-fat dairy and meat at 1 to 22 µg/100 g. One pack of natto exceeds any commercial MK-7 dose, and no food comes within three orders of magnitude of the 45 mg MK-4 dose used clinically in Japan.

items.dose_gap: The two forms give opposite answers, which is why they must not be merged. MK-7 at the doses used in supplements and trials, 90 to 180 µg/day, is fully covered by food: one 50 g pack of natto is 470 µg of MK-7, so a pack every second or third day matches a 180 µg capsule. Nothing else does. Matching 180 µg/day from cheddar at 2.7 µg/100 g would take 6.7 kg of cheese a day, and from butter about 4.3 kg. MK-4 is the reverse. The clinical dose in Japan, menatetrenone for osteoporosis, is 45 mg/day (45,000 µg), typically 15 mg three times daily. At the richest measured food value, barbecue chicken at 22.1 µg/100 g, that is about 204 kg of chicken per day. Even a modest 1.5 mg consumer MK-4 pill needs 6.8 kg of chicken or 58 kg of whole milk. Measured whole-diet MK-4 intake sits around 17 µg/day (7.3% of a mean total vitamin K intake of about 230 µg/day in Japanese women, Kamao 2007), which is roughly one 2,600th of the pharmacological dose. MK-4 at supplement strength is unreachable by eating, and no amount of butter, egg yolk or chicken changes that.
items.form_caveat: MK-7 supplements are made by Bacillus subtilis natto fermentation, the same organism that makes natto, or synthesised; the active species is all-trans MK-7 and cis-isomer contamination is a documented quality problem in commercial products that the fermented food does not have. MK-4 supplements are wholly synthetic, derived from menadione, because no food is or could be concentrated to 45 mg per dose. Natto also brings the fermentation matrix, fibre and nattokinase, and circulating K2 after eating natto is around ten times the circulating K1 after eating spinach (Schurgers LJ, Vermeer C, Haemostasis 2000;30:298-307, PMID 11356998). The common 'cheese is a K2 food' claim needs unpicking: cheese total vitamin K is genuinely high, 282 µg/100 g for hard cheese and up to 506 µg/100 g for soft cheese, but roughly 90% of it is MK-9, MK-10 and MK-11 from starter bacteria (Fu et al. 2017, PMID 29955705), forms that no clinical trial has tested, while the MK-7 fraction is only a few µg/100 g. Animal MK-4 also tracks the animal's feed: menadione is a routine poultry feed additive and Elder et al. attribute poultry MK-4 to alkylation of that menadione, so brand, country and production system shift the numbers, and the two chicken hot dog and chicken broth samples in the same study contained no detectable MK-4 at all.
items.bioavailability: MK-4 and MK-7 behave so differently that microgram-for-microgram comparison is meaningless. A single 420 µg dose of MK-7 was well absorbed and remained detectable in serum for 48 hours, whereas the identical 420 µg dose of MK-4 was undetectable in serum, and over seven days of 60 µg/day only MK-7 raised serum concentrations (Sato T et al., Nutr J 2012;11:93, PMID 23140417, DOI 10.1186/1475-2891-11-93). MK-7's long half-life comes from its extended isoprenoid side chain and tight lipoprotein binding. This is the mechanistic reason MK-4 must be dosed in milligrams while MK-7 works in micrograms, and it means the 1 to 22 µg/100 g of MK-4 in butter, egg yolk, cheese and chicken contributes almost nothing to circulating vitamin K2 even though it is real and measurable. All menaquinones need dietary fat for absorption, which is why they are found in and absorbed from the fat phase of dairy and eggs; the reduced-fat versions lose most of it, with reduced-fat cheddar at 1.8 µg MK-4 per 100 g against 9.5 µg for full fat (PMID 29955705).

misclassifications: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d classified RICH: wrong for the item as scoped. The classification describes the nutrient, but the item is defined by its dose, and the entry's own dose_gap says 'This is a pharmacological dose with no dietary analogue, and it cannot be reached by eating.' A label of RICH sitting above that sentence is self-contradictory. Alpha-tocopherol at RDA level is genuinely rich in food; 400 IU is not obtainable from any diet. This needs a dose-aware class (nutrient rich in food, supplement dose unreachable), not RICH.

Vitamin K2 '(MK-7 and MK-4)' classified RICH as one merged item: two forms with opposite answers cannot share one availability class. MK-7 at 90 to 180 µg is genuinely food-reachable, but only from natto, so the RICH label rests on exactly one food that most of the target population never eats; every other MK-7 source listed is trace (cheddar 2.7, butter 4.2 µg/100 g). MK-4 at the 45 mg clinical dose is unreachable by a factor of thousands and the entry itself concedes 'MK-4 supplements are wholly synthetic, derived from menadione, because no food is or could be concentrated to 45 mg per dose.' Split into MK-7 = RICH (single-food dependency flagged) and MK-4 = synthetic/unreachable at clinical dose, trace in food.

Vitamin D3 classified RICH: defensible but borderline, and the entry does not acknowledge the tension. Two of the twelve 'foods' are not natural food sources at all: cod liver oil is conceded in the same entry to 'behave as a supplement', and fortified orange juice is a manufactured delivery vehicle. Strip those and one trace entry (untreated white mushrooms at 0.1 µg/100 g, under 1% of RNI), and the genuine dietary base narrows to oily fish plus egg yolk plus UV-treated mushrooms. Against that, the entry's own evidence is that population intake is 28 to 33% of the RNI and SACN concluded the RNI is 'difficult to achieve from natural food sources'. RICH is not wrong, but it should be qualified as 'rich in a narrow set of foods, and demonstrably not delivering the RNI at population level'.

Vitamin D3 food list omits the farmed-versus-wild distinction, which functions as a misclassification in practice: the entry anchors on wild sockeye at 16.7 µg/100 g, but farmed Atlantic salmon (what most shoppers actually buy) runs several-fold lower. Presenting sockeye as 'salmon' overstates what the typical purchase delivers.

Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU classified RICH: correct, and correctly reasoned. Liver genuinely exceeds the supplement dose and the entry draws the right conclusion (public-health warning, not recommendation). No change.

Beta-carotene supplements classified RICH: correct on mass, and the entry handles the absorbed-dose distinction unusually well rather than hiding behind the label. No change to the class. The supporting food values are where the problems are (see number_checks).
missing_foods: Vitamin D: UV-treated maitake, up to 56.1 µg/100 g. The entry cites this figure in its own form_caveat but leaves it out of the food list, where it would outrank every fish listed by more than 3x. Conspicuous omission.
Vitamin D: eel (unagi), among the richest natural D3 foods at roughly 18 to 23 µg/100 g, above every fish in the list.

Vitamin D: fortified margarine and fat spreads. Given the entry's explicit UK framing, omitting the fortified-spread category is a real gap, since it has been a statutory UK vitamin D vehicle for decades and contributes far more to UK intake than the fortified US orange juice that was included.
Vitamin D: fortified breakfast cereals, a larger real-world UK and US contributor than fortified orange juice.

Vitamin D: kippers and other smoked/cured herring, a UK staple; also canned red sockeye (higher than the canned pink that was listed), herring and cod roe, swordfish (about 14 µg/100 g), and sun-dried shiitake for D2.
Vitamin E: paprika and chilli powder at roughly 29 to 38 mg alpha-tocopherol/100 g, the densest common non-oil sources by weight and higher than every nut in the list.
Vitamin E: hazelnut oil (about 47 mg/100 g) and almond oil (about 39 mg/100 g), both above the sunflower oil that was listed.
Vitamin E: safflower oil (about 34 mg/100 g) and cottonseed oil (about 35 mg/100 g), both comparable to sunflower seeds and omitted entirely.
Vitamin E: peanuts and peanut butter (about 8 to 9 mg/100 g). Modest per 100 g but a far bigger real-world intake contributor than the wheatgerm the entry included at 1.3 mg per portion.

Vitamin E: corn oil (about 14 mg/100 g) and soybean oil (about 8 mg/100 g), the two highest-volume vitamin E vehicles in the Western diet, plus red palm oil (tocotrienol-rich), rice bran oil, pine nuts and Brazil nuts.

Preformed vitamin A: fortified margarine and fat spreads at roughly 800 to 900 µg retinol/100 g. A serious omission when butter at 671 to 958 µg/100 g was included, since fortified spread matches or beats butter and is eaten in the same way.

Preformed vitamin A: canned cod liver (Icelandic and Polish tinned cod liver), eaten as an ordinary food and carrying retinol in the same range as the cod liver oil the entry treats as a supplement. This is the sharpest real-world version of the entry's own 'cod liver oil is the common trap' point.
Preformed vitamin A: goose and duck liver, and foie gras, all in the same range as the livers listed; also liver sausage/liverwurst and haggis, which are how liver is most often eaten unnoticed.

Preformed vitamin A: hard cheese (Cheddar around 325 µg retinol/100 g), whole milk and cream. Omitting the dairy tier while including butter and egg yolk leaves the everyday retinol baseline understated.
Preformed vitamin A: halibut liver oil, substantially more concentrated in retinol than cod liver oil and sold in the same aisle.
Beta-carotene: red palm oil, the densest ordinary source at roughly 20,000 to 40,000 µg total carotenes/100 g, several times carrot. Its absence is the single biggest gap in that list.

Beta-carotene: carrot juice at roughly 9,300 µg/100 g. Matters more than any solid here because it is the one food that can be consumed in the volume needed to approach a 20 mg dose, which directly tests the entry's dose-gap argument.
Beta-carotene: butternut squash and pumpkin (roughly 4,000 to 6,900 µg/100 g), both above every green listed.
Beta-carotene: dried parsley, basil and coriander, plus paprika, all very high per 100 g; and cantaloupe melon (about 2,000 µg/100 g), fresh apricots, persimmon and papaya.

Beta-carotene: sweet red pepper, spring greens/collards, watercress, Swiss chard and romaine lettuce, all reasonable everyday sources that outrank the baby spinach the entry chose as its green exemplar.

Vitamin K2: goose liver paste at roughly 369 µg MK-4/100 g, the richest MK-4 food in the standard food-composition literature and about 17x the barbecue chicken the entry calls 'the richest measured food value'. This omission produces an outright false statement in the dose_gap and form_caveat.

Vitamin K2: Gouda, Edam, Jarlsberg and other long-ripened Dutch and Norwegian cheeses, the canonical MK-9-rich cheeses. The entry builds its whole 'cheese is a K2 food' rebuttal on Cheddar, which is the weaker exemplar; using Gouda would test the claim properly.
Vitamin K2: curd cheese and quark, listed as K2 sources in the very Schurgers and Vermeer paper the entry cites.

Vitamin K2: other fermented soy foods, tempeh, fermented soy pastes and Korean cheonggukjang, which would show whether natto is uniquely high or merely the best-measured; plus sauerkraut and fermented salami for modest MK-7.
dose_gap_errors: Beta-carotene, 30 mg from carrot: stated 'about 312 g of carrot', wrong. The sentence establishes raw carrot at 9,149 µg/100 g and computes 20 mg as 219 g of raw carrot, then silently switches to the boiled value for the 30 mg figure. At raw 9,149 µg/100 g, 30 mg needs 327.9 g. Corrected: about 328 g of raw carrot (312 g is the boiled-carrot answer, 30,000/9,616 x 100 = 312.0 g). Against USDA's raw carrot value of 8,285 µg/100 g it is 362 g.

Vitamin K2, 1.5 mg MK-4 from whole milk: stated 'or 58 kg of whole milk', wrong by a factor of 2.6. At the entry's own whole-milk value of 1.0 µg MK-4/100 g, 1,500 µg needs 150,000 g. Corrected: 150 kg of whole milk, not 58 kg. Even using the upper variant the entry mentions (1.3 µg/100 g) it is 115 kg. No value in the entry yields 58 kg, which would require 2.59 µg/100 g. The error understates the gap, so fixing it strengthens the entry's conclusion.

Vitamin D, 4,000 IU from UV-treated portabella: stated 'about 1 kg', loose by 12%. At 11.2 µg/100 g, 100 µg needs 892.9 g. Corrected: about 890 g. Minor, but it is the only rounding in the entry that goes in the direction of exaggerating the gap.

Beta-carotene, knock-on from the wrong sweet potato value: the entry's '360 g of boiled sweet potato' for 20 mg uses 5,560 µg/100 g. Against USDA baked sweet potato at 11,509 µg/100 g the requirement is 174 g, and the listed 130 g portion covers 75% of a 20 mg dose rather than 33%. The stated arithmetic is internally correct; the input is what fails.

Vitamin D, knock-on from the wrong egg yolk value: '46 large egg yolks' for 4,000 IU is arithmetically correct on the entry's 12.8 µg/100 g (100/2.176 = 46.0), but at USDA's 5.4 µg/100 g a yolk carries 0.92 µg and the requirement is 109 yolks. Corrected: about 109 large yolks.

Vitamin D, knock-on from the contested herring value: '155 g of grilled herring' for 1,000 IU and '7.8 kg' for 50,000 IU both recompute correctly on 16.1 µg/100 g, but at USDA's cooked Atlantic herring value of 5.40 µg/100 g they become 463 g and 23.1 kg. Either widen to a range or drop herring as a dose-gap anchor.
Beta-carotene, knock-on from the dried apricot value: '1.3% of a 20 mg dose' for 40 g is correct on 640 µg/100 g but becomes 4.3% at USDA's 2,163 µg/100 g.

Vitamin E, knock-on from the wheatgerm oil value: '201 g / about 15 tablespoons' for 268 mg is correct on 133.0 mg/100 g but becomes 179 g / about 13 tablespoons at USDA's 149.4 mg/100 g. Similarly the synthetic '10 tablespoons' becomes 8.9.

Verified as correct, for the record: all 400 IU vitamin E conversions (268 mg natural, 180 mg synthetic) and every vitamin E food requirement (720 g sunflower seeds at 4,207 kcal, 1.05 kg almonds, 550 g sunflower oil, 484 g synthetic-equivalent); the entire vitamin A series (10,000 IU = 3,000 µg, 11.9 g calf liver, 3.5 to 8.4x range, 9,733 IU pate portion, 8,160 IU cod liver oil tablespoon, every retinol-to-IU conversion); vitamin D 150 g and 600 g sockeye, 7.76 kg herring, 28% and 33% of RNI; beta-carotene 219 g and 1.31 kg raw carrot, 360 g sweet potato, 6x IOM ratio, and all twelve per-portion and percentage figures; K2 6.67 kg cheddar, 4.29 kg butter, 203.6 kg and 6.79 kg chicken, 16.8 µg/day MK-4 intake, 1/2,647 of the clinical dose, and all ng/g conversions.
verdict.net_assessment:
Process caveat first: the session's WebSearch quota was already fully consumed (200/200) before this task began, so the requested 8-plus searches were impossible. I substituted roughly 24 targeted WebFetch calls against PubMed, gov.uk and USDA FoodData Central mirrors. FDC's own site returned 404 on every food-detail route and the API rate-limited DEMO_KEY, so USDA values were read through an FDC mirror rather than the primary source, and no FDC ID could be resolved.

Strongest part of the submission by a wide margin is the literature. Every one of the ten checkable citations survived: Huang 2003 (400 IU, 184 nonsmokers, median 58% gamma-tocopherol fall), Kamao 2007 (natto 939 µg/100 g, 230 µg/d total K, MK-4 7.3%), Fu 2017 (hard cheese 282, soft 506 µg/100 g, MK-9/10/11 dominance), Sato 2012 (420 µg MK-4 undetectable), Tripkovic 2012 (D3 over D2, bolus-specific), Schurgers 2000, Roberts 2008, ATBC/CARET, and the Nutrients 2019 DOI, which resolves to a genuine Reboul review. The CARET figure is the notable case: I expected RR 1.36 to be an error against the commonly quoted 1.28, and the cited JNCI paper genuinely reports 1.36 for weighted incidence. Whoever wrote this read the papers.

Arithmetic is also strong. Of roughly 90 recomputable figures, only two are actually wrong: 30 mg beta-carotene from raw carrot is 328 g not 312 g (raw/boiled values silently swapped mid-sentence), and 1.5 mg MK-4 from whole milk is 150 kg not 58 kg, an error by a factor of 2.6 that understates the entry's own case. One rounding is loose (890 g of UV portabella, stated as 1 kg). The CoFID total-vitamin-D convention (cholecalciferol + 5 x 25-OH-D3) and the alpha-tocopherol-equivalents convention both make several figures look like addition errors when they are not, and the submission applies both correctly.

The real weakness is the food-composition layer, and it is systematic rather than random. CoFID carries most of the numeric load and not one of its 35 food codes could be confirmed. Where USDA was reachable, six foods diverged by 2x to 4x, and five of the six run in the direction that flatters the entry's narrative: egg yolk vitamin D overstated 2.4x, butter beta-carotene overstated 3.9x, butter retinol 43% high, while olive oil vitamin E is understated 2.8x, baked sweet potato beta-carotene 2.24x and dried apricots 3.4x. Raw spinach is understated 3.6x, which falsifies an explicit comparative claim ('well under a fifth of carrot' is really about two-thirds against USDA). Herring vitamin D, an anchor for two dose-gap calculations, is 3x above USDA's Atlantic herring. Two citations could not be found at all: COT TOX-2021-57 and the NDNS 2.8/3.3 µg intake figures.

Two classification calls need changing. Vitamin E at 400 IU is labelled RICH directly above a dose_gap that says it 'cannot be reached by eating', which is self-contradictory for a dose-defined item. And merging MK-7 and MK-4 under one RICH label buries the fact that MK-4 at 45 mg is synthetic-only by the entry's own admission, while MK-7's RICH status depends entirely on natto. Vitamin D3's RICH is defensible but should be qualified, since three of its twelve entries are a supplement, a fortified vehicle and a trace food.

One factual error carries real weight: barbecue chicken is not the richest MK-4 food. Goose liver paste at roughly 369 µg/100 g is about 17x higher and also defeats the claim that 'no food comes within three orders of magnitude' of the 45 mg dose (it is about 2.1 orders). The conclusion still holds at 12.2 kg/day, so the argument survives, but the supporting statement is wrong and the food is missing from the list. Alongside it, the omission of UV maitake at 56.1 µg/100 g is odd because the entry cites that number in its own caveat, and the UK-framed vitamin D and vitamin A entries both omit fortified fat spreads, which is where a large share of UK intake actually comes from.

Verdict: the reasoning, the pharmacology and the citation discipline are well above average, and the qualitative conclusions are all sound and would survive every correction above. The numbers are not yet trustworthy at the precision they are quoted to. Before publication I would require a direct read of the CoFID spreadsheet to confirm the 35 codes, replacement of the six USDA-divergent values with sourced ranges, the two arithmetic fixes, the two classification splits, correction of the richest-MK-4-food claim, and removal or replacement of the TOX-2021-57 and NDNS references. Confidence in my own USDA comparisons is moderate rather than high, since they came through a mirror; the citation verifications are high confidence.

items.availability_note: Folic acid (pteroylmonoglutamic acid) is a manufactured molecule that does not occur in natural food. It is made by chemical synthesis (Waller condensation of a triaminopyrimidinone with a three-carbon unit and p-aminobenzoyl-L-glutamic acid) and is fully oxidised with a single glutamate. Natural foods contain reduced folate polyglutamates, chiefly 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, which is a different compound with different handling. The only folic acid in the food supply is what fortification put there, so the foods listed below are fortified products carrying analytically measured folic acid (USDA reports 'folic acid' and 'folate, food' as separate components). Rich natural food-folate sources exist and are listed with numbers in the dose_gap field, but they supply food folate, not folic acid.

items.dose_gap: DFE arithmetic first: 1 ug food folate = 1 ug DFE, 1 ug folic acid in a fortified food = 1.7 ug DFE, and folic acid taken fasting = 2.0 ug DFE (the 1.7 multiplier comes from assuming 85% availability for folic acid against 50% for food folate; Suitor and Bailey, PMID 10646010). So the standard 400 ug/day periconceptional folic acid tablet is worth about 680 ug DFE with food, 800 ug DFE fasting. Matching 680 ug DFE from natural food folate, per day, every day: 376 g cooked lentils (1.9 cups; 181 ug DFE/100 g, 358 ug per 198 g cup, FDC 172421), or 219 g prepared edamame (1.4 cups; 311 ug/100 g, 482 ug per 155 g cup, FDC 168411), or 269 g braised beef liver (253 ug/100 g, 172 ug per 68 g slice, FDC 168626), or 395 g cooked chickpeas (172 ug/100 g, 282 ug per 164 g cup, FDC 173757), or roughly 351 g raw spinach, about twelve 30 g cups (194 ug/100 g, FDC 168462), or 456 g cooked asparagus, about thirty spears (149 ug/100 g, 89 ug per 4-spear 60 g portion, FDC 168390), or 630 g boiled broccoli (108 ug/100 g, 84 ug per 78 g half-cup, FDC 169967). Technically reachable, practically not sustained. The UK high-risk dose of 5 mg/day is 8,500 ug DFE, about 4.7 kg of cooked lentils a day: unreachable by any diet. And the quantitative gap is not the main problem. Cuskelly, McNulty and Scott randomised 62 women to an extra 400 ug/day as a folic acid supplement, as folic-acid-fortified food, as natural food folate, or as dietary advice: red cell folate rose only in the supplement and fortified-food arms, and did not change in the food-folate arms despite documented increases in intake (Lancet 1996;347:657-9, PMID 8596381). The two trials that established the effect used synthetic folic acid: 4 mg/day (MRC Vitamin Study, Lancet 1991;338:131-7, PMID 1677062) and 0.8 mg/day in a multivitamin (Czeizel and Dudas, N Engl J Med 1992;327:1832-5, PMID 1307234). No trial has shown that food folate prevents neural tube defects. Telling a woman planning pregnancy to eat leafy greens instead of taking the tablet is not a conservative substitution, it is an untested one.
items.form_caveat: Folic acid is not bioidentical to food folate and the difference cuts both ways. It must be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase before it can enter one-carbon metabolism, and human DHFR capacity is low: unmetabolised folic acid appears in serum above a threshold of about 266 ug of folic acid per meal (Kelly et al., Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65:1790-5, PMID 9174474), which a 400 ug tablet exceeds. That is why the adult UL is set at 1,000 ug/day of folic acid from supplements and fortified food, with no UL on food folate: high folic acid can correct the megaloblastic anaemia of B12 deficiency while the neurological damage continues, so it masks the diagnosis. The concentrated-extract concern runs the other way here. Food folate has no toxicity ceiling; the synthetic form does. Separately, L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (calcium methylfolate) supplements are marketed as the 'natural' or 'MTHFR-friendly' alternative, but no periconceptional trial has been run on them and the DFE conversion factors for them were only formally derived later (EFSA, PMC9399872); the neural-tube-defect evidence base is specifically folic acid (Czeizel, Ann Nutr Metab 2011, PMID 21865678).
items.bioavailability: Food folate is roughly 50% available against about 85% for folic acid eaten with food and close to 100% fasting; a long-term controlled feeding study in young women found food folate about 60% as effective as added folic acid in a mixed diet, supporting the 1.7 multiplier. Food folate is a polyglutamate that must be deconjugated at the brush border before absorption, and it is chemically fragile. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors, Release 6 (2007) gives folate retention of 45% for legumes boiled 45-75 min and drained (retention code 0521), 30% for legumes boiled 2-2.5 h (code 0541), 60% for greens boiled in water to cover and drained (code 3005), and 90% for potatoes baked in the skin (code 3301). A cup of dried lentils simmered for an hour loses over half its folate, and the composition table value describes the cooked food only if the cooking matches. Folic acid in a fortified food or a tablet is stable and its dose is what the label says.

items.availability_note: Rich in animal foods and effectively absent from plant foods. Cobalamin is synthesised only by bacteria and archaea; plants have no pathway for it and no requirement for it. Every reliable dietary source is an animal that accumulated bacterial B12, or a bacterially fermented or fortified product. On the four contested claims: SPIRULINA IS NOT USABLE. Watanabe et al. showed that 83% of the cobamide in spirulina tablets is pseudovitamin B12 (adeninylcobamide), which is inactive in humans, and only 17% is real B12 (J Agric Food Chem 1999;47:4736-41, PMID 10552882, DOI 10.1021/jf990541b). Microbiological assays cannot distinguish the two, which is why spirulina labels claim high B12. Pseudovitamin B12 can also compete with the real thing. NORI IS USABLE, and is the only credible plant source: dried purple laver contains five biologically active cobalamin forms, with coenzyme forms (adenosyl- and methylcobalamin) about 60% of the total, and it corrected B12 status in deficient rats (PMID 11430774). Reported contents range from 32.3 ug/100 g dry weight (Japanese Porphyra) to 133.8 ug/100 g (Korean purple laver), with 51.7 ug/100 g for seasoned toasted Korean laver (Watanabe et al., Nutrients 2014;6:1861-73, PMID 24803097). TEMPEH IS NOT RELIABLE: 0.7-8.0 ug/100 g, entirely dependent on which bacteria happened to contaminate the Rhizopus fermentation, so a given batch may contain none. MUSHROOMS ARE NOT USABLE: dried shiitake averages 5.61 ug/100 g dry weight (range 1.3-12.7), black trumpet and golden chanterelle 1.09-2.65 ug/100 g dry weight, and most other species about 0.09 ug/100 g or trace; lion's mane contains the inactive B12[c-lactone] analogue. Chlorella varies from zero to several hundred ug/100 g between products and cannot be relied on. Kimchi and fermented vegetables are below 0.1 ug/100 g.

items.dose_gap: Two different gaps, and conflating them is the usual error. Against the 2.4 ug/day RDA there is no gap at all for anyone eating animal food: a single 3 oz portion of cooked clams supplies 35 times the RDA, a slice of liver 20 times, a can of sardines 3.4 times. Against the supplement dose there is an unbridgeable gap. Oral B12 supplements are typically 500-1,000 ug, and 1,000-2,000 ug for treating deficiency. To have 1,000 ug of B12 physically present in a meal you would need 1.01 kg of cooked clams, or 1.42 kg of braised beef liver, or 11.2 kg of canned sardines, or 35.7 kg of cooked salmon, or 222 litres of whole milk. That is the wrong comparison anyway: intrinsic-factor-mediated absorption saturates at about 1.5-2.0 ug per meal (Watanabe, Exp Biol Med 2007;232:1266-74, PMID 17959839, DOI 10.3181/0703-mr-67), so everything above roughly 2 ug in any single sitting is absorbed only by passive diffusion at on the order of 1%. A 1,000 ug tablet works precisely because 1% of 1,000 ug bypasses the receptor route. No food can deliver that, and no food needs to unless the receptor route is broken. For a strict vegan the picture inverts: no food reliably supplies even the 2.4 ug RDA except dried nori, and Watanabe puts the requirement at about 4 g/day of dried purple laver, which is roughly one and a half sheets eaten every day of a product whose content varies fourfold by origin and degrades with toasting and storage. That is a thin thread to hang a neurological outcome on. Fortified foods or a tablet are the honest answer.
items.form_caveat: Supplements use cyanocobalamin, which is not a form found in food; the cyanide ligand is a manufacturing artefact of the purification step and is removed intracellularly. Food B12 is protein-bound and needs gastric acid and pepsin to release it before intrinsic factor can take it up, so proton pump inhibitors, atrophic gastritis, gastric surgery and metformin knock out food B12 while leaving free crystalline B12 in a tablet or fortified cereal largely usable. This is the one case in this set where the supplement is the correct choice on mechanism, not just convenience. The dangerous form issue is the reverse of the usual concentration worry: algae supplements are not too strong, they are inactive. A spirulina capsule labelled as a B12 source delivers mostly pseudovitamin B12, and the assay that generated the label number could not tell the difference. Note also that the USDA figure for yeast extract spread is only 0.50 ug B12/100 g (FDC ID 167717), which is 0.03 ug per 6 g teaspoon: yeast itself does not make B12, so any yeast product that is a real B12 source is fortified, and the number belongs to the fortification, not the yeast.
items.bioavailability: About 50% of dietary B12 is assumed absorbed from a normal meal, but it varies sharply by food: fish 42%, sheep meat 56-89%, chicken 61-66%, and eggs under 9% (Watanabe 2007, PMID 17959839). The last figure matters because eggs are routinely offered to vegetarians as a B12 food; on absorbed B12 a large egg delivers well under 0.05 ug, which is under 2% of the RDA rather than the 19% the content figure implies. Cooking costs real B12 too. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007) gives B12 retention of 70% for roasted beef (code 1301 group), 60% for beef braised or simmered without the drippings, 65% for roasted chicken, 60% for liver simmered without drippings, 90% for baked lean finfish, 60% for shellfish boiled in the shell against 90% steamed, and only 30% for milk held at heat for an hour. Keeping the pan juices recovers much of it, which is why the with-drippings factors run 15 points higher.

items.availability_note: Vitamin B6 itself is abundant and widely distributed: fish, organ meat, poultry, potatoes, bananas, pistachios and fortified cereals all carry useful amounts, and dietary deficiency is uncommon in people eating normally. The high-dose supplement is a different object. It is pyridoxine hydrochloride, a manufactured crystalline salt, sold at 50, 100 and sometimes 250-500 mg per tablet, which is 40 to 400 times the 1.3 mg adult RDA. Food is a rich source of the vitamin and not a source of the dose.

items.dose_gap: A 100 mg pyridoxine tablet is 77 times the RDA. Matching it by eating, in one day: 8.93 kg of pistachios, or 9.80 kg of braised beef liver, or 10.7 kg of raw yellowfin tuna, or 16.7 kg of roasted chicken breast, or 27.2 kg of banana, which is about 231 medium bananas. A 50 mg tablet still needs 4.5 kg of pistachios or 116 bananas. Even the regulatory ceiling is out of dietary reach: EFSA's 2023 tolerable upper intake level of 12 mg/day for adults corresponds to about 1.07 kg of pistachios or 3.27 kg of banana, roughly 28 bananas, every day. Ordinary diets deliver a few mg per day, an order of magnitude below the UL and two to three orders below the supplement. This is the mechanical reason for the requested point: dietary B6 has never produced the sensory neuropathy that supplements produce, because no food is concentrated enough to get near the toxic range. The syndrome was first described at 2-6 g/day of pyridoxine (Schaumburg et al., N Engl J Med 1983, PMID 6308447), cases have since been reported at far lower supplemental doses, and EFSA cut the adult UL from the SCF's 25 mg/day to 12 mg/day on peripheral neuropathy grounds (EFSA NDA Panel, EFSA J 2023;21:e8006, PMID 37207271, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2023.8006). Not one case has been attributed to food B6.
items.form_caveat: This is a genuine case where the food is safe and the concentrated form is not, and the reason is dose plus kinetics rather than any exotic compound. Food B6 arrives as pyridoxal phosphate and pyridoxamine phosphate bound in the matrix, plus glycosylated pyridoxine in plant foods, released and absorbed gradually across a meal. A tablet delivers a bolus of free pyridoxine. The accepted mechanism for the neuropathy is that free pyridoxine at high concentration outruns conversion to pyridoxal 5-phosphate and acts at PLP-dependent sites in the dorsal root ganglion, which lack a blood-nerve barrier. Pyridoxal-5-phosphate supplements are marketed as the safe alternative on the strength of that mechanism, but the human evidence is thin and EFSA applies the 12 mg/day UL to total B6 regardless of form, so treating P5P as exempt is not supported. One practical consequence: because B6 is added to energy drinks, fortified cereals and B-complex products, people accumulate supplemental doses without intending to, and the UL is easy to cross by stacking products while eating a diet that contributes almost nothing to the risk.
items.bioavailability: Roughly 75% of dietary B6 is absorbed. Plant B6 is partly pyridoxine-5'-beta-D-glucoside, which is about half as available as free pyridoxine and can act as a weak antagonist: women fed a diet high in pyridoxine glucoside showed a measurable decline in B6 status indicators (J Nutr 1996, PMID 8857512). So plant-source B6 numbers overstate the delivered amount, and the gap between a plant food and a tablet is wider than the composition table suggests. Cooking removes more. USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007) gives B6 retention of 50% for roasted beef, 35% for beef braised or simmered without the drippings, 45% for liver simmered without drippings, 80% for roasted chicken, 50% for legumes boiled 2-2.5 h, 65% for legumes boiled 45-75 min and drained, and 85% for greens boiled in water to cover. A raw-basis figure such as the 0.933 mg/100 g for raw tuna is not what lands on the plate.

items.availability_note: Genuinely rich and cheap in ordinary food. A single medium red pepper or one guava exceeds the 90 mg adult RDA on its own, and a cup of strawberries or one medium orange comes close. This is the one ingredient in this set where a normal diet not only meets the requirement but can approach supplement territory. Synthetic ascorbic acid is manufactured (Reichstein or two-step fermentation from glucose), but it is the identical molecule, so the synthetic label carries no penalty here.

items.dose_gap: Unlike the other three, the supplement dose here is physically reachable by eating, which makes the honest answer more interesting than a flat impossibility. A 1,000 mg tablet equals 781 g of raw red pepper (about 6.6 medium peppers), or 439 g of guava (8 fruits), or 552 g of blackcurrants, or 1.70 kg of strawberries, or 1.88 kg of orange (14 medium oranges), or 2.0 litres of fresh orange juice. A 500 mg dose is 3.3 red peppers or 7 oranges. Eccentric, but not fantasy. The real gap is that the dose above about 200 mg is pointless rather than unreachable. Levine et al. gave 30-2,500 mg/day under depletion-repletion control: bioavailability was complete at a 200 mg single dose, fell off at 500 mg and above with the absorbed excess appearing in urine, leucocytes saturated at 100 mg/day and plasma at 1,000 mg/day (PNAS 1996;93:3704-9, PMID 8623000, DOI 10.1073/pnas.93.8.3704). So the honest framing is that four or five servings of ordinary fruit and vegetables reach the physiologically useful plateau, and the 1,000 mg tablet mostly funds expensive urine. The one number that should temper any composition table, though, is what survives handling: see cooking and storage below.
items.form_caveat: Effectively NONE on the molecule. Synthetic and food-derived vitamin C are chemically identical and all steady-state human comparative bioavailability studies show no difference; some acute pharmacokinetic studies show minor transient differences of no physiological consequence (Carr and Vissers, Nutrients 2013;5:4284-304, PMID 24169506, DOI 10.3390/nu5114284). This kills the 'natural vitamin C is better absorbed' claim, and it also means acerola, camu-camu and rose hip products carry no absorption advantage; most such products are in any case standardised by adding synthetic ascorbic acid, so the consumer is buying the synthetic molecule with fruit powder attached. What the whole food genuinely adds is the rest of the matrix, potassium, folate, carotenoids, flavonoids and fibre, none of which is in the tablet, and none of which the vitamin C evidence is actually about. Where a caveat does bite is the classic textbook recommendation. Spinach is the folklore answer for vitamins in green vegetables, but its vitamin C is modest at 28.1 mg/100 g, a realistic 30 g cup gives 8.4 mg, and boiling extracts most of what is there: in fresh-cut spinach, boiling moved 60% of the vitamin C and 50% of the flavonoids into the cooking water (Gil et al., J Agric Food Chem 1999, PMID 10794612). Recommending boiled spinach for vitamin C is close to recommending the cooking water.
items.bioavailability: Absorption is near-complete up to about 200 mg per dose via the sodium-dependent transporter SVCT1, declines above 500 mg, and the plateau is reached at 1,000 mg/day (PMID 8623000). Absorption is therefore not the variable that matters; retention before eating is. Cooking and storage losses, all from USDA Table of Nutrient Retention Factors Release 6 (2007), ascorbic acid column: greens boiled in water to cover and drained retain 55% (code 3005), greens boiled in a little water and drained 60% (code 3004), greens stir-fried 85% (code 3008), greens cooked from frozen and drained 60%; other vegetables boiled in water to cover and drained 75%, steamed 85%; potatoes baked in the skin 80%, boiled pared and drained 75%, and only 25% when boiled after storage and browned (code 3311); canned fruit 50% and dried fruit 20%. Steaming beats boiling and draining, consistently: in broccoli every method except steaming caused significant vitamin C loss (Yuan et al., J Zhejiang Univ Sci B 2009, PMID 19650196, DOI 10.1631/jzus.b0920051). Storage compounds it, since refrigerated storage of fruit and vegetables lowers vitamin C along with anthocyanins and total phenolics (PMID 28737734). Practical upshot: a week-old boiled vegetable can deliver a quarter of its table value, so the 27% loss between raw broccoli at 89.2 mg/100 g and boiled broccoli at 64.9 mg/100 g is the optimistic case, not the worst one.

misclassifications: Not a wrong tag, but an inconsistent convention: folic acid is tagged SYNTHETIC because the marketed molecule is manufactured, while 'High-dose vitamin B6' is tagged RICH even though the marketed object is 50-500 mg pyridoxine hydrochloride, a manufactured crystalline salt with no dietary counterpart at that dose. The submission's own note concedes this ('Food is a rich source of the vitamin and not a source of the dose'). Either the tag describes the nutrient (in which case folic acid's group should be labelled by folate, which is RICH) or it describes the product as sold (in which case high-dose pyridoxine is closer to SYNTHETIC). Pyridoxine itself does occur in food, so RICH is defensible for the molecule; the inconsistency is in what the field is measuring.

Vitamin B12 tagged RICH is correct for omnivores but the tag is population-dependent in a way the single word hides. For an unfortified plant-based diet the same evidence in the note makes B12 effectively absent: the only credible source is dried nori at 2.33 ug per 3 g sheet, from a product whose content varies about elevenfold by origin and degrades with toasting and storage. A reader taking RICH at face value gets the wrong answer for exactly the population that needs the right one.

Folic acid tagged SYNTHETIC survives challenge and should stand. I looked for a genuine dietary source and there is none: USDA's own component structure separates 'folic acid' from 'folate, food', and every food in FDC with non-zero folic acid is fortified or enriched (beef liver, lentils, spinach, chickpeas, asparagus and broccoli all read folic acid 0 and folate food = folate total). The three foods listed in the item are correctly identified as fortification vehicles.

Vitamin C tagged RICH survives challenge and is the strongest classification in the set: one 119 g red pepper (152 mg) or one 55 g guava (125 mg) exceeds the 90 mg RDA, verified against FDC. No trace-amount inflation anywhere in that food list.
missing_foods: Fortified ready-to-eat breakfast cereal is missing from the folic acid item, and it is the archetypal folic acid vehicle. US brands fortified to 100% DV carry 400 ug folic acid per serving, an entire periconceptional dose in one bowl, which is a stronger illustration of 'the only folic acid in the food supply is what fortification put there' than yeast extract, oatmeal and bread combined. Enriched pasta and enriched white rice, the mandated US enrichment vehicles, are also absent. Numbers are label-dependent and should be cited per product.

Chicken liver, all classes, cooked, simmered: 578 ug food folate/100 g (FDC 171061), more than twice the braised beef liver used in the folate dose gap. This omission is load-bearing, not cosmetic: 680 ug DFE needs only 118 g of chicken liver, under three 44 g livers, which is a plausible portion and materially weakens the 'technically reachable, practically not sustained' framing. Lamb liver, pan-fried, is 400 ug DFE/100 g (FDC 172533).

Sunflower seed kernels, dried: 227 ug DFE/100 g (FDC 170562), a folate source in the same class as the legumes listed, and 1.34 mg B6/100 g, which is richer per 100 g than the dry-roasted pistachios that head the B6 list. Raw garlic is 1.24 mg B6/100 g (FDC 169230).

Mollusks, mussel, blue, cooked, moist heat: 24.0 ug B12/100 g (FDC 174217). The submission used the raw entry and a retention factor instead of the cooked entry that USDA publishes, which halves the figure for the food people actually eat. Pacific oyster, raw is 16.0 ug/100 g (FDC 174219) and lamb liver, pan-fried is 85.7 ug/100 g (FDC 172533); the class the submission skips entirely (octopus, mackerel, herring, beef kidney, crab, caviar) all sit well above the salmon and milk rows that were included.

Fortified nutritional yeast and fortified plant milks and cereals are absent from the B12 food rows even though the item's own dose_gap concludes 'fortified foods or a tablet are the honest answer'. The one practical answer for the one population with a real gap never gets a row. Contents are label-dependent, which is the reason to name the category and cite the label rather than omit it.

Acerola, raw: 1,680 mg vitamin C/100 g (FDC 171686), roughly 81 mg from a single 4.8 g fruit. It appears in the vitamin C item only as something being debunked, never as the richest verified source in the database. Raw kale at 93.4 mg/100 g (FDC 168421) is also missing, which matters because the item spends a paragraph on spinach as the folklore green (28.1 mg, and boiling takes 60% of that) without naming the green that actually delivers. Rose hips, camu-camu, chilli peppers, papaya and Brussels sprouts round out the omitted set.
dose_gap_errors: Vitamin B12: '222 litres of whole milk' to reach 1,000 ug. The division is right but the unit is not. 1,000 / 0.0045 = 222,222 g, which is 222 kg of milk, and at a density of about 1.03 kg/L that is roughly 216 litres. Corrected figure: about 216 L (222 kg).

Vitamin C: '2.0 litres of fresh orange juice' for a 1,000 mg dose. Same unit slip. 1,000 / 0.50 = 2,000 g of juice, which at about 1.04 kg/L is roughly 1.9 litres. Corrected figure: about 1.9 L (2.0 kg).

Vitamin B12, mussels row: per_portion 10.2 ug and '425% of the 2.4 ug RDA' do not follow from the row's own stated basis. Applying the declared 90% steaming retention to the raw value gives 9.18 ug (383%); using the cooked USDA entry that should have been used gives 20.4 ug per 85 g (850%). Corrected figure: 20.4 ug, 850% of the RDA.

Vitamin B12 nori: 'a product whose content varies fourfold by origin'. The 4.1-fold ratio only holds inside the submission's own truncated 32.3-133.8 range. Against the cited paper's full spread (12.3 ug/100 g New Zealand karengo to 133.8 ug/100 g Korean laver) the variation is about elevenfold. Corrected figure: roughly elevenfold.

Vitamin B12 nori: 'about 4 g/day of dried purple laver, which is roughly one and a half sheets'. At the 3 g sheet weight used in the same item's food row, 4 g is 1.33 sheets. Corrected figure: about one and a third sheets.

Everything else recomputes. I re-ran all four dose_gap blocks line by line: 400 ug x 1.7 = 680 DFE and x 2.0 = 800 fasting; 376 g lentils, 219 g edamame, 269 g beef liver, 395 g chickpeas, 351 g spinach (11.7 thirty-gram cups), 456 g asparagus (30.4 spears), 630 g broccoli, and 4.7 kg lentils for 8,500 DFE; 1.01 kg clams, 1.42 kg liver, 11.2 kg sardines, 35.7 kg salmon; 100 mg B6 = 76.9x RDA, 8.93 kg pistachios, 9.80 kg liver, 10.7 kg tuna, 16.7 kg chicken, 27.2 kg banana = 231 bananas, 50 mg = 4.46 kg or 116 bananas, 12 mg UL = 1.07 kg pistachios or 3.27 kg banana (27.7 bananas); 1,000 mg vitamin C = 781 g red pepper (6.6), 439 g guava (8.0), 552 g blackcurrant, 1.70 kg strawberries, 1.88 kg orange (14.4), and 500 mg = 3.3 peppers or 7 oranges. All correct to the stated precision.
verdict.net_assessment:
Unusually accurate submission. Of roughly 60 numeric food figures I could check against source, every per-100 g composition value and every portion gram weight matched USDA FoodData Central exactly, including details that are normally where fabrication shows up: the pistachio B6 data-point count (13) and analytical range (0.484-1.80), the separate folic acid and food folate components for the three fortified foods, the 92 g drained sardine can, the 86 g half breast, the 4-spear 60 g asparagus portion, and the split between raw (89.2 mg) and boiled (64.9 mg) broccoli. Every one of the 16 PMIDs I checked resolves to a real paper with the stated journal, year, volume and pages, and the quoted findings match the abstracts (266 ug/meal threshold, 83%/17% spirulina cobamides, eggs under 9% absorbed, IF saturation at 1.5-2.0 ug/meal, complete vitamin C bioavailability at 200 mg, 60% of spinach vitamin C into the cooking water, EFSA's 12 mg/day from a 50 mg reference point with UF 4). Roughly 30 retention factors from USDA Release 6 are all correct, verified row by row in the actual table. I found no invented sources.

Four things need fixing. The one substantive error is the mussels row: the submission used the raw entry (12.0 ug/100 g) plus a hand-applied retention factor, then failed to apply the factor anyway, when USDA publishes the cooked food at 24.0 ug/100 g. The correct row is 20.4 ug per 3 oz and 850% of the RDA, not 10.2 ug and 425%, and the general lesson is that a retention factor is the wrong tool when a cooked composition entry exists. Second, food folate in the yeast extract row is 793 ug, not 797. Third, two unit slips where grams were reported as litres (222 kg of milk is about 216 L; 2,000 g of juice is about 1.9 L). Fourth, three retention CODES are misattributed even though their values are right (stir-fried greens is 3015 not 3008, steamed in-shell shellfish is 2702 not 2770, roasted beef is 0601 not 1301) and the nori range floor is 12.3 ug/100 g in the cited paper, making the variation elevenfold rather than fourfold.

On classification: SYNTHETIC for folic acid and RICH for vitamin C both survive adversarial challenge cleanly. RICH for B12 is right for omnivores but hides a population-dependent reversal for unfortified plant diets. RICH for high-dose B6 is inconsistent with the convention that produced SYNTHETIC for folic acid, since the object being classified is a 50-500 mg manufactured salt. The most consequential omission is a substantive one rather than a decorative one: chicken liver at 578 ug food folate/100 g means 680 ug DFE takes 118 g of liver, which weakens the folate item's central rhetorical move about the food-folate route being impractical, and it should be addressed head-on rather than left out. Fortified breakfast cereal (400 ug folic acid per serving) and fortified nutritional yeast are missing from the two items whose conclusions depend on fortification being the honest answer.

items.availability_note: Iron is genuinely abundant in ordinary food, in two chemically distinct forms that behave completely differently. Haem iron (offal, red meat, shellfish, black pudding) is absorbed by a dedicated transporter and is largely indifferent to what else is on the plate. Non-haem iron (legumes, seeds, greens, fortified flour) is the majority of most people's intake and is absorbed at a fraction of the rate, heavily modified by vitamin C, polyphenols, phytate and calcium. Haem accounts for 77 percent of total iron in raw lean beef, 81 percent in lamb, 88 percent in pork and 74 percent in chicken (PMID 26433293), which is higher than the 40 percent commonly assumed in the older Monsen equation. Reference point used below: EFSA PRI 16 mg/d for premenopausal women, 11 mg/d for men (EFSA Overview on Dietary Reference Values for the EU population, v4, Sept 2017, Table 7; underlying opinion EFSA Journal 2015;13(10):4254).

items.dose_gap: Two different supplement doses need two different answers. A nutritional-dose supplement (14 to 18 mg elemental iron, the EU labelling reference level) is comfortably reachable by eating: 1 cup of boiled lentils (6.6 mg) plus 85 g of lamb's liver (7.0 mg) plus 1 oz of pumpkin seeds (2.3 mg) is 15.9 mg in one day. A therapeutic dose is not. Ferrous sulfate at the doses used in absorption and treatment trials delivers 60 to 65 mg elemental iron in a single hit (60 mg and 120 mg ferrous sulfate doses in PMID 29032957). Matching 65 mg of iron by total content requires about 785 g of lamb's liver, 3.3 kg of sirloin steak, 1.95 kg (roughly 10 cups) of boiled lentils, or 2.4 kg (about 80 cups) of raw spinach in one day. Matching it by ABSORBED iron is the honest calculation and it is worse for plants and better for meat than the raw numbers suggest. A 65 mg ferrous sulfate dose absorbed at roughly 10 percent in iron-depleted women delivers about 6.5 mg. To absorb 6.5 mg as haem iron at 25 percent absorption you need 26 mg of haem iron, which is about 1.19 kg of braised lean lamb shoulder (2.7 mg total iron per 100 g, 81 percent of it haem; FDC ID 174331 and PMID 26433293). To absorb the same 6.5 mg from non-haem food at 5 percent you need 130 mg of non-haem iron, roughly 3.9 kg of cooked lentils per day. Verdict: correcting a diagnosed deficiency cannot be done with food. Preventing one can.
items.form_caveat: Three separate traps. (1) Liver is the best iron food and the worst thing to recommend blindly, because raw beef liver carries 4,970 ug retinol activity equivalents per 100 g (FDC ID 169451). An 85 g portion of braised liver delivers several thousand micrograms of preformed retinol, which is why liver is contraindicated in pregnancy in most national guidance. The iron benefit and the vitamin A hazard travel together and cannot be separated. (2) Liver's iron is largely ferritin and haemosiderin iron, so its headline 8.28 mg is less absorbable than the haem fraction of plain muscle meat implies. Muscle meat with a smaller number can deliver more absorbed iron. (3) Supplement iron behaves unlike food iron: a 60 mg dose raises hepcidin and suppresses absorption of the next dose, which is why alternate-day dosing absorbs more per milligram given than consecutive-day dosing (PMID 29032957). Food iron arriving in small amounts across the day never triggers that. Spinach is a bad recommendation, though for a different reason than the textbook gives. Isotope work in humans found that potassium oxalate added to a low-oxalate kale meal did not change non-haem iron absorption at all (11.5% vs 10.7%), and the authors concluded that oxalic acid in fruit and vegetables is of minor relevance to iron nutrition (PMID 17440529). The spinach meal in the same study absorbed 24 percent less than the matched kale meal, attributable to its much higher polyphenol and calcium content, not oxalate. So spinach iron is genuinely poorly absorbed, the mechanism is polyphenols plus calcium plus the ferritin-bound form of the iron, and the oxalate explanation everyone repeats does not survive isotope testing. Either way, a 30 g bowl of raw spinach leaves contains 0.81 mg of iron and yields a rounding error.
items.bioavailability: Haem iron is absorbed at roughly 15 to 35 percent and non-haem at 2 to 20 percent, with iron status the dominant variable. Across whole diets rather than single meals, bioavailability is 14 to 18 percent for mixed diets and 5 to 12 percent for vegetarian diets in people with no iron stores, and the authors note that iron status generally has a greater effect than diet composition (PMID 20200263). Vitamin C enhancement: 25 to 50 mg of ascorbic acid eaten with a meal multiplies non-haem absorption several-fold in single-meal studies, with the effect strongest in high-phytate meals (PMID 3700141). The important correction is that when the same amount of ascorbic acid is given across a complete diet over days, the facilitating effect is far less pronounced (PMID 11124756). Squeezing lemon on your lentils helps; it does not turn plant iron into meat iron. Tea and coffee inhibition, with numbers: a cup of coffee cut non-haem absorption from a hamburger meal by 39 percent and tea by 64 percent; instant coffee at double strength drove absorption from 5.88 percent down to 0.53 percent; coffee taken one hour BEFORE the meal did no harm, while coffee one hour AFTER inhibited as much as coffee with the meal (PMID 6402915). Black tea inhibited non-haem absorption by 79 to 94 percent, peppermint tea by 84 percent, cocoa by 71 percent, chamomile by 47 percent, dose-dependently on total polyphenols, and adding milk made no difference (PMID 10999016). Note that this is polyphenol inhibition, not phytate: phytate is the separate inhibitor in the wholegrains and legumes themselves. Practical consequence: the single highest-yield change for someone with low iron stores is moving tea and coffee to between meals rather than with or after them.

items.availability_note: Iodine is one of the very few supplement ingredients where the supplement dose is fully and easily reachable from food, but only from a narrow set of foods: dairy, white fish, eggs, shellfish and iodised salt. Nothing else contributes meaningfully. Iodine in milk is not intrinsic to the cow, it comes from fortified cattle feed and iodophor teat disinfectants, which is why it is seasonal (higher in winter housing) and why organic milk is lower. Reference point below: EFSA AI 150 ug/d for adults, 200 ug/d in pregnancy and lactation (EFSA Overview on Dietary Reference Values for the EU population, v4, Sept 2017, Tables 5 and 7; underlying opinion EFSA Journal 2014;12(5):3660).

items.dose_gap: There is essentially no gap. A standard iodine supplement or prenatal multivitamin supplies 150 ug, exactly the EFSA adult AI. One 115 g cod fillet delivers 131 ug. About 400 ml of milk (1.6 cups) delivers 151 ug. Six large eggs deliver 148 ug. Half a teaspoon of iodised salt (3 g) delivers 152 ug. Iodine belongs in the small category of supplements a normal eater does not need. The gap opens the moment those specific foods leave the diet, and here the UK numbers are stark. Substituting three dairy portions a day (milk, yoghurt, cheese) with unfortified plant alternatives cuts the iodine those portions supply from 124 ug to 2.6 ug, a 97.9 percent loss, taking the contribution to the 150 ug recommendation from 83 percent down to 1.8 percent (PMID 35373723). That is not a shortfall, it is a near-total removal. The same market survey found only 28 percent of 146 UK milk alternatives and 6 percent of 76 yoghurt alternatives were iodine-fortified, against 88 percent and 73 percent fortified with calcium; no cheese alternative and no fish alternative was iodine-fortified at all; and organic plant alternatives cannot legally be fortified. This is measurable in real people, not just on paper: in NDNS years 7 to 9, adults and children who consumed milk alternatives exclusively had an iodine intake of 94 ug/d against 129 ug/d for cows' milk consumers, and a median urinary iodine concentration of 79 ug/l against 132 ug/l, which classifies the milk-alternative group as iodine deficient by the WHO criterion while the milk drinkers were sufficient (PMID 32993817). Unfortified milk-alternative concentrations were a median 7.3 ug/kg, 1.7 percent of winter conventional cows' milk; the three fortified products found in 2015 were much better at 266 to 287 ug/kg (PMID 28946925).
items.form_caveat: Kelp is the dangerous answer, and the danger is dosing variability rather than iodine itself. Across 12 species of commercially sold edible seaweed, iodine ranged from 16 ug/g in nori to over 8,165 ug/g in processed kelp granules from Laminaria digitata sold as a salt substitute, a 500-fold spread, and within a single species iodine varied with preharvest conditions (514 ug/g in sun-bleached blades against much higher in fresh blades) (PMID 15588380). One gram of those kelp granules is more than fifty times the adult AI. A 2021 survey of 96 commercial macroalgae products found iodine of 128 to 62,400 ug per portion in wholefood kelp products and 5 to 5,600 ug per day in supplement doses, that for more than half the products a single serving or dose would exceed the tolerable upper intake level, and that species labelling and declared iodine content were frequently inadequate or inaccurate (PMID 33889064). A kelp tablet is therefore an unlabelled dose of a potent thyroid-active substance, and excess iodine causes both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. If iodine is the goal, potassium iodide at a known 150 ug, or milk, fish and eggs, are the correct answers and kelp is not. Second caveat, milk: iodine in milk comes from feed and dairy hygiene, so it moves with farming practice. Organic milk was 42.1 percent lower in iodine than conventional in a 172-sample UK retail survey (PMID 21781365), and winter milk runs higher than summer. Someone who switches to organic milk has quietly cut their main iodine source by nearly half without changing anything visible. Third, iodised salt: the USDA entry above is a US product. The UK has no salt iodisation programme, which is precisely why the Bath group repeatedly identify milk, dairy and fish as the main UK iodine sources; a UK reader cannot assume their salt contributes anything.
items.bioavailability: Iodine bioavailability is the simple case. Iodide from milk, iodised salt and potassium iodide supplements is almost completely absorbed, and urinary iodine excretion is used directly as the intake biomarker on the standard assumption that about 90 percent of ingested iodine is excreted in urine (PMID 25274294). There is no meaningful absorption advantage to any form, and no matrix effect worth chasing: 150 ug from a fillet of cod, a pot of yoghurt or a tablet are close to interchangeable systemically. The one real form difference is at the top end rather than the bottom. Organically bound iodine in seaweed is released variably during digestion and cooking, and boiling kelp leaches a large fraction of its iodine into the water, so a seaweed dose is uncertain in both directions. Two further practical points: iodine and selenium interact, because the deiodinase enzymes that convert thyroxine to the active hormone are selenoproteins, so iodine repletion in a selenium-poor person behaves differently; and goitrogens in raw brassicas and cassava compete with iodide uptake, which matters only when iodine intake is already marginal.

items.availability_note: Zinc the nutrient is abundant in ordinary food. Zinc lozenges are not a nutritional product, and this distinction is the whole answer. The trials that show a benefit used more than 75 mg/day of elemental zinc, most commonly 80 to 92 mg/day, some 192 to 207 mg/day, delivered as slowly dissolving zinc acetate or zinc gluconate lozenges taken roughly every two hours while awake (PMID 28515951). That is eight to twelve times the EFSA PRI for an adult woman. The mechanism also depends on the delivery route: free zinc ions released in the mouth and throat over 20 to 30 minutes, in contact with the pharyngeal mucosa. Food zinc is swallowed and absorbed in the small intestine, so it cannot reproduce the intended local effect at any dose. Reference point below: EFSA PRI 7.5 mg/d for adult women and 9.4 mg/d for adult men at a phytate intake of 300 mg/d (EFSA Overview on Dietary Reference Values for the EU population, v4, Sept 2017, Tables 5 and 7; underlying opinion EFSA Journal 2014;12(10):3844).

items.dose_gap: To hit the 80 mg/day of elemental zinc used in the lozenge trials (PMID 28515951) you would need, every day for the duration of a cold: 204 g of raw oyster meat, roughly 14 to 15 medium oysters; or 102 g of cooked oysters; or 88 g of canned oysters, about 11 of them; or 989 g of braised lean beef chuck; or 1.10 kg of braised lamb shoulder; or 1.05 kg of pumpkin seed kernels; or 5.23 kg of boiled chickpeas. Only oysters make it look even arithmetically plausible, and 14 raw oysters a day for a week is a Vibrio and norovirus decision, not a nutrition one. The deeper point is that closing the arithmetic gap would still not reproduce the product. The lozenge trials work (to whatever extent they do) through free Zn2+ released in the oropharynx and held in contact with the mucosa; swallowed zinc, from food or from a capsule, bypasses that entirely. So the answer is not that food falls short of the dose. It is that food cannot deliver this dose by this route at all. Separately, the nutritional dose is trivially food-reachable: 85 g of braised beef (6.9 mg) or 6 raw oysters (33.4 mg) meets or vastly exceeds the 7.5 to 9.4 mg PRI in one portion. Zinc lozenges and zinc nutrition are two unrelated questions that share a mineral name.
items.form_caveat: Zinc gluconate lozenges shortened colds by 28 percent and zinc acetate lozenges by 40 percent, a difference that was not statistically significant, and there is no evidence that doses above 100 mg/day do better than 80 to 92 mg/day (PMID 28515951). The salt matters less than people claim; the lozenge format matters more. Zinc capsules, tablets, syrups and food are not substitutes for lozenges in this indication, because the local contact is the point. Two safety notes that follow directly from the numbers above: 80 to 92 mg/day is roughly ten times the EFSA PRI and well above nutritional upper levels, defensible only for a few days, because sustained high zinc antagonises copper absorption; and unlike a nutrient, this is a short-course pharmacological use with an actual end date. Cooking and canning concentrate oyster zinc dramatically (39.3 mg/100 g raw against 78.6 cooked and 91.0 canned, FDC IDs 171978, 171980, 171981), because water is lost rather than zinc gained, so per-100 g comparisons across preparation states are misleading unless you track the yield.
items.bioavailability: Oysters are the outlier of the entire food composition table. At 39.3 mg/100 g raw and up to 91.0 mg/100 g canned, they carry four to twelve times the zinc of red meat, which is itself the next best category, and they are the reason oysters are the answer to every zinc question. Beyond oysters, absorption efficiency does most of the work, and phytate is the variable. Human whole-body-retention studies of matched cereal meals found fractional zinc absorption of 26.8 percent from a rye bread meal containing 100 umol of phytic acid, falling to 8.4 percent from oatmeal porridge containing 600 umol, a threefold loss driven by phytate alone (PMID 2824731). A related study found that less zinc was absorbed in absolute terms from wholemeal bread than from white bread despite wholemeal containing more zinc, and that adding milk products improved zinc absorption from the wholemeal meal (PMID 7361691). Replacing 25 percent of the beef protein in a composite meal with defatted soy flour lowered both the zinc content and the zinc absorbed (PMID 6893252). EFSA has built this straight into the requirement rather than treating it as a footnote: the adult male PRI rises from 9.4 mg/d at 300 mg phytate/day to 11.7, 14.0 and 16.3 mg/d at 600, 900 and 1,200 mg phytate/day, and the female PRI from 7.5 to 12.7 mg/d across the same range (EFSA DRV Summary v4 2017, Tables 5 and 7). A high-legume, high-wholegrain diet therefore needs about 70 percent more zinc on the label to deliver the same absorbed zinc. Practical mitigations with real effect sizes: soaking, sprouting, sourdough fermentation and added phytase degrade phytate and measurably raise both zinc and iron absorption (PMID 24050000); animal protein and milk in the same meal raise it; and vegetarians consequently sit at the top of the EFSA PRI range rather than the bottom (PMID 12936958).

items.availability_note: Selenium is the one item on this list where the exact supplement dose is reachable with two nuts, and that is a problem rather than a reassurance. Brazil nuts are the richest known food source of selenium and the USDA average is 1,920 ug/100 g, about 96 ug in a single 5 g kernel, so two average nuts is 192 ug and effectively the entire 200 ug trial dose. The catch is that Brazil nut selenium is set by the soil the tree grew in and varies by more than thirty-fold between Amazon regions, so nobody eating them knows their dose. Reference points below: EFSA AI 70 ug/d for adults, and the EFSA tolerable upper intake level of 255 ug/d for adult men and women including pregnancy and lactation, set from alopecia as the critical endpoint with a LOAEL of 330 ug/d taken from the SELECT trial and an uncertainty factor of 1.3 (EFSA Journal 2023, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2023.7704; AI from EFSA DRV Summary v4 2017, Tables 5 and 7). The 200 ug/d dose itself comes from the two landmark trials: selenised yeast in the Nutritional Prevention of Cancer trial and 200 ug/d L-selenomethionine in SELECT.
