items.dose_gap: There is almost no gap, and that is the finding. 200 ug/d is met by 2.1 average Brazil nuts (10 g), or 64 g of braised pork kidney, or 185 g of cooked yellowfin tuna, or 180 g of lamb's liver, or 532 g of cooked cod, or 4 tins of sardines, or 13 eggs. Kidney and Brazil nuts overshoot in a single normal portion: one 85 g portion of pork kidney is 265 ug, already 133 percent of the supplement dose and above the EFSA upper level on its own. Because the dose is so easy to reach, the useful calculation runs the other way. The EFSA AI is 70 ug/d and the EFSA upper level is 255 ug/d, a working margin of only about 185 ug. A person on a 200 ug/d supplement plus an ordinary diet is at roughly 270 ug and already over the upper level; add two Brazil nuts and they are near 460 ug. The UL was derived from alopecia observed in SELECT at a LOAEL of 330 ug/d, so this is an observed human effect at achievable intakes, not a theoretical ceiling (DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2023.7704). Selenium is the case where food easily matches the supplement and the honest advice is to pick one route, not both.
items.form_caveat: Brazil nuts are the textbook answer and a genuinely bad way to dose selenium deliberately, because the dose is unknowable at the point of eating. Median selenium in Brazil nuts varied from 2.07 mg/kg in Mato Grosso state to 68.15 mg/kg in Amazonas, so depending on origin a single nut supplies from 11 percent to 288 percent of a 70 ug adult requirement, and the authors attribute this to soil selenium, soil pH and texture, location and genotype (PMID 28923728). Nuts from the two extremes are visually identical, are not labelled by state of origin, and are routinely blended. Advice like 'two Brazil nuts a day' is therefore a dose that ranges from about 20 ug to about 680 ug depending on a fact the eater cannot access, which spans deficient to well over the upper level. On form equivalence, selenium is unusual in a helpful way: the dominant species in Brazil nuts and cereals is selenomethionine, which is the same species used as the supplement in SELECT, so food and that supplement are pharmacologically comparable (PMID 18346307). But 200 ug of selenium is not one thing. The selenised yeast used in the earlier NPC trial was a poorly speciated mixture whose delivered selenium was variable, and the two trials produced opposite results, so the number 200 ug carries no single meaning across the literature (PMID 18346308, PMID 18346307). Finally, the whole point of supplementing collapses in a selenium-replete person: SELECT tested 200 ug/d L-selenomethionine in selenium-replete men and found no protection against prostate or other major cancers, while the alopecia signal that defines the modern UL came from that same trial.
items.bioavailability: Selenium bioavailability depends on chemical species more than on food matrix. Selenomethionine, the form in Brazil nuts, cereals and meat, is absorbed almost completely and is incorporated non-specifically into body proteins as a storage pool, which is why it raises plasma selenium readily and why its kinetics differ from inorganic selenite and selenate (PMID 18346307, PMID 28412747). This has a practical consequence the composition tables hide: the selenium content of any plant food is a proxy for the soil it grew in, not a property of the species. The USDA wholemeal bread figure of 25.7 ug/100 g reflects North American wheat grown on selenium-rich soils. European and UK wheat is grown on selenium-poor soils, so the same bread cannot be assumed to deliver the same selenium, and the wide between-country variation in intake driven by exactly this mechanism is the central theme of the food-chain intake review (PMID 18346308). Animal foods are more stable, because livestock feed is commonly selenium-supplemented, which is why kidney, liver, tuna and eggs hold their values better across countries than bread or nuts do. The ranking for a reader who wants reliable selenium without a variable dose: offal and marine fish first, eggs as a steady background contributor, Brazil nuts last on the list rather than first, precisely because they are the richest source.

number_checks.claim: Ferrous sulfate doses of 60 and 120 mg in PMID 29032957 described as '60 mg and 120 mg ferrous sulfate doses'
number_checks.authoritative_value: The trials gave 60 mg and 120 mg of IRON as labelled ferrous sulfate, not 60/120 mg of the salt (325 mg ferrous sulfate = 65 mg iron)
number_checks.correction: Say '60 mg and 120 mg elemental iron given as ferrous sulfate'. As written it reads as salt weight, which would be a sixth of the actual dose.

number_checks.authoritative_value: The review covers added Aspergillus niger phytase (12 iron studies, 5 zinc studies) and notes 'for zinc, not enough information is available to determine optimal activities'

misclassifications: Zinc lozenges classified RICH is the one real misclassification. The classification is applied to the nutrient while the item under review is a route-limited pharmacological product: 80-92 mg/d elemental zinc released as free Zn2+ over 20-30 minutes in the oropharynx, dosed every two hours. The submission's own text concedes the point ('food cannot deliver this dose by this route at all'), which is the definition of a supplement whose effect is not food-reachable. RICH plus a caveat lets a reader conclude oysters substitute for lozenges. The honest coding is two rows, or a NOT-FOOD-REACHABLE classification with a note that nutritional zinc separately is RICH (85 g braised beef = 6.9 mg against a 7.5-9.4 mg PRI).

Iodine RICH is defensible but the evidence base is jurisdictionally mismatched. Three of the four largest rows are US-analysed foods, and the single largest, iodised table salt at 5,080 ug/100 g, does not exist as a dietary source in the UK, which the item itself states in its own form_caveat ('The UK has no salt iodisation programme'). The classification should carry the qualifier that it rests on dairy, white fish and eggs for a UK reader, and the salt row should be marked as not transferable rather than left in the table at 51% of the AI.

The iron form_caveat's central claim, 'The iron benefit and the vitamin A hazard travel together and cannot be separated', is wrong and is only wrong because kidney was omitted. Braised lamb kidney is 12.4 mg iron per 100 g with 137 ug RAE (FDC 174355) and braised pork kidney is 5.29 mg iron with 78 ug RAE (FDC 167860). Both are offal, both beat the tabulated lamb liver on iron per 100 g in the case of kidney, and neither carries a retinol problem. The hazard separates cleanly by organ.

Iron RICH and Selenium at 200 ug/d RICH are both correct and well supported. Nothing in this group is classified SYNTHETIC, so there is no case of a synthetic label hiding a genuine dietary source; and no food in any of the four tables is a trace-amount source dressed up as rich - the lowest entries (raw spinach 0.81 mg iron, wholemeal bread 0.57 mg zinc) are explicitly presented as small.
missing_foods: Iron, the big one: pig's liver, braised, 17.9 mg/100 g (FDC 167863) - 2.2 times the lamb liver the item calls 'the best iron food', with lower vitamin A (5,400 ug RAE) than braised lamb liver (7,490). Also lamb kidney braised 12.4 mg (FDC 174355) and chicken liver simmered 11.6 mg (FDC 171061). All three outrank every row in the iron table.

Iron, non-haem omissions: tahini 8.95 mg and sesame seed kernels toasted 7.78 mg (FDC 170189, 170152), hemp seed hulled 7.95 mg (170148), toasted wheat-germ cereal 9.09 mg (173896), wheat germ crude 6.26 mg (168892), blue mussels cooked 6.72 mg (174217), molasses 4.72 mg (168820), and enriched white wheat flour 4.64 mg (168894) - the last one matters for a UK-framed item because UK white and brown flour carry mandatory iron fortification while wholemeal does not. Worth noting the folklore exception: clams are NOT a rich iron food in current USDA data (cooked 2.81 mg, canned 2.68 mg), so their absence is correct.

Iodine: haddock is the single most conspicuous omission for a UK-oriented item, at 390 ug per 120 g portion (about 325 ug/100 g, 260% of the AI in one fillet), with scampi 160 ug per 170 g. Both come from the same UK data that the item's own Bath-group citations rest on. Also missing: an iodine-FORTIFIED plant drink row at 266-287 ug/kg (PMID 28946925), which is the one actionable food answer for the exact group the item identifies as deficient; and kombu, oarweed and sugar kelp at 2,276-7,800 ug/g (PMID 33889064), which appear only as a hazard and never as the richest sources they are.

Zinc: toasted wheat-germ cereal 16.7 mg/100 g (FDC 173896) and wheat germ crude 12.3 mg (168892) are the richest plant zinc foods and both beat every plant row in the table; then sesame seed kernels toasted 10.2 mg (170152), hemp seed hulled 9.9 mg (170148), dried shiitake 7.66 mg (168436), and cheddar cheese 3.67 mg (328637) as the everyday dairy contributor that also improves zinc absorption from phytate meals, the mechanism the item itself cites from PMID 7361691.

Selenium: lamb kidney braised 219 ug/100 g (FDC 174355) is the standout omission - second only to pork kidney, cheap, and with negligible vitamin A. Then blue mussels cooked 89.6 ug (174217), chicken liver 82.4 ug (171061), sunflower seed kernels dry roasted 79.3-80.4 ug (170563, 325524), wheat germ 79.2 ug (168892), light tuna canned in oil 76.0 ug (173708), and clams 50.5-64.0 ug (171976, 171975). Canned tuna and sunflower seeds in particular answer the item's own closing question (reliable selenium without a variable dose) better than the fresh yellowfin steak it does list.
dose_gap_errors: Iron therapeutic gap, the substantive one: the calculation assumes 'roughly 10 percent' absorption for a 65 mg dose in iron-depleted women, but the trial it cites for that population (PMID 29032957) measured cumulative fractional absorption of 16.3% on consecutive days and 21.8% on alternate days at 60 mg/d, and 11.8% for a single 120 mg dose. Using the source's own 16.3%, absorbed iron is 10.6 mg, not 6.5 mg; the haem requirement becomes 42.4 mg, which is about 1.94 kg of braised lean lamb shoulder (not 1.19 kg), and the non-haem requirement becomes 212 mg, which is about 6.4 kg of cooked lentils (not 3.9 kg). The error runs in the direction that flatters food.

Selenium, internal contradiction: the form_caveat states 'a single nut supplies from 11 percent to 288 percent of a 70 ug adult requirement' (a correct quote from PMID 28923728) while the same item's food table gives 10.4 ug and 341 ug per kernel, which are 14.8% and 487% of 70 ug. The two cannot both stand: the paper's percentages imply a 3.0-3.7 g kernel, the table uses USDA's 5.0 g kernel. On the table's own basis the sentence should read 'about 15 percent to about 490 percent'. The later '20 ug to about 680 ug for two nuts' is consistent with the 5 g basis (20.7 and 681.5), so the 11%/288% sentence is the outlier.
Iodine, egg arithmetic: 49.1 ug/100 g x 50 g = 24.55 ug, not 24.7 ug; consequently 'Six large eggs deliver 148 ug' should be 147 ug, and the percentage is 16.4% not 16%.

Zinc, dose framing: '80 to 92 mg/day... is eight to twelve times the EFSA PRI for an adult woman' should be about 11 to 12 times (7.5 mg PRI gives 10.7x and 12.3x). Eight times corresponds to the male PRI of 9.4 mg/d, not the female one named in the sentence.

Iodine, unit slip: 'About 400 ml of milk (1.6 cups) delivers 151 ug' silently equates 400 ml with 398 g. At milk density, 400 ml is about 412 g and delivers 156 ug; 151 ug is what 1.6 USDA cups (398 g) gives. Same slip in the UK milk rows, where a '200 ml glass' is costed as 200 g (88 ug rather than 90 ug).

Zinc, incomplete list: the 80 mg/day comparison lists chickpeas at 5.23 kg but drops lentils, which are in the same table and would need 6.30 kg (80/1.27 x 100). Including the worse of the two legumes strengthens the argument being made.

Everything else recomputes correctly. All 46 per-portion conversions and all 46 percent-of-reference figures reproduce to the rounding shown; the iron 785 g / 3.3 kg / 1.95 kg (9.86 cups) / 2.4 kg (80 cups) equivalents, the 15.9 mg one-day stack, the zinc 204 g / 102 g / 88 g / 989 g / 1.10 kg / 1.05 kg / 5.23 kg equivalents, the selenium 10.4 g / 64 g / 185 g / 180 g / 532 g / 4.1 tins / 13 eggs equivalents, the 255 minus 70 = 185 ug margin, the 270 and 462 ug totals, the 97.9% dairy-substitution loss, the 1.7% milk-alternative ratio, and the 54-fold kelp-granule multiple all check out.
verdict.net_assessment: This is an unusually clean submission on the two axes fabrication normally shows up on. Every one of the 46 numeric food figures matched FoodData Central to the digit when pulled from the FDC record endpoint (I verified 30 records including all cited FDC IDs), all 25 PMIDs resolved to real papers that say what they are cited as saying, all five DOIs resolved through Crossref, and every EFSA reference value (iron 16/11, iodine 150/200, zinc 9.4-16.3 and 7.5-12.7 across the phytate range, selenium AI 70, UL 255 from a 330 ug LOAEL with UF 1.3) matched the EFSA source text verbatim. Nothing is UNVERIFIABLE. Three defects are substantive. First, the zinc bioavailability section reverses PMID 7361691: the paper found LESS absolute zinc absorbed from white bread than from wholemeal, the submission says the opposite, and the reversed version is doing argumentative work. Second, zinc lozenges are classified RICH when the submission's own reasoning establishes the dose is not food-reachable by the required route, which is a classification that contradicts its own text. Third, the iron therapeutic gap uses a 10% absorption assumption that its own cited trial contradicts (16.3-21.8%), understating the food burden by roughly 1.6x in the direction that flatters food. Below those: the claim that iron and vitamin A cannot be separated is refuted by the kidney entries the table omits (lamb kidney 12.4 mg iron, 137 ug RAE); pig's liver at 17.9 mg iron is 2.2x the food the item calls the best iron source; two portion descriptors are wrong (85 g of cooked oysters is about 12 medium, not 6; USDA's 81 g of tofu is a quarter block, not a block); the Brazil nut 11%/288% quote contradicts the item's own 15%/487% table; a non-significant 24% spinach result is presented as established with a mechanism the source does not support; the plant drinks are called unfortified when USDA shows them calcium- and vitamin-fortified; and the milk-alternative fortification percentages are quoted against the wrong denominators. Fixing the PMID 7361691 reversal, the zinc classification, and the iron absorption assumption would leave a submission I would consider sound.

items.availability_note: Magnesium sits in the chlorophyll molecule and in the outer layers of seeds and grains, so every unrefined plant food carries some. Nuts, seeds, cocoa, wholegrains, legumes and dark leafy greens are all meaningful contributors, and a mixed diet built on them reaches the adult RDA (420 mg/day men 31+, 320 mg/day women 31+, Institute of Medicine 1997) with no supplement. Refining is what strips it: wheat bran holds 389 mg/100 g while white bread holds 22 mg/100 g (CoFID 11-906 and 11-1145).

items.dose_gap: There is effectively no gap. Supplements are sold at 200 to 400 mg elemental magnesium, which is the whole daily requirement, and food covers that range easily. A worked day: 1 oz pumpkin seeds (156 mg) plus 1 cup cooked black beans (120 mg) plus 1 oz 70-85% dark chocolate (65 mg) is 341 mg before anything else on the plate is counted. Single-food routes are absurd by comparison: 400 mg from dark chocolate alone means 175 g of bar, roughly 1,000 kcal, and 400 mg from wholemeal bread alone means 533 g, about 17 slices. The safety asymmetry matters more than the arithmetic. The Institute of Medicine set the 350 mg/day upper limit for supplemental magnesium only, and it explicitly excludes magnesium naturally present in food and water; the EU Scientific Committee on Food set a comparable 250 mg/day limit for magnesium added through supplements or fortified foods. So 700 mg of magnesium from seeds and beans carries no upper limit, while 400 mg from tablets is already over the supplemental ceiling.
items.form_caveat: The difference is dose kinetics rather than chemistry. Food delivers magnesium in small amounts across a day inside a matrix that slows release, so the unabsorbed fraction stays small and osmotic diarrhoea does not happen. A 400 mg bolus of a soluble magnesium salt leaves a large unabsorbed load in the gut lumen, and that load is the mechanism of the laxative effect that set the upper limit in the first place. Magnesium citrate and magnesium hydroxide are marketed as laxatives at doses close to supplement doses. In anyone with reduced renal clearance (CKD stage 4-5, elderly patients on multiple drugs) supplements can cause symptomatic hypermagnesaemia, while food magnesium is handled by renal excretion across the normal intake range. There is no situation where the food form is the risky one.
items.bioavailability: Net absorption of dietary magnesium from a mixed diet is about 50%, falling to 15-36% at higher intakes (Institute of Medicine DRI report, NCBI Bookshelf NBK109816). Phytate is the main food inhibitor and can cut fractional absorption by up to 60% in a dose-dependent way, so the magnesium in bran, seeds and legumes is not fully realised. Oxalate does the same, which is why cooked spinach at 157 mg per cup delivers materially less than the number implies, and why spinach is the classic textbook answer that should not be the recommendation. Supplement forms differ sharply among themselves: Firoz and Graber (Magnesium Research 2001;14(4):257-262) measured fractional absorption of about 4% for magnesium oxide against 9-11% for the lactate, aspartate and chloride forms, and magnesium oxide is the cheapest and most widely sold form. A 400 mg magnesium oxide tablet can therefore deliver less absorbed magnesium than a handful of pumpkin seeds while producing the loose stools.

items.supplement: Calcium supplements on top of an adequate diet
items.availability_note: Calcium is among the easiest nutrients to get from ordinary food. Dairy, calcium-set tofu, tinned fish eaten with the bones, fortified plant milks and fortified juice each deliver 200 to 860 mg per normal portion, and low-oxalate brassicas add 150 to 270 mg per cooked cup with better fractional absorption than milk. The adult reference intake of 1,000 mg/day (1,200 mg for women 51+, Institute of Medicine 2011) is reachable in three or four food choices. This entry concerns adding a supplement to a diet that already meets that target, which is a different question from correcting a real deficit.

items.dose_gap: There is no gap to close, which is the whole point of this entry. Calcium supplements are sold at 500 to 600 mg elemental per tablet, and the trials that generated the safety signals gave 1,000 to 1,200 mg/day on top of whatever participants were already eating. Matching 1,000 mg from food takes: 3.6 cups of milk, or 141 g of Cheddar, or one 1/2-cup serving of calcium-set tofu (861 mg) plus one cup of cooked kale (177 mg), or three pots of yogurt, or two small cans of sardines plus a glass of fortified soy drink. Every one of those is a normal day of eating. So in a person whose diet already provides 1,000 mg, a 1,000 mg supplement does not fill a deficit, it doubles the intake and delivers the added half as a single soluble bolus. The correct framing is that the supplement is additive rather than corrective.
items.form_caveat: The harms recorded in the trials attach to supplements, not to dietary calcium, and the proposed mechanism is the form itself. Food calcium arrives in small amounts inside a matrix across a whole meal and produces no sharp rise in serum calcium; a 500-1,000 mg dose of calcium carbonate or citrate produces a measurable postprandial spike, and that spike is the hypothesised driver of the vascular signal. The specific findings: in the Women's Health Initiative randomised trial, 36,282 postmenopausal women given 1,000 mg calcium carbonate plus 400 IU vitamin D3 daily for a mean 7 years had more clinically diagnosed urinary tract stones, hazard ratio 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.34), unrelated to baseline calcium intake (PMID 21525191). Bolland and colleagues' meta-analysis of calcium supplements without co-administered vitamin D reported a 27-31% relative increase in myocardial infarction (BMJ 2010, DOI 10.1136/bmj.c3691). In the 10-year MESA follow-up of 5,448 adults, supplement users had higher incident coronary artery calcification while the highest quintile of dietary calcium was associated with lower risk (Anderson et al., DOI 10.1161/JAHA.116.003815). Observational work in the same populations consistently finds higher dietary calcium associated with fewer kidney stones, the opposite direction to the supplement result. This is contested territory: a 2016 National Osteoporosis Foundation and American Society for Preventive Cardiology review concluded there was no demonstrable cardiovascular harm at total intakes up to 2,000-2,500 mg/day, and the meta-analyses have been criticised for relying on secondary endpoints and self-reported events. The defensible summary is that food calcium has no such signal attached to it in any dataset, so where the diet already reaches the target the supplement carries risk without a corresponding benefit. Two practical form points: calcium carbonate requires gastric acid and must be taken with food, so it is a poor choice for anyone on a proton pump inhibitor or with achlorhydria (calcium citrate does not have this dependency), and doses above about 500 mg saturate absorption, so a single 1,000 mg tablet is worse value than two 500 mg doses.
items.bioavailability: Fractional absorption is where the food ranking is decided, and it inverts the raw milligram ranking. From the tabulated absorption studies (Nutrients 2022 review, PMC8746734; Heaney et al., J Food Sci 1993;58:1378-1380): bok choy 51.9-52.0%, kale 40.9% at a 288 mg load and 52.7% at 83 mg, broccoli 47.8%, calcium-set tofu 39.0-49.3%, cow milk 21.7-54.8% depending on load (about 30-32% at a typical 250 mg load), Cheddar 37.4%, yogurt 24.2%, calcium carbonate supplement roughly 22-24%, calcium citrate roughly 24%, and spinach 5.1%. Two consequences. First, low-oxalate brassicas beat both milk and supplements per milligram consumed, so a cup of bok choy at 158 mg delivers about the same absorbed calcium as 250 ml of milk. Second, spinach, rhubarb, beet greens and Swiss chard should be struck off calcium lists entirely; the oxalate precipitates the calcium in the gut and the food is close to useless for this purpose despite good label numbers. Fortified plant milks carry a specific practical failure: the added calcium salt is insoluble and sediments to the bottom of the carton, and the fortificant itself absorbs less well than dairy calcium (soy drink fortified with calcium carbonate 21.1%, with tricalcium phosphate 18.1%). An unshaken carton delivers a fraction of the label value, and the last glass delivers a dose nobody intended.

items.availability_note: This is a product category rather than a molecule, and almost every nutrient inside it is abundant in ordinary food. A varied diet plus targeted correction of the two or three things a given person actually lacks covers the same ground, which is why the US Preventive Services Task Force concluded in 2022 that evidence is insufficient to recommend multivitamins for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer, and recommended against beta-carotene and vitamin E supplements outright. One qualification on the RICH label: the molecules in the tablet are manufactured, and two of them (folic acid and cyanocobalamin) do not occur in food in those forms at all, so the nutrients are food-abundant while the pill is entirely synthetic. The nutrients people genuinely fall short on are a short list. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines for Americans name calcium, potassium, vitamin D and dietary fibre as nutrients of public health concern, with iron and folate added in pregnancy. UK NDNS data adds magnesium (9% of men and 13% of women below the LRNI), selenium (25.8% of males and 50.3% of females below the LRNI) and iron in younger women (about a quarter below the LRNI), with mean vitamin D intakes below the RNI in every age and sex group. The food answers below are given for that handful rather than for all 25 tablet ingredients.

items.dose_gap: There is no food equivalent of a multivitamin, because a multivitamin is not a nutrient. One tablet supplies roughly 100% of the reference intake for 20 or more nutrients simultaneously, and the only thing matching that profile is a varied diet, which by definition already supplies them. So the useful arithmetic is per nutrient, for the short list where shortfalls are real. Vitamin D is the one with a genuinely unbridgeable food gap at temperate latitudes in winter: 15 ug/day (US RDA) needs about 90 g of cooked sockeye salmon every day, or 1.15 litres of fortified milk, or 14 large eggs. The UK 10 ug/day RNI needs about 60 g of oily fish daily or 770 ml of fortified milk. UV-treated mushrooms are the only food that reaches it in one normal portion (24.4 ug per cup). This is where a supplement is defensible, and it argues for vitamin D on its own rather than a 25-ingredient tablet. Periconceptional folic acid is the second real case: 400 ug/day is food-achievable in bulk (about 220 g of cooked lentils daily) but the trial evidence that prevents neural tube defects is for supplemental folic acid, and food folate is both less bioavailable and more variable, so food substitution is not supported. B12 on a vegan diet is the third: there is no reliable unfortified plant source, so a supplement or fortified food is mandatory. For the rest of the tablet (vitamin C, vitamin A, thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, B6, vitamin E, vitamin K, zinc, selenium, copper) the food gap for anyone eating a normal mixed diet is zero. Two further mismatches: the potassium in a multivitamin is capped at about 99 mg against a 3,500 mg reference intake, so it cannot address the potassium shortfall the guidelines name, and the calcium is typically 100-200 mg, a fifth of a calcium supplement, so it does not function as one either. Fibre, the fourth named shortfall, is absent from every tablet.
items.form_caveat: This category contains the clearest documented case of a whole food being safe while the isolated concentrate is harmful. Carotenoid-rich vegetables are consistently associated with lower lung cancer risk, while beta-carotene as a supplement increased lung cancer incidence in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers in the ATBC and CARET trials, and the USPSTF now recommends against it with moderate certainty that harms exceed benefits. Vitamin E supplements carry the same recommendation against. Preformed vitamin A as retinol in a tablet counts toward the 3,000 ug/day upper limit and is teratogenic at high intake, while beta-carotene in carrots does not convert quickly enough to reach toxicity. Folic acid in a tablet can partially mask the haematological signs of B12 deficiency while neurological damage continues, an effect food folate has not been shown to produce. Stacking is the underappreciated risk: a multivitamin alongside fortified breakfast cereal and a fortified plant drink can push folic acid, retinol, niacin and iron past their upper limits in someone who believes they are taking one tablet. Within the tablet itself, iron competes with zinc and copper for shared transporters and calcium interferes with iron uptake, so a combined product delivers less of each than the label states. And no tablet carries the fibre, the food-level potassium, or the polyphenols that account for much of the association between diet quality and outcomes, which is the structural reason a pill is not a diet.
items.bioavailability: Form differences run in both directions, so blanket claims fail here. Iron: haem iron from meat and fish absorbs at roughly 15-35% and is largely insensitive to the rest of the meal, while non-haem iron from plants and from the ferrous salts in tablets ranges from about 2% to 20% depending on phytate, polyphenols, calcium and vitamin C eaten at the same time. Spinach iron sits at the bottom of that range because oxalate binds it, so the textbook answer is the wrong answer. Folate: folic acid from a supplement taken with food is roughly 85% bioavailable against about 50% for naturally occurring food folate, so here the synthetic form genuinely outperforms the food. Vitamin B12: food B12 is protein-bound and needs gastric acid and pepsin to release it, so older adults with atrophic gastritis and long-term proton pump inhibitor or metformin users often absorb crystalline B12 from a tablet better than B12 from a chop. Vitamin D: the D2 in UV-treated mushrooms raises and sustains serum 25(OH)D less efficiently than the D3 in oily fish and most supplements, so the 24.4 ug per cup is not fully equivalent to 24.4 ug from salmon. Vitamin K: the K1 in leafy greens is poorly released from the plant matrix and cleared fast, while the long-chain MK-7 in natto reaches higher and far longer-lasting serum concentrations, so a portion of natto and a portion of kale are not interchangeable despite sharing the label term. All four fat-soluble vitamins need fat in the same meal, which is why a multivitamin swallowed with black coffee delivers less than the panel claims.

misclassifications: Bok choy, calcium entry: labelled as having the 'highest measured fractional absorption of any calcium food at 51.9-52.0%', citing Heaney et al. J Food Sci 1993. That paper measured broccoli 47.8%, bok choy stems 51.9%, bok choy leaves 52.0% and kale 52.7% at an identical 83 mg load, and states the differences were 'absolutely small and statistically insignificant'. Kale ranked highest, and the submission's own bioavailability list contains the contradicting 52.7% figure two lines later. The superlative is unsupported by its own source.

Spinach as a magnesium source, magnesium entry: classified as a nominal-only contributor ('oxalate binds a large share of this', 'the classic textbook answer that should not be the recommendation'). The primary study behind the oxalate claim (Bohn et al., Br J Nutr 2004;91:601-606, spinach 26.7% vs kale 36.5% fractional Mg absorption) concludes the opposite: 'the lower fractional apparent Mg absorption from the test meal served with spinach can be assumed to be, at least partly, counterbalanced by the higher native Mg content of spinach as compared with kale.' Absorbed magnesium works out at roughly 42 mg per cooked cup of spinach (157 x 0.267) against roughly 11 mg for a cooked cup of kale (29.5 x 0.365). The 5.1%-absorption logic that correctly disqualifies spinach for calcium does not transfer to magnesium, where a 27% relative penalty leaves spinach one of the better absorbed-magnesium portions on the list.

Fortified plant milks, calcium entry: 'the fortificant itself absorbs less well than dairy calcium' is contradicted by the cited data. Zhao et al. (J Nutr 2005, PMID 16177199) found calcium-carbonate-fortified soymilk equivalent to cow's milk (21.1% vs 21.7% at a 250 mg load) and titled the paper accordingly; the Nutrients 2022 review the submission cites says the same. Only the tricalcium phosphate form (18.1%) is genuinely lower. The sedimentation point about unshaken cartons is separate and stands.

Vitamin D within the multivitamin entry: presented as a 'genuinely unbridgeable food gap' with UV mushrooms 'the only food that reaches it in one normal portion'. Three ordinary portions clear the 15 ug RDA on USDA data (canned sockeye 3 oz = 17.9 ug; farmed rainbow trout 3 oz = 16.2 ug; a USDA half-fillet of the entry's own sockeye = 25.9 ug), and cod liver oil delivers ~11 ug per teaspoon. The entry's own dose-gap line concedes 90 g of salmon per day, which is a normal portion, so the internal logic already contradicts 'unbridgeable'. The defensible claim is behavioural (few people eat oily fish daily at temperate latitudes in winter), not compositional.

Nigari tofu row, calcium entry: the food is described as 'set with nigari (magnesium chloride) rather than calcium sulfate', but USDA describes FDC 172448 as 'Tofu, firm, prepared with calcium sulfate AND magnesium chloride (nigari)'. The row is doing the work of showing that the coagulant determines the calcium content, and a dual-coagulant product is the wrong exhibit for that argument even though the 201 mg figure is correct.

Multivitamin entry classified RICH: defensible as a statement about the nutrients, and the entry is transparent that it is a product category rather than a molecule. But the classification sits alongside an in-entry claim that one constituent has an unbridgeable food gap. Once that claim is corrected (see above), RICH holds; as written the entry argues against its own label.

Overstated synthetic-form claim: 'folic acid and cyanocobalamin do not occur in food in those forms at all'. Folic acid is fair. Cyanocobalamin is reported in trace amounts in foods, and more directly, both forms are present in fortified foods, which the same entry treats as a legitimate B12 route ('a supplement or fortified food is mandatory'). Soften to 'are not the predominant natural food forms'.

No item on any of the three lists is a trace-amount food dressed up as a rich source. All 42 composition figures describe genuinely rich sources, and the two deliberate anti-recommendations (spinach for calcium and iron, kelp for iodine) are correctly framed as warnings rather than sources.
missing_foods: Magnesium: sunflower seed kernels, dried, 325 mg/100 g (FDC 170562) and 390 mg/100 g in CoFID 14-845 (about 92-111 mg per oz) - a commonly eaten seed that would rank third on the list.
Magnesium: flaxseed/linseed, 392 mg/100 g (FDC 169414), higher than every nut listed and also 255 mg calcium.
Magnesium: wheat germ, crude, 239 mg/100 g (FDC 168892); and wheat bran itself, quoted at 389 mg/100 g in the availability note but never given a row (USDA crude wheat bran is 611 mg/100 g).

Magnesium: mineral and hard tap water. The entry's own upper-limit sentence excludes 'magnesium naturally present in food and water', yet no water source appears; some European mineral waters supply over 100 mg/L, which is a material share of a 420 mg target.
Magnesium: pine nuts 270 mg/100 g (CoFID 14-839) and melon seeds 510 mg/100 g (CoFID 14-826).

Calcium: hard cheeses, which beat the Cheddar row substantially. Parmesan 1,184 mg/100 g (FDC 170848), CoFID Parmesan 1,025 (12-526), Emmental 1,025 (12-493), Gruyere 950 (12-164). A 30 g piece of Parmesan is about 355 mg, more than the 1 oz Cheddar slice at 199 mg.

Calcium: UK bread. Because non-wholemeal flour is fortified with calcium carbonate by law, CoFID white bread average is 155 mg/100 g (11-1145) and wholemeal 106 mg/100 g (11-981), i.e. about 50 mg per 32 g slice. Bread is one of the largest contributors to UK calcium intake and is absent from a list that otherwise uses CoFID throughout.

Calcium: whitebait, in flour, fried, 860 mg/100 g (CoFID 16-231) - the whole-small-fish archetype, richer than either canned fish listed; also canned jack mackerel with bones, 241 mg/100 g (FDC 175121).

Calcium: fortified dried skimmed milk 1,280 mg/100 g (CoFID 12-521) and fortified instant hot oat cereal 1,336 mg/100 g (CoFID 11-792). Broccoli is discussed in the bioavailability paragraph at 47.8% absorption but never given a row, and almonds (269 mg/100 g) appear only under magnesium.

Vitamin D: cod liver oil, 250 ug/100 g (FDC 173577), about 11 ug per teaspoon - the most concentrated entry in the entire USDA vitamin D table and the historical answer to winter deficiency. Also canned sockeye salmon 21.0 ug/100 g (FDC 173693), farmed rainbow trout 19.0 ug/100 g (FDC 173718), salted mackerel 25.2 ug/100 g (FDC 168149), and fortified fat spread 17.5 ug/100 g (FDC 171415), the main UK non-fish vehicle. UV-exposed crimini mushrooms (31.9 ug, FDC 168557) outrank the portabella chosen.

Iodine: iodised salt, the global public-health iodine vehicle, is absent entirely from an entry that names only milk, cod, and kelp-as-hazard. Haddock is also omitted despite being much richer than the cod used - 421 ug/100 g grilled (CoFID 16-376) against 161 ug for baked cod - along with crab brown meat 333 ug (16-391), and the eggs and shellfish that the NHS lists among the four main sources.

Folate: the entry gives only lentils and liver. Fortified breakfast cereals, chickpeas, asparagus and edamame are omitted, and spinach's own 146 ug/100 g folate goes unmentioned while the spinach row is used solely as an iron warning.
dose_gap_errors: Calcium, 'three pots of yogurt' as a route to 1,000 mg: 3 x 311 mg = 933 mg, which is 93% of the target, not a match. Corrected figure: 3.2 pots, i.e. about 546 g of low-fat yogurt.

Multivitamin, iodine denominators throughout the entry: percentages are computed against '150 ug RNI', but the UK RNI is 140 ug/day (NHS). Corrected figures: milk 1 cup 76 ug = 54% (stated 50%); cod fillet 290 ug = 207% (stated 193%); kombu 1 g 4,407 ug = 3,148% (stated 2,938%) and a 31.5-fold overshoot of the reference intake.

Multivitamin, vitamin D: 'UV-treated mushrooms are the only food that reaches it in one normal portion' is arithmetically false. Corrected figures: 3 oz canned sockeye salmon = 17.9 ug (119% of the 15 ug RDA), 3 oz farmed rainbow trout = 16.2 ug (108%), one USDA half-fillet (155 g) of the entry's own cooked sockeye = 25.9 ug (173%), 1 tsp cod liver oil = 11.3 ug (75%).

Calcium, bioavailability paragraph: the milk range used in the food-versus-supplement comparison is given as 21.7-54.8% where the cited table reads 21.7-66.0%. This is the number that decides the paragraph's central claim, since the corrected upper bound exceeds every brassica figure quoted.

Everything else reconciles. All 46 per-portion multiplications reproduce to within rounding, all 46 percentage-of-reference figures reproduce to within 1 percentage point, and the remaining dose-gap arithmetic is exact: magnesium 156+120+65 = 341 mg; 400 mg from dark chocolate = 175.4 g and 1,049 kcal ('roughly 1,000'); 400 mg from wholemeal bread = 533 g and 16.7 slices ('about 17'); 1,000 mg calcium = 3.62 cups of milk, 140.8 g of Cheddar, tofu 861 + kale 177 = 1,038 mg, two sardine cans plus soy drink = 1,001 mg; 15 ug vitamin D = 89.8 g sockeye, 1,154 ml fortified milk, 13.6 eggs; 10 ug = 59.9 g oily fish, 769 ml milk; 400 ug folate = 221 g cooked lentils; six Brazil nuts = 543 ug selenium against the 400 ug upper limit.
verdict.net_assessment: Unusually strong on data, weaker on inference. I verified all 41 cited FDC IDs against the SR Legacy April 2018 dataset directly (food.csv, food_nutrient.csv, food_portion.csv) and all 24 cited CoFID codes against the CoFID 2021 dataset: every food description matches, every per-100 g nutrient value matches exactly, and every portion weight matches USDA's own portion table rather than being invented (including awkward ones like the 27 g third-cup of oats, the 92 g sardine can, the 68 g liver slice, the '1 oz = 23 whole kernels' almond portion, and the 110-276 ug iodine span across CoFID's ten cod entries, which reproduces precisely). Not one fabricated identifier and not one wrong composition figure. Arithmetic is equally clean: 46 of 46 per-portion multiplications and all percentage figures reproduce. Citations are real and accurately characterised where I could check them: PMID 21525191 (WHI, 36,282 women, HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02-1.34, baseline calcium intake unrelated), BMJ 2010 c3691 (MI 1.31 patient-level, 1.27 trial-level, supporting '27-31%'), JAHA 116.003815 (MESA, 5,448 adults), PMC8746734 (Nutrients 2022;14(1):180), Firoz and Graber (PMID 11794633, magnesium oxide 4%), NBK109816 (DRI 1997 Ch. 6, '15 to 36 percent' verbatim), and the 2022 USPSTF statement. The failures are almost all one type: a cited source says something different from, or narrower than, the claim built on it. Three cases are substantive. The bok choy superlative is refuted by the very experiment cited, where kale absorbed highest and the authors declined to rank the vegetables. The soy fortificant claim inverts a study whose title states equivalence with cow's milk. And the spinach-magnesium write-down inverts Bohn 2004, which concluded the oxalate penalty is partly offset by spinach's higher magnesium content, so absorbed magnesium from a cup of spinach (about 42 mg) beats a cup of kale (about 11 mg) roughly fourfold. Alongside these: the vitamin D 'only food' claim is false against USDA's own table, the iodine percentages use a US reference value labelled as a UK RNI, one yogurt dose-gap route lands 7% short, and the NDNS shortfall statistics are given to one decimal place with no survey year, age band, or table, which makes them uncheckable. Recommended disposition: accept the composition tables and the arithmetic essentially as they stand; require correction of the four inference errors and the iodine denominator; require a citation for the NDNS figures; and add the omitted sources, most importantly hard cheeses and UK fortified bread for calcium, sunflower seeds and flaxseed for magnesium, cod liver oil and oily-fish canned forms for vitamin D, and iodised salt and haddock for iodine.

items.availability_note: Oily fish supply EPA and DHA in gram quantities per ordinary portion, so this is one of the few supplement categories where food genuinely competes with capsules at physiological doses. One 130 g portion of salmon or one herring fillet delivers 2.4-2.9 g EPA+DHA, about ten times a single day's EFSA Adequate Intake of 250 mg (EFSA DRVs summary 2017; EFSA Journal 2010;8(3):1461, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1461). One caution on the composition data: the USDA farmed-salmon entry reflects older analyses. In 3,000 Scottish farmed salmon, EPA+DHA fell from 2.74 g/100 g in 2006 to 1.36 g/100 g in 2015 as feed shifted from fish oil to vegetable oil (Sprague 2016, DOI 10.1038/srep21892), so treat the farmed-salmon figures below as an upper bound and roughly halve them for current farmed fish.

items.dose_gap: Two separate gaps. (1) The physiological dose (EFSA AI 250 mg/day EPA+DHA, evidence range 250-500 mg/day) is easily met by food: one 143 g herring fillet per week averages 410 mg/day, one 130 g farmed salmon portion 399 mg/day, one wild salmon portion 342 mg/day. Two mackerel fillets, two 92 g tins of sardines or two 45 g tins of anchovies per week give 258-302 mg/day. Trout needs about 3 fillets/week (266 mg/day) and tinned light tuna needs 7-14 tins/week, which makes it unusable for this purpose. In portion terms: 250-500 mg/day = 0.6-1.3 salmon portions, 0.6-1.2 herring fillets, 1.7-3.3 mackerel fillets, 1.9-3.9 tins of sardines, 1.9-3.8 tins of anchovies, or 2.8-5.6 trout fillets per week. (2) The pharmacological dose of 4 g/day used in trials and in FDA-approved prescription products (AHA Science Advisory, Circulation 2019, DOI 10.1161/CIR.0000000000000709; REDUCE-IT used 4 g icosapent ethyl) cannot be eaten. It requires 199 g/day of herring (1.4 kg/week), 186 g/day of farmed salmon on 2006-era composition or 294 g/day on 2015 composition (1.3-2.1 kg/week), 333 g/day of mackerel (3.8 fillets a day), 407 g/day of sardines (4.4 tins a day), 195 g/day of anchovies (4.3 tins a day, with the sodium load that implies), or 464 g/day of tinned albacore, which would supply about 160 ug of methylmercury a day against FDA/EPA advice of one albacore serving a week for sensitive groups. Above roughly 1 g/day of EPA+DHA, supplements are the only realistic route.
items.form_caveat: Whole fish and fish oil are not interchangeable in the evidence base. VITAL randomised 25,871 adults to 1 g/day of marine n-3 and found no reduction in major cardiovascular events (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.80-1.06) or cancer (Manson 2019, PMID 30415637), while the benefit at 4 g/day in REDUCE-IT came from purified prescription EPA, not a food-equivalent mixture. High-dose omega-3 also carries an atrial fibrillation signal that eating fish does not. Contaminant tradeoff for large predatory fish: mean mercury is 1.45 ppm for Gulf of Mexico tilefish, 1.00 ppm for swordfish, 0.98 ppm for shark and 0.73 ppm for king mackerel, all above the FDA/EPA 0.46 ug/g 'avoid' cutoff, versus 0.01 ppm for sardine, 0.02 ppm for salmon and anchovy, 0.05 ppm for Atlantic mackerel, 0.07 ppm for trout, 0.08 ppm for herring and 0.13 ppm for canned light tuna, all inside the 0.15 ug/g 'Best Choices' band (EPA-FDA fish advice technical information; independent synthesis in Karimi 2012, PMID 22732656, gives grand means of 0.882 ppm for shark, 0.883 ppm for tilefish and 0.450 ppm for tuna). The tradeoff is unfavourable in a specific way: the high-mercury predators are also mediocre omega-3 sources (cooked swordfish supplies 108 mg EPA per 85 g, USDA SR Legacy abridged EPA table), so choosing small oily fish improves both sides at once. Dioxins are the opposite case, concentrating in the fat of oily fish. EFSA cut the tolerable weekly intake to 2 pg TEQ/kg body weight and reported it exceeded 5 to 15 fold across all European age groups, with fatty fish among the top contributors (EFSA Journal 2018;16(11):5333, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5333). Refined fish oils must meet 1.75 pg WHO-TEQ/g fat for dioxins and 6.0 pg/g fat for dioxins plus dioxin-like PCBs (Regulation (EU) 2023/915), so a purified concentrate can carry a lower contaminant load per gram of EPA+DHA than the fish it came from. One processing detail: draining oil-packed tuna pours away omega-3. Canned white tuna in oil retains only about 66 mg EPA/100 g after draining versus 233 mg/100 g for the water-packed product (USDA SR Legacy abridged EPA table).
items.bioavailability: Chemical form changes absorption measurably. Using natural triglyceride fish oil as the 100% reference at matched doses of 3.1-3.6 g/day, the bioavailability index was 124% for re-esterified triglyceride, 91% for free fatty acid and 73% for ethyl ester (Dyerberg 2010, PMID 20638827). Most cheap concentrates are ethyl esters, which also depend more on a fat-containing meal for absorption, so a 1,000 mg ethyl-ester capsule taken on an empty stomach does not deliver what the label implies. Fish is delivered as natural triglyceride inside a fat and protein matrix and needs no such allowance. Cooking method matters less than preparation: canning in oil and then draining removes omega-3, whereas canning in water and draining does not (see form caveat).

items.availability_note: The molecules krill oil delivers, EPA and DHA, are abundant in ordinary oily fish, and a 1-2 g/day krill oil dose is smaller than what a single tin of sardines provides. Krill itself is close to a non-food: Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) is eaten as okiami in Japan and to a small extent in Russia and the Philippines, but the global catch is largely rendered into meal and oil, and the shell carries fluoride at roughly 4,260 mg F/kg fat-free dry matter in the carapace versus 570 mg/kg in raw muscle, so the exoskeleton has to be stripped before human consumption (Can J Fish Aquat Sci 1979, DOI 10.1139/f79-204; Tou 2007, PMID 17345959). Nobody reaches a krill oil dose by eating krill; they reach it by eating fish or by taking capsules. What is genuinely unavailable from food is the delivery form, EPA and DHA esterified to phospholipids rather than triglycerides, at 39.29-80.69% phospholipid in krill oil (Xie 2019, DOI 10.1111/1541-4337.12427), plus the astaxanthin that gives it its colour.

items.dose_gap: There is effectively no gap, which is the useful finding. Measured EPA plus DHA in 20 commercial krill oils spanned 14.2-34.8% w/w of total fatty acids (Lee 2024, PMID 39233519, DOI 10.4014/jmb.2406.06026), so a 1 g capsule carries at most roughly 140-350 mg EPA+DHA and usually less once the phospholipid head groups are accounted for. Two capsules (2 g) therefore deliver about 280-700 mg, which is matched or beaten by one 92 g tin of sardines (903 mg), one 45 g tin of anchovies (924 mg) or one mackerel fillet (1,059 mg). Even at the top of the trial range, 4 g/day of krill oil supplies roughly 570-1,400 mg EPA+DHA, equal to 0.6-1.5 tins of sardines. Going the other way, matching a krill oil dose by eating krill is not a real option: the catch is not sold as food outside a small Japanese and Russian market, and the shell must be removed for fluoride reasons.
items.form_caveat: Two things separate krill oil from both fish and fish oil. First, the phospholipid form, which is the actual product claim and cannot be obtained from fish, since fish store EPA and DHA mainly as triglycerides. Second, astaxanthin, which no oily fish portion supplies in comparable concentration. Neither has been shown to produce a clinical outcome that fish or fish oil does not. Against that, krill oil is the most expensive way to buy EPA and DHA per milligram, capsule doses are small enough that many products deliver less omega-3 than one tin of fish, it is a crustacean allergen, and whole krill or poorly processed krill meal carries the fluoride load of the exoskeleton. Sustainability is a genuine consideration given that Antarctic krill is the base of the Southern Ocean food web.
items.bioavailability: The phospholipid form does appear to be absorbed at least as well as triglyceride and better than ethyl ester. In a crossover trial in 12 healthy men at a matched 1,680 mg EPA+DHA dose, incorporation into plasma phospholipids by area under the curve was 80.03% for krill oil, 59.78% for re-esterified triglyceride fish oil and 47.53% for ethyl ester fish oil, though with wide variance and no statistically significant difference for DHA or EPA+DHA combined (Schuchardt 2011, Lipids Health Dis, PMC3168413). The practical implication is modest: a krill capsule may deliver its contents somewhat more efficiently, but it contains so much less EPA and DHA than a portion of fish that absorption efficiency does not close the gap.

items.availability_note: Cod liver oil is itself a traditional food-grade oil with a USDA composition entry, and everything it supplies is available from ordinary foods: EPA and DHA from oily fish, vitamin D from oily fish, vitamin A from any liver. What makes it distinctive is the concentration. One teaspoon (4.5 g) carries 806 mg EPA+DHA, 1,350 ug RAE of preformed vitamin A (4,500 IU) and 11.2 ug of vitamin D (450 IU). Cod liver is also eaten as a food in Nordic, Baltic and Russian cuisine (tinned cod liver), though a per-portion composition value from an authoritative table was not obtainable here, so no figure is given rather than an estimate.

items.dose_gap: At physiological doses there is no gap and cod liver oil is efficient: 250-500 mg/day of EPA+DHA needs only 1.4-2.8 g of oil, about a third to two thirds of a teaspoon, carrying 419-838 ug RAE of vitamin A, comfortably inside the 3,000 ug/day UL. The gap opens at pharmacological doses, and it is a toxicity gap rather than a volume one. Reaching 4 g/day of EPA+DHA takes 22.3 g of cod liver oil, about 1.6 tablespoons, which delivers 6,704 ug RAE of preformed vitamin A, 2.2 times the EFSA adult UL, every day. Traditional cod liver oil therefore cannot be dose-escalated to the level used in triglyceride-lowering trials. That is what plain fish oil and purified concentrates exist for.
items.form_caveat: This is the clearest case in this group where the concentrated product is hazardous in a way the food behaviour does not suggest. The vitamin A is preformed retinol, so it accumulates and is teratogenic. Anyone already taking a multivitamin, or pregnant, can exceed the 3,000 ug RAE/day UL on one tablespoon alone (4,080 ug). Doubling up cod liver oil with a separate vitamin D supplement is the other common stacking error. Note also that many modern products labelled cod liver oil are refined and have the vitamin A and D partly stripped and re-standardised, so the USDA generic entry above describes traditional oil and not necessarily what is in a given bottle: the label governs. Contaminants concentrate in liver, which is why the EU sets separate limits for fish liver and derived products (20.0 pg WHO-TEQ/g wet weight) alongside the 1.75 pg/g fat dioxin and 6.0 pg/g fat dioxin plus dioxin-like PCB limits for marine oils (Regulation (EU) 2023/915). Commercial cod liver oil is refined to meet those limits; home-rendered or artisanal liver oil is not.
items.bioavailability: Cod liver oil is a natural triglyceride and was one of the natural-triglyceride comparators assigned the 100% reference index in the Dyerberg bioavailability comparison, against 124% for re-esterified triglyceride and 73% for ethyl ester at matched doses (PMID 20638827). Its fat-soluble vitamins come dissolved in the oil, which is the ideal vehicle, and that is precisely why the vitamin A is so efficiently absorbed and why overdose is easy. There is no absorption advantage over eating oily fish for the EPA and DHA.

items.availability_note: ALA is one of the easiest nutrients in this entire reference to obtain from food. EFSA sets the Adequate Intake at 0.5% of energy, about 1.1-1.4 g/day for a 2,000-2,500 kcal diet (EFSA DRVs summary 2017; DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1461). A single tablespoon of ground flaxseed exceeds it. The real question is not whether you can eat ALA but whether ALA becomes EPA and DHA in the body, and the answer is largely no for DHA.

items.dose_gap: For ALA itself, zero gap: one tablespoon of ground flaxseed (1.60 g), one ounce of walnuts (2.57 g) or one tablespoon of walnut oil (1.41 g) each exceed the 1.1-1.4 g/day AI, and one tablespoon of flaxseed oil supplies 7.26 g. The gap appears when ALA is sold as a substitute for EPA and DHA. Tracer studies bracket the conversion: in young women given 700 mg of labelled ALA, net fractional conversion was 21% to EPA, 6% to DPA and 9% to DHA (Burdge and Wootton 2002, PMID 12323090, DOI 10.1079/BJN2002689), while in young men roughly 33% of the dose was oxidised within 24 hours, EPA and DPA were the only meaningful products, and there was no detectable labelled DHA in plasma at any point over 21 days (Burdge, Jones and Wootton 2002, PMID 12323085, DOI 10.1079/bjn2002662). Whole-body estimates are lower still, commonly 0.1-0.5% for DHA. Working the arithmetic for a 250 mg/day target: at the optimistic 8-9% figure you need 2.8-3.1 g ALA/day, which is 1.2-1.3 tablespoons of whole flaxseed, so replacing EPA is plausible. At the 0.5% figure for DHA you need 50 g ALA/day, which is 219 g of flaxseed or roughly 100 mL of flaxseed oil daily, and at 0.1% you need 250 g ALA/day, over a kilogram of seed. No one eats that. State it plainly: flaxseed, chia and walnut oil can substitute for EPA at modest intakes and cannot supply DHA at any realistic intake. Feeding trials agree, with plasma DHA unchanged after a month of flaxseed in any form (Austria 2008, PMID 18689552).
items.form_caveat: Form determines whether the ALA is absorbed at all, which is unusual among plant supplements. Over one month at matched ALA doses, flaxseed oil and milled flaxseed both raised plasma ALA significantly (oil higher than milled, P=0.004), while whole flaxseed produced no significant rise, and no group raised EPA or DHA (Austria 2008, PMID 18689552, DOI 10.1080/07315724.2008.10719693). Sprinkling whole seeds on food is close to decorative. Practical consequences: grind flaxseed, store it cold and use it quickly, because ALA at 53% of an oil is highly oxidisable and rancid flax oil is a pro-oxidant load rather than a benefit; flaxseed oil supplies ALA with none of the fibre or lignans of the seed; and conversion to EPA is suppressed by high dietary linoleic acid, so an ALA supplement taken alongside a diet heavy in sunflower or corn oil performs worse than the tracer figures suggest. Milled seed was also the best-tolerated form, with the oil and whole seed both causing gastrointestinal discomfort in that trial.
items.bioavailability: Two sequential losses. First, absorption and delivery: oil beats milled seed beats whole seed, with whole seed showing no measurable plasma ALA response (Austria 2008). Second, metabolic conversion, where the same enzyme chain (delta-6 desaturase, elongase, delta-5 desaturase, then peroxisomal beta-oxidation for DHA) is shared with linoleic acid and is the real bottleneck: EPA yields of 8-21%, DPA 6-8%, and DHA anywhere from 9% down to undetectable, with women converting better than men, which is thought to reflect the demands of pregnancy and lactation. A third of an oral ALA dose is simply burned for energy within 24 hours.

items.availability_note: Classified TRACE because of who this supplement is for. Marine microalgae are the original producers of EPA and DHA in the ocean food web, and fish carry these fatty acids because they eat, directly or through zooplankton, the same organisms algal oil is grown from. Algal oil simply skips the fish. For an omnivore the compounds are RICH in food (see the Omega-3 entry: one herring fillet supplies 2,873 mg). For the vegan or vegetarian this product actually serves, no plant or fungal food supplies a meaningful amount. Raw laver (nori) has 80 mg EPA per 100 g and zero DHA, which is 2 mg of EPA per standard sheet. Dried spirulina, routinely marketed as an omega-3 food, contains 0.000 g of both EPA and DHA. The production organism itself is not a food: Schizochytrium sp. is a single-cell marine microalga cultured in fermenters and authorised in the EU as a novel food, with DHA at 40.5-46.3% of total fatty acids and EPA at only 0.5-0.6% in the strain assessed (EFSA Journal 2020;18(10):6242, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6242).

items.dose_gap: For a vegan diet the gap is effectively infinite for DHA and absurd for EPA. Typical algal oil products and the EU authorised supplement conditions sit at 250 mg/day of DHA for the general adult population and 450 mg/day for pregnancy and lactation (EFSA Journal 2020;18(10):6242). Matching 250 mg of EPA from nori would take 312 g of raw laver, about 120 sheets a day. Matching any amount of DHA from nori is impossible, since the USDA value is 0.000 g, and spirulina supplies zero of both. There is no seaweed portion, no fermented food and no oilseed that closes this gap, which is why algal oil is one of the few supplements in this reference with a real and unavoidable role rather than an expensive alternative to a food. For an omnivore the same dose is one 45 g tin of anchovies (580 mg DHA, FDC 174183) or half a tin of sardines.
items.form_caveat: The strain determines what you actually get. A DHA-dominant Schizochytrium oil at 40.5-46.3% DHA and 0.5-0.6% EPA is not an EPA supplement, so a product labelled vegan omega-3 may supply almost no EPA even though the label implies both, and buyers wanting EPA need a strain or blend selected for it. On the positive side, this is one case where the concentrated product is cleaner than the food: because the algae are grown in closed fermenters rather than harvested from the sea, algal oil avoids the methylmercury of predatory fish and the dioxin and PCB burden that makes fatty fish the leading dietary contributor to European dioxin exposure (EFSA Journal 2018;16(11):5333). The usual oxidation caveat applies, since a highly unsaturated oil in a clear bottle or an old capsule degrades, and the fishy aftertaste of an oxidised product is the tell. Do not substitute algae biomass powders (spirulina, chlorella) for algal oil, since they are different organisms with no DHA.
items.bioavailability: Algal oil DHA is nutritionally equivalent to DHA from fish. A randomised trial comparing algal-oil capsules with cooked salmon found the two to be equivalent sources of DHA in terms of blood incorporation (Arterburn 2008, PMID 18589030, DOI 10.1016/j.jada.2008.04.020). Absorption follows the same rules as other marine oils, so the triglyceride forms behave like natural fish oil and take-with-a-meal advice applies. Some DHA retroconverts to EPA in the body, which partly offsets the very low EPA content of DHA-dominant algal oils, though not reliably enough to treat a DHA-only product as an EPA source.

misclassifications: Krill oil RICH: the verdict survives but two of the three factual claims holding it up are false, and one of them is false in the direction that would have strengthened the entry. 'The phospholipid form, which is the actual product claim and cannot be obtained from fish, since fish store EPA and DHA mainly as triglycerides' is wrong. Fish roe is exactly that food: USDA FDC 175132 'Fish, roe, mixed species, raw' gives EPA 983 mg + DHA 1,360 mg = 2,343 mg/100 g, and FDC 174188 'Fish, caviar, black and red, granular' gives EPA 2,740 + DHA 3,800 = 6,540 mg/100 g. Roe and caviar are membrane-lipid tissues in which a large share of the EPA and DHA is phospholipid-bound, and in lean white fish such as cod the majority of the (small) EPA+DHA pool sits in phospholipid rather than triglyceride. The triglyceride generalisation holds for fatty fish flesh only. A single tablespoon of caviar (16 g, 1,046 mg EPA+DHA) beats a 2 g krill oil dose on both quantity and form.

Krill oil RICH, second false unavailability claim: 'astaxanthin, which no oily fish portion supplies in comparable concentration'. Wild sockeye and other red-fleshed Pacific salmon carry astaxanthin in flesh at roughly 25-40 mg/kg, so a 130 g portion supplies about 3-5 mg, which meets or exceeds the astaxanthin in a typical 1-2 g krill oil dose (commonly 0.1-1.5 mg per gram of oil). I could not re-verify the sockeye concentration in this session, so treat this as a challenge to be checked rather than a settled correction, but the flat 'no oily fish portion' should not stand as written. Note the entry's own bioavailability section already concedes neither the phospholipid form nor astaxanthin has produced a clinical outcome fish or fish oil does not.

Algal oil TRACE: correct for vegans, overstated for the vegetarians the entry names in the same sentence. 'For the vegan or vegetarian this product actually serves, no plant or fungal food supplies a meaningful amount' is literally true only because eggs are neither plant nor fungal. USDA FDC 171287 'Egg, whole, raw, fresh' gives DHA 58 mg/100 g, so one large 50 g egg supplies 29 mg preformed DHA and two supply 58 mg, which is 23% of the 250 mg/day target; DHA-enriched eggs run several times higher. For a lacto-ovo vegetarian the honest classification is closer to LOW or PARTIAL than TRACE, and the foods list should carry an egg row. TRACE remains right for strict vegans, which the entry should say explicitly rather than eliding vegan and vegetarian.

Cod liver oil RICH: partly circular as constructed. The first and largest 'food' in the list is cod liver oil itself, so only two of the three entries (herring, sardines) are actually alternatives to the supplement. The classification is defensible because cod liver oil genuinely is a traditional food-grade oil with its own USDA record, but the entry should either drop the self-referential row or label it as the reference product. The entry also names 'vitamin A from any liver' and tinned cod liver in its note, then lists neither as a food.
Omega-3 (EPA and DHA) RICH and ALA RICH: both correct and well supported. No change. No item in this group is classified SYNTHETIC, so there is nothing to reclassify upward on that axis.
missing_foods: Caviar, black and red, granular (USDA FDC 174188): EPA 2,740 mg + DHA 3,800 mg = 6,540 mg/100 g, the richest EPA+DHA food in SR Legacy, and 1 tablespoon (16 g) = 1,046 mg, more than one 92 g tin of sardines. Absent from all three EPA/DHA entries. Its omission is most costly in the krill oil entry, where it is the direct counterexample to the phospholipid claim.

Fish roe, mixed species, raw (USDA FDC 175132): EPA 983 mg + DHA 1,360 mg = 2,343 mg/100 g, above cooked Atlantic herring, with a USDA tablespoon measure of 14 g. Cod roe, herring roe and salmon roe are ordinary foods in exactly the Nordic, Baltic and Japanese cuisines the submission already invokes for cod liver and krill.

Herring, Atlantic, pickled (USDA FDC 175118): EPA 843 mg + DHA 546 mg = 1,389 mg/100 g. The entry gives only cooked fresh herring, but pickled and kippered herring is the form in which most herring is actually eaten in the UK and Northern Europe, and it sits between mackerel and salmon on omega-3 content.

Rapeseed (canola) oil: the single largest omission in the ALA entry, because in UK and Northern European diets it is the dominant dietary ALA source by a wide margin, ahead of flaxseed, chia and walnuts combined. USDA SR Legacy lists it at roughly 9 g ALA/100 g, i.e. about 1.2 g per tablespoon, which alone meets the 1.1 g/day AI. I could not re-verify the exact figure in this session (the FDC ID probes returned sunflower, safflower, corn, almond and avocado oil), so confirm the value before publishing. An ALA entry that lists only supplement-shaped foods and omits the cooking oil people already use misrepresents how easy the AI is to hit.

Perilla oil: the highest-ALA edible oil in common culinary use at roughly 54-64% ALA, above flaxseed oil, and a staple in Korean and Japanese cooking. Absent entirely, which leaves the entry's implicit claim that flaxseed oil is the ALA ceiling unchallenged.
Seeds, hemp seed, hulled (USDA FDC 170148): ALA 8.68 g/100 g, verified. Comparable to walnuts per 100 g and a better ALA-per-calorie buy than walnut oil, which the entry does include at 10.4 g/100 g.

Egg, whole (USDA FDC 171287): DHA 58 mg/100 g, 29 mg per large 50 g egg, verified. The only meaningful preformed-DHA food available to lacto-ovo vegetarians and the missing row in the algal oil entry. DHA-enriched eggs, sold specifically for this purpose, carry several times more.

Also absent from the EPA/DHA entries, in rough order of how much they would change the picture: sablefish/black cod and Pacific or jack mackerel (both above Atlantic mackerel); canned pink and red salmon, which is what most people actually buy and which the entry ignores in favour of fresh fillets (FDC 175138 raw pink salmon is EPA 182 + DHA 333 = 515 mg/100 g, so canned is a genuinely weaker choice worth saying so); oysters and mussels; and the fish body oils (menhaden, herring, salmon oil at roughly 10-20 g EPA+DHA/100 g), which would put cod liver oil's 17.9 g/100 g in context and show that the vitamin A problem is specific to liver oil rather than intrinsic to concentrated fish oil.

Coho salmon, wild, raw (USDA FDC 175136, EPA 429 + DHA 656 = 1,085 mg/100 g) is worth a mention only as a caution: the entry's Atlantic-salmon-only treatment implies all salmon are 1.8-2.1 g/100 g fish, and Pacific species are roughly half that.
dose_gap_errors: Tinned light tuna, '100% of one day's 250 mg AI' and 'needs 7-14 tins/week': both rest on a 112 g drained tin that is not in the USDA record cited. FDC 173709's own portion is 1 can = 165 g. Corrected: 224 mg/100 g x 1.65 = 370 mg per tin, which is 148% of the 250 mg AI (not 100%) and 9% of a 4 g dose (not 6%), and the weekly requirement becomes 5 tins/week at 250 mg/day and 9 tins/week at 500 mg/day, not 7-14. The qualitative conclusion (light tuna is a poor route) survives but is weaker than stated.

Canned albacore, '386% of one day's AI; 24% of a 4 g/day dose': same 112 g problem. On USDA's 1 can = 172 g the tin gives 1,483 mg EPA+DHA = 593% of the AI and 37% of a 4 g dose. On USDA's 3 oz = 85 g it gives 733 mg = 293% and 18%. The 112 g figure sits between the two USDA measures with no stated basis.

ALA entry, 'at the optimistic 8-9% figure you need 2.8-3.1 g ALA/day ... so replacing EPA is plausible': the 8-9% band is the DHA (9%) and DPA (6%) conversion from Burdge & Wootton 2002, not the EPA figure, which the same paper puts at 21%. Sizing an EPA target with a DHA conversion rate inflates the requirement roughly 2.5-fold. Corrected on the paper's own EPA figure: 250 mg EPA/day needs 1.19 g ALA/day, which is about half a tablespoon of whole flaxseed or three quarters of a tablespoon ground. The stated division (250/0.09 = 2.78 g; 250/0.08 = 3.13 g) is arithmetically correct, so this is a wrong-input error rather than a wrong-sum error.

Same sentence, 'which is 1.2-1.3 tablespoons of whole flaxseed': internally contradicted by the entry's own form_caveat and bioavailability sections, which state on Austria 2008 that whole flaxseed produced no significant rise in plasma ALA and that 'sprinkling whole seeds on food is close to decorative'. The requirement should be expressed in milled seed at 1.60 g ALA/tbsp: 2.8-3.1 g ALA = 1.8-2.0 tablespoons ground, or on the corrected 21% EPA conversion, 0.7 tablespoons ground.

Krill oil, sardine row '129-320% of the EPA+DHA in a typical 2 g/day krill oil dose (280-700 mg)': the upper bound should be 323%, since 903/280 = 322.5%. The other three rows recompute exactly on the same 280-700 mg basis (anchovy 132-330%, mackerel 151-378%, herring 410-1,026%), so this is an isolated slip, not a systematic one.

Krill oil, '14.2-34.8% w/w of total fatty acids ... so a 1 g capsule carries at most roughly 140-350 mg EPA+DHA': this converts a percentage of total fatty acids into a percentage of capsule mass, which is not the same quantity, since total fatty acids are less than capsule mass once phospholipid head groups, free sterols, astaxanthin and excipients are counted. The entry hedges correctly ('usually less'), but then carries 280-700 mg, 570-1,400 mg and '0.6-1.5 tins of sardines' forward as point estimates. Every one of those is an upper bound, so the real gap runs further in favour of fish than the entry claims. Label them as ceilings.

Omega-3 availability_note, 'One 130 g portion of salmon or one herring fillet delivers 2.4-2.9 g EPA+DHA, about ten times a single day's ... 250 mg': the range excludes the very fish the same paragraph then tells you to assume. On the entry's own Sprague correction, a 130 g portion of current farmed salmon delivers 1.36 x 1.3 = 1.77 g, i.e. 7.1 times the AI, below the stated range. Sprague's own text gives 1.8 g for exactly this portion. State the range as 1.8-2.9 g and 'roughly seven to twelve times', or the headline contradicts the caveat two sentences later.

Everything else recomputes exactly. Verified as correct: all nine per-portion conversions and all nine percent-of-AI figures in the omega-3 foods table (herring 1,149%, farmed salmon 1,116%, wild salmon 957%, anchovy tin 370%, mackerel 424%, sardine 361%, trout 248%); the weekly averaging arithmetic (herring 410, farmed salmon 399, wild salmon 342, mackerel/sardine/anchovy pairs 258-302, trout 266 mg/day); the portions-per-week ranges (0.6-1.3 salmon, 0.6-1.2 herring, 1.7-3.3 mackerel, 1.9-3.9 sardine tins, 1.9-3.8 anchovy tins, 2.8-5.6 trout fillets); every 4 g/day figure (herring 199 g/day and 1.4 kg/week, farmed salmon 186 and 294 g/day and 1.3-2.1 kg/week, mackerel 333 g and 3.8 fillets, sardines 407 g and 4.4 tins, anchovies 195 g and 4.3 tins, albacore 464 g, methylmercury 162 ug); the entire cod liver oil block (1 tsp 806 mg / 1,350 ug RAE / 11.2 ug D; 1 tbsp 2,434 mg / 4,080 ug RAE / 34 ug D; 322% of AI, 45% and 136% of the vitamin A UL, 11% of the vitamin D UL; 1.4-2.8 g of oil for 250-500 mg carrying 419-838 ug RAE; 22.3 g for 4 g/day carrying 6,704 ug RAE = 2.2x UL; herring 3.6 tsp and sardines 1.1 tsp equivalence); every ALA per-portion and percent-of-AI figure; the ALA 0.5%-of-energy to 1.1-1.4 g/day conversion; the DHA-conversion extremes (50 g ALA/day at 0.5% = 219 g flaxseed or about 100 mL oil; 250 g ALA/day at 0.1% = over 1 kg of seed); and the nori figures (2 mg EPA/sheet, 0.8% of a 250 mg dose, 312 g or about 120 sheets to reach 250 mg).
verdict.net_assessment:
Unusually strong on composition data and weak in a few specific, fixable places. Every one of the 19 USDA records I could pull matched the submission: 18 cited FDC IDs resolved to exactly the described food with the stated EPA, DHA and ALA values, plus the uncited tuna-in-oil comparison (FDC 175157, EPA 66 mg/100 g) which also checked out. All nine PMIDs and all six DOIs resolved to the papers claimed, and the load-bearing numbers inside Sprague 2016 (2.74 to 1.36 g/100 g, over 3,000 fish, EFSA's 130 g portion), Karimi 2012 (0.882 / 0.883 / 0.450 ppm), Schuchardt 2011 (12 men, 1,680 mg, 80.03 / 59.78 / 47.53, all non-significant) and VITAL (25,871, HR 0.92, 0.80-1.06) were confirmed verbatim. Roughly 60 dose-gap calculations recompute correctly. That is a better hit rate than these submissions usually manage.

Five defects need fixing. One is a hard miscitation: EFSA Journal 2020;18(10):6242 is an infant-formula opinion for strain WZU477 at 20-50 mg DHA/100 kcal and contains neither the 250 mg/day nor the 450 mg/day supplement condition attributed to it (those belong to the Union list, Regulation (EU) 2017/2470); the same opinion also undercuts the entry's EPA generalisation by recording 1.3-6% EPA in other authorised strains. Two are invented portion weights: both tuna rows use a 112 g drained tin that is not in the USDA records cited, and because the light-tuna headline ('100% of one day's AI', '7-14 tins/week') is built on it, the corrected figures are 148% and 5-9 tins. One is a conversion-rate mismatch: the ALA entry sizes an EPA target with the 8-9% DHA conversion rate instead of Burdge & Wootton's 21% EPA rate, then expresses the answer in whole flaxseed, the one form its own bioavailability section says does not work. One is a pair of false unavailability claims in the krill oil entry: phospholipid-bound EPA and DHA are obtainable from food (fish roe 2,343 mg/100 g, caviar 6,540 mg/100 g), and wild red-fleshed salmon does supply astaxanthin at doses comparable to a krill capsule.

The FDA mercury block is the largest unverifiable region: four FDA and EPA URLs returned 404, so the eleven per-species means and the 0.15/0.46 ug/g band cutoffs are unconfirmed, and the Gulf of Mexico tilefish figure of 1.45 ppm should be re-checked against FDA's usually cited 1.123 ppm. The EPA page did confirm the qualitative placement of anchovies, Atlantic mackerel, sardines and trout in Best Choices. Also unverified: the two krill fluoride values (whose 1979 journal name is wrong), the Xie 2019 phospholipid range, the Regulation (EU) 2023/915 dioxin limits, the EFSA vitamin A and D ULs, and the uncited swordfish EPA figure.

The biggest content gap is caviar and fish roe. They are the richest EPA+DHA foods in the database, they are ordinary foods in the cuisines the submission already cites, and they are the direct refutation of the krill oil entry's central claim, so omitting them costs the submission twice. After that: rapeseed oil and perilla oil in the ALA entry, pickled herring in the omega-3 entry, and eggs in the algal oil entry. Availability calls are all defensible as verdicts; the krill oil and algal oil justifications need rewriting even though their labels stand.

items.availability_note: Creatine is genuinely present in ordinary food, but only in skeletal muscle of animals. Harris et al. measured about 30 mmol/kg (roughly 393 mg/100 g) in uncooked chicken, beef and rabbit muscle, and essentially none in plant foods. The catch is dose: normal portions deliver a few hundred milligrams, while trials use 3-5 g/day. Organ meat is the classic wrong answer, ox liver held only 2.3 mmol/kg (about 30 mg/100 g) despite the liver being where creatine is synthesised.

Harris RC, Lowe JA, Warnes K, Orme CE, Res Vet Sci 1997;62(1):58-62. PMID 9160426; DOI 10.1016/s0034-5288(97)90181-8

foods.food: Ox liver, uncooked (the textbook answer that fails)

items.dose_gap: BEEF EQUIVALENT: at 393 mg/100 g raw (Harris 1997), 3 g/day of creatine requires 763 g of raw lean beef and 5 g/day requires 1,272 g, i.e. 1.3 kg of raw steak every day, about six 200 g steaks. Using Balsom's slightly higher 4.5 g/kg figure for beef the numbers are 667 g and 1,111 g. That 1.3 kg of beef also carries roughly 280 g of protein and its full fat and calorie load, so the creatine dose cannot be separated from a diet nobody would eat. Raw herring is the single best food (650-1,000 mg per 100 g fillet), and even then 5 g/day needs 500-770 g of herring daily. Cooking makes the real plate-equivalent worse: creatine falls and creatinine rises about four-fold after 90 min at 70 C, and losses grow with final internal temperature, so the raw-basis figures above are the optimistic case. VEGETARIAN BASELINE: muscle total creatine was significantly lower in vegetarians than non-vegetarians at baseline (117 vs 130 mmol/kg dry mass), and vegetarians gained more from supplementation, so the group with the biggest gap is exactly the group with no food route at all (Burke DG et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2003;35(11):1946-55, PMID 14600563, DOI 10.1249/01.mss.0000093614.17517.79). Verdict: the supplement dose is not achievable by eating normally.
items.form_caveat: NONE in chemical terms. Supplemental creatine monohydrate is the same molecule found in muscle; it is manufactured by reacting sarcosine salts with cyanamide rather than extracted from meat, so there is no plant-versus-extract issue and no concentrated phytochemical to worry about. The meaningful caveats run the other way. First, cooking converts food creatine into creatinine, which is metabolically inert, so the label value of a raw cut overstates what reaches the plate (Purchas RW et al., Meat Sci 2004;66(3):629-37, PMID 22060873, DOI 10.1016/S0309-1740(03)00181-5; Purchas RW, Busboom JR, Meat Sci 2004;68(2):201-7, PMID 22062229, DOI 10.1016/j.meatsci.2004.02.018). Second, only muscle stores creatine: liver, kidney and other offal are poor sources despite being the synthetic organs, and dried or rendered meat products have largely degraded to creatinine (Harris 1997). Third, plant foods contain none, so 'eat more real food' is not advice a vegetarian can act on.
items.bioavailability: Creatine monohydrate is close to completely absorbed and dietary creatine from meat is also efficiently absorbed, so absorption is not the limiting step; dose size is. The responsive variable is baseline muscle store: vegetarians started at 117 mmol/kg dry mass versus 130 in non-vegetarians and showed larger increases in total creatine, phosphocreatine, lean tissue and work performance after supplementation (PMID 14600563). Habitual omnivore intake is roughly 1-2 g/day against a whole-body turnover of about 2 g/day in a 70 kg male, with the balance made endogenously (PMID 7817065), which is why a supplement of 3-5 g/day is a two- to five-fold multiple of anything a diet delivers. Cooking losses are the one real bioavailability penalty for the food form: creatine and taurine are the two compounds most reduced by cooking beef, partly by conversion to creatinine and partly by loss into cooking juices (PMID 22062229).

items.availability_note: This is the one item on the list where ordinary food comfortably beats the supplement. A 1.6 g/kg target is 112 g/day for a 70 kg adult, and single household portions of everyday foods deliver 8-53 g each. Protein powder is itself a food fraction (whey and casein are dairy by-products), so there is no molecule here that food lacks.
