items.dose_gap: ZERO. There is no dose gap for a 1.6 g/kg target. A worked day for a 70 kg adult needing 112 g: 2 boiled eggs (14.1 g) plus a 170 g pot of Greek style yogurt (9.7 g) plus a 130 g grilled chicken breast (41.6 g) plus 200 g cooked red lentils (16.2 g) plus 250 mL semi-skimmed milk (9.0 g) plus 30 g Cheddar (7.6 g) totals 98.2 g; add one 100 g can of tuna in brine and it reaches 123 g, over target, with no powder. Even a 100 kg athlete at 1.6 g/kg (160 g) gets there by adding a 170 g steak (52.7 g). The gap only appears at very high targets combined with a poor appetite, a low-calorie diet, or exclusively plant sources, where the volume of food becomes the binding constraint rather than the protein content. Powder solves convenience and calorie density, not availability.
items.form_caveat: NONE in the sense that matters: whey and casein isolates are dairy fractions, soya and pea isolates are legume fractions, and the amino acids arriving in the blood are the same ones food delivers. Two real form differences remain. Isolates strip the matrix, so you get the amino acids without the calcium, fat, B12 and satiety that come with dairy or meat, which makes it easy to add protein and easier still to add unnoticed calories in flavoured, maltodextrin-containing products. And a powder is dosed by scoop rather than eaten as a meal, so it is the only protein source people routinely take on top of an already adequate intake. Plant isolates also need blending or a higher dose to match dairy on lysine and methionine, which is a formulation issue food solves by variety.
items.bioavailability: Absorption differences between food and powder are about speed and amino acid pattern, not quantity absorbed. Animal-source protein is more digestible and more leucine-dense per gram than most plant sources: roast chicken breast is 31.0 g protein and 2.33 g leucine per 100 g, that is 7.5% of protein as leucine (USDA FoodData Central FDC ID 171477, SR Legacy NDB 5064). Whey is faster and more leucine-rich per gram than whole food, casein and whole-food meals are slower, and for total daily protein this difference is small. One genuine food-form penalty: composition tables report protein as nitrogen multiplied by a conversion factor, so figures for plant foods with non-protein nitrogen slightly overstate usable protein, and cooking method changes yield per gram bought (raw beef mince is 19.7 g/100 g versus 21.8 g/100 g stewed as water is lost, CoFID 18-469 and 18-470).

items.availability_note: Free beta-alanine, the molecule in the tub, has no meaningful food source and is manufactured. The dietary route is indirect: meat supplies beta-alanine bound into the histidine dipeptides carnosine and anserine, which are hydrolysed after ingestion. Chicken breast is the richest ordinary food at 258 mg carnosine plus 660 mg anserine per 100 g in commercial broilers, together about 346 mg of beta-alanine equivalent per 100 g. That is roughly a tenth of a single day's supplement dose per 100 g of meat, and the dose has to be repeated daily for four weeks or more, so the practical gap is one to two orders of magnitude. Poultry dark meat, often assumed to be similar, holds only 20-36 mg carnosine per 100 g.

items.dose_gap: CARNOSINE ROUTE COMPUTED: carnosine is 39.4% beta-alanine by mass (89.09 / 226.23) and anserine is 37.1% (89.09 / 240.26). The lowest dose shown to work is 3.2 g/day of beta-alanine for 4 weeks, which raised muscle carnosine 42.1% (6.4 g/day raised it 64.2%). From commercial broiler breast at 346 mg beta-alanine equivalent per 100 g, counting both carnosine and anserine, 3.2 g/day requires 923 g of raw chicken breast every day for a month. Counting carnosine alone it is 3.15 kg/day. From beef at 84 mg/100 g it is 3.8 kg of raw steak per day, and from chicken thigh it is over 20 kg. Nine hundred grams of chicken breast is roughly 210 g of protein and would have to be eaten daily for the whole loading period. Not achievable by eating normally. Note also that no food delivers free beta-alanine in the form the supplement uses.
items.form_caveat: MAJOR, and it cuts both ways. Ingested carnosine does not reach muscle intact: after histidine dipeptides were given in chicken broth at 40 mg/kg beta-alanine equivalent, carnosine was undetectable in plasma while plasma beta-alanine peaked at 428 uM, because serum carnosinase hydrolyses the dipeptide. So the food form works only by liberating beta-alanine, and it does so at roughly half the peak concentration of an equal weight of free beta-alanine (833 uM at the same 40 mg/kg dose). Reassuringly, isomolar oral L-carnosine raised muscle carnosine as much as 6.4 g/day beta-alanine (65.8% versus 64.2%), so the dipeptide route is biologically equivalent and only the volume of food is impossible (Harris RC et al., Amino Acids 2006;30(3):279-89, PMID 16554972, DOI 10.1007/s00726-006-0299-9). Two further points: cooking significantly reduces meat carnosine (Purchas RW et al., Meat Sci 2004;66(3):629-37, PMID 22060873), and the paraesthesia that makes people split beta-alanine doses is a property of a large free-amino-acid bolus that food never produces.
items.bioavailability: Quantified head to head. At 40 mg/kg body weight, plasma beta-alanine peaked at 833 uM from free beta-alanine and at 428 uM from an equivalent load of histidine dipeptides in chicken broth, with both returning to baseline by 2 h and urinary loss of beta-alanine under 5% (PMID 16554972). Muscle carnosine responses after 4 weeks: 42.1% at 3.2 g/day, 64.2% at 6.4 g/day, and 65.8% for isomolar L-carnosine. The practical implication is that the food matrix costs about half the peak plasma concentration per gram but does not block the pathway; the binding constraint is that meat contains only 0.08-0.35% beta-alanine equivalent by weight. Beta-alanine content also varies severalfold with muscle type and breed: carnosine in beef ranged from 0.003 to 418.7 mg/100 g across 21 muscles (PMID 30811817), and glycolytic (white) muscle holds far more than red oxidative muscle, so 'chicken' is not one number.

items.availability_note: Caffeine is the one supplement on this list where the usual dose is what ordinary drinks already deliver. An ergogenic 3-6 mg/kg is 210-420 mg for a 70 kg adult, and USDA gives home brewed coffee 40 mg per 100 g, so two to four mugs covers it. The problem is not availability but dose control: the same beverage from the same outlet on six consecutive days ranged from 259 to 564 mg.

items.dose_gap: NONE for the dose, LARGE for the precision. A 200 mg pre-workout dose is about two mugs of home brewed coffee (96 mg each) or three single espresso shots. What food cannot deliver is a known dose. Measured caffeine in caffeinated specialty coffees ranged 58-259 mg per dose, mean 188 mg (SD 36) for a 16 oz cup, and critically the same beverage bought from the same outlet on six consecutive days ranged 259-564 mg, a 2.2-fold swing in what the customer thought was an identical drink (McCusker RR, Goldberger BA, Cone EJ, J Anal Toxicol 2003;27(7):520-2, PMID 14607010, DOI 10.1093/jat/27.7.520). Decaffeinated versions still contained up to 17.7 mg per dose, so decaf is not caffeine-free. Tea adds steep-time variance on top of leaf variance (14-61 mg per serving across 20 commercial products, Chin 2008). Matcha spans 18.9-44.4 mg/g, so one teaspoon is anywhere from 38 to 89 mg. Practical conclusion: reaching the dose from drinks is trivial, hitting it within plus or minus 20% is not, which is why trials use capsules.
items.form_caveat: The caveat is inverted here. Anhydrous caffeine powder is the same molecule but is dangerous precisely because it is concentrated: a level teaspoon is several grams, in the range associated with fatal poisoning, whereas the same amount as brewed coffee would be 30 to 50 mugs and physically self-limiting. Whole-drink forms also carry matrix effects that change the experience and the risk profile. Coffee brings chlorogenic acids and, when unfiltered, diterpenes that raise LDL; tea and matcha bring L-theanine and catechins that alter the subjective stimulation; energy drinks bring sugar, taurine and often glucuronolactone, so a 'caffeine dose' from a can is never only caffeine. Tea and coffee polyphenols also inhibit non-haem iron absorption when taken with meals, a cost the capsule does not impose. Finally, energy drink and specialty coffee servings are large and easy to stack, and label values are nominal rather than analysed.
items.bioavailability: Caffeine is essentially completely absorbed from every form tested, so there is no meaningful absorption penalty for the food route; the differences are in rate and in dose certainty. Liquids reach peak plasma concentrations faster than capsules, chewing gum faster still, and a hot drink sipped over 20 minutes produces a flatter curve than a capsule swallowed at once, which matters for timing a pre-exercise dose but not for total exposure. Analytical values differ between databases for the same drink because brewing dominates: USDA lists brewed coffee at 40 mg/100 g and espresso at 212 mg/100 g (FDC 171890, 171891), while the Brazilian table lists espresso at 279 mg/100 mL (DOI 10.3390/nu14204417). Both are correct for what they measured, which is the whole point: the food is the variable, not the absorption.

items.availability_note: Vegetables are the dietary source and some reach supplement-level concentrations. EFSA pooled 25,306 leafy vegetable samples and found rocket (rucola) had the highest median nitrate of any vegetable at 4,800 mg/kg, with beetroot at 1,100 mg/kg, butterhead lettuce 1,978 mg/kg, iceberg lettuce 844 mg/kg, spinach 785 mg/kg and celery 693 mg/kg. This is the only entry on this list where a normal portion of a normal food can match the dose used in trials.

items.dose_gap: SMALL, and for one vegetable it closes entirely. Using 1 mmol nitrate = 62 mg, a 6 mmol target is 372 mg. HOW MUCH BEETROOT JUICE EQUALS 6 mmol: exactly 100 mL of concentrated beetroot shot, since 70 mL was measured at 4.2 mmol and 140 mL at 8.4 mmol; that is one and a half standard shots. From whole vegetables at EFSA median concentrations: 78 g of rocket, 188 g of butterhead lettuce, 338 g of cooked beetroot, 441 g of iceberg lettuce, 474 g of raw spinach, or 537 g of celery. Rocket is the only food where the trial dose fits inside a portion a person would actually eat, and a single 80 g bag already gives 6.19 mmol. Worth flagging against the trial data: in Wylie's dose-response study 70 mL (4.2 mmol) did not change any exercise response, while 140 mL (8.4 mmol) reduced steady-state oxygen uptake 1.7% and extended time to task failure 14%, and 280 mL (16.8 mmol) gave no further performance gain. So a 6 mmol target sits between the ineffective and the effective dose in that trial, and roughly 8 mmol (about 130 g of rocket or 130 mL of concentrate) is the better food target.
items.form_caveat: SUBSTANTIAL, mostly about dose uncertainty and a regulatory conflict. Vegetable nitrate varies enormously: rocket ran from 1,528 mg/kg at the 5th percentile to 7,340 at the 95th, and the highest single leafy sample EFSA saw was 19,925 mg/kg in an oak-leaf lettuce grown under cover. Beetroot's mean (1,379 mg/kg) is well above its median (1,100) because of a long tail, so a salad or a home-pressed juice cannot be dosed. The regulatory tension is concrete: EFSA calculated that eating more than 47 g of rocket at the median nitrate concentration would on its own exceed the acceptable daily intake for nitrate (and a rocket-heavy salad pattern pushed modelled intake to 330 mg/person/day). So the food route to 6 mmol means routinely exceeding the nitrate ADI, which EFSA judged acceptable in the context of overall vegetable benefits but which is not nothing. Processing matters too: nitrate in red beet and kohlrabi was reduced by up to 50% by fermentation, and boiling leaches nitrate into the water, so pickled beetroot and boiled-and-drained spinach are weaker than the raw figures suggest. Finally, the pathway depends on oral bacteria reducing nitrate to nitrite, so antibacterial mouthwash blunts the effect regardless of the source. Spinach is the classic textbook nitrate answer and is a mediocre one: its median is six times lower than rocket, and it is separately a bad iron recommendation because its oxalate binds the iron.
items.bioavailability: Nitrate from vegetables and from a juice concentrate behave the same because it is a small inorganic anion, absorbed essentially completely in the upper small intestine, then concentrated in saliva by the enterosalivary circulation and reduced to nitrite by oral bacteria before any nitric oxide is formed. Wylie's dose-response work showed plasma nitrite rising dose-dependently with peak change at 2-3 h after 4.2, 8.4 and 16.8 mmol, but the physiological response saturating: 8.4 and 16.8 mmol produced similar improvements, so more nitrate is not more effect. The practical bioavailability differences are therefore in the food, not the gut: concentration varies severalfold with species, season, greenhouse versus open-field growing and region (EFSA 2008), juice concentrates are standardised while salad is not, and cooking water discards nitrate. A whole-food route is entirely viable, it just needs rocket rather than beetroot to be efficient.

items.availability_note: HMB (beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate) is a leucine metabolite. No food composition database, USDA FoodData Central, CoFID or any national table, carries an HMB value, and the frequently repeated claim that it occurs in catfish, grapefruit and alfalfa is not backed by any quantified composition analysis I could source. What is quantified is the internal route: healthy adults produce only 0.3-0.4 g/day endogenously, because roughly 5-10% of leucine flux goes down the HMB pathway while about 80% goes to protein synthesis. Against a supplement dose of 3-6 g/day, the body's own whole-day output is 8 to 20 times too small, and food contributes no measurable preformed HMB at all.
items.dose_gap: QUANTIFIED VIA THE LEUCINE ROUTE, because there is no food HMB figure to work from. At the 5% conversion rate, generating 3 g of HMB would require about 60 g of leucine per day. Roast chicken breast provides 2.33 g leucine per 100 g (USDA FDC ID 171477, SR Legacy NDB 5064), so 60 g of leucine is 2.6 kg of cooked chicken breast per day, which carries roughly 800 g of protein. Even at the optimistic 10% conversion figure it is 30 g of leucine, about 1.3 kg of cooked chicken breast and 400 g of protein daily. And these calculations are theoretical ceilings: measured endogenous production in healthy adults is only 0.3-0.4 g/day, meaning real conversion never approaches the arithmetic. The 3-6 g/day used in trials therefore cannot be reached by eating anything, in any quantity, and cannot be reached by eating more leucine or more whey either, because the bottleneck is the branched-chain metabolic pathway rather than the intake. Verdict: unreachable through food, by a factor of at least 8 to 20 against the body's entire daily output.
items.form_caveat: The supplement is a manufactured molecule, not a food extract. Industrial routes are chemical synthesis by halogenation of diacetone alcohol with sodium hypobromite, or esterification approaches from diacetone alcohol and acetic acid derivatives, at output scales around 1.5 tonnes per month; microbial routes using Galactomyces reessii (29.0 g/L) and engineered E. coli (17.7 g/L) are emerging. Regulatory reviews treat 3-6 g/day as generally safe while noting that no international consensus on an optimal dose exists. Because there is no food form, there is no whole-food-versus-extract comparison to make, and equally no reason to describe HMB as something a diet can supply. The one form question that matters commercially is calcium HMB monohydrate versus free-acid HMB, which differ in absorption kinetics rather than in origin. Primary source for the manufacturing, endogenous production and conversion figures: Foods 2025;14(8):1294, PMID 40282696, DOI 10.3390/foods14081294.
items.bioavailability: There is no food form whose absorption can be compared, so the only meaningful statement is about the pathway. Dietary leucine is not a usable precursor at supplement scale: 80% is directed to protein synthesis and only 5-10% enters the HMB pathway, which is why increasing protein or leucine intake raises endogenous HMB only marginally and total endogenous output stays at 0.3-0.4 g/day (DOI 10.3390/foods14081294). Between the two supplement forms, free-acid HMB is reported to reach peak plasma concentration faster and higher than calcium HMB monohydrate, which is the main practical bioavailability distinction; both bypass the leucine pathway entirely, which is precisely why the supplement exists.

items.availability_note: Both compounds occur in ordinary food at meaningful concentrations, and both sit far below their supplement doses. Quercetin: capers are extraordinary at 234 mg/100 g raw and red onion is the everyday source at 39 mg/100 g, against habitual intakes of tens of milligrams and trial doses of 500-1,000 mg/day. Taurine: it is present in animal foods only, detectable in meats and dairy and absent from plant products, with shellfish the richest source and dark poultry meat around 47 mg/100 g, against trial doses of 1-6 g/day. Neither dose is reachable by eating, but neither is a manufactured molecule with no dietary presence.

items.dose_gap: QUERCETIN: trials use 500-1,000 mg/day. From the richest food, raw capers at 233.84 mg/100 g, that is 214-428 g of capers per day, which is 14 to 29 tablespoons of a brine-packed condiment and a salt load nobody should take. From raw red onion at 39.21 mg/100 g it is 1.28-2.55 kg of onion per day. From apples with skin at 4.01 mg/100 g it is 12.5-25 kg of apples, about 70-140 apples. Habitual dietary quercetin intake is on the order of tens of milligrams, so a 500 mg capsule is roughly 25-50 times anything a diet delivers. Not achievable. TAURINE: trials use 1-6 g/day, commonly 3 g. From beef at 61.1 mg/100 g that is 4.9 kg of raw steak per day; from chicken thigh at 47.34 mg/100 g it is 6.3 kg; from clam meat at roughly 450 mg/100 g as eaten it is about 670 g of clam meat daily, which is the only route within an order of magnitude of feasible and still nothing a person eats. Vegans and vegetarians get essentially none from food, since taurine was detected in meats, dairy products and infant feeding solutions but not in any plant product tested (Laidlaw SA, Grosvenor M, Kopple JD, JPEN J Parenter Enteral Nutr 1990;14(2):183-8, PMID 2352336, DOI 10.1177/0148607190014002183). Verdict for both: the supplement dose is not reachable by eating normally, though both compounds are real dietary constituents rather than inventions.
items.form_caveat: QUERCETIN, MAJOR. Supplements are almost always the aglycone, extracted from Sophora japonica flower buds or Dimorphandra mollis pods, which are not foods anyone eats; food quercetin is glycosides (glucosides in onions, rutin in tea and apples). The forms are not interchangeable in the gut (see bioavailability), and a 500-1,000 mg aglycone dose is a pharmacological exposure that inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, whereas 10-30 mg/day from onions and apples never approaches it. Capers are the technically richest source and the worst practical recommendation: the value is for a salt-cured condiment eaten a tablespoon at a time, and the canned figure ranges 45.05-519.85 mg/100 g across 20 samples, an elevenfold spread. Apples with skin are the classic textbook answer and are roughly 60 times too dilute; peeling drops them from 4.01 to 1.05 mg/100 g. TAURINE, MODERATE. The supplement is synthetic and chemically identical to food taurine, so there is no extract-versus-food problem. The two real caveats are analytical and culinary. Shellfish taurine numbers circulating online are often dry-weight figures presented as if they were per 100 g of food, which inflates them four- to sixfold; the values above are labelled explicitly. And taurine is a free amino acid, not protein-bound, so it leaches: taurine and creatine were the compounds most reduced by cooking beef, with losses partly into the cooking juices (Purchas RW, Busboom JR, Meat Sci 2004;68(2):201-7, PMID 22062229; Purchas RW et al., Meat Sci 2004;66(3):629-37, PMID 22060873). A stew keeps its taurine in the broth; a grilled steak with the juices discarded does not.
items.bioavailability: QUERCETIN, quantified and decisive. In healthy ileostomy volunteers absorption was 52 plus or minus 15% for quercetin glucosides from fried onions, 17 plus or minus 15% for quercetin rutinoside (the main form in tea and apples) and 24 plus or minus 9% for pure quercetin aglycone, the form used in supplements; conjugation with glucose enhances absorption (Hollman PC et al., Am J Clin Nutr 1995;62(6):1276-82, PMID 7491892, DOI 10.1093/ajcn/62.6.1276). So per milligram, onion quercetin is roughly twice as absorbable as the capsule and three times as absorbable as tea or apple rutin, which narrows the effective gap a little but nowhere near enough to close it, since urinary recovery was only 0.5% of the amount absorbed. TAURINE. It is present in food as the free amino acid rather than bound in protein, absorbed by the TauT transporter with high oral bioavailability, and the supplement form is identical, so absorption is not where food loses. Food loses on concentration and on cooking: the practical content of a portion depends heavily on whether cooking liquid is consumed, and reported values vary severalfold with muscle type (beef taurine ranged 0.552 to 23.861 umol/g across 21 muscles, PMID 30811817) and with breed in poultry (39.29-47.34 mg/100 g, PMID 36230082). Reading dry-weight shellfish values as wet-weight is the single commonest error in this literature.

misclassifications: BETA-ALANINE labelled TRACE is wrong, and it is wrong by the submission's own yardstick. Its own numbers put commercial broiler breast at 346 mg beta-alanine equivalent per 100 g, i.e. 589 mg in a 170 g portion, i.e. 18% of a 3.2 g daily dose. Compare the items it labelled RICH: creatine delivers 13-20% of a 5 g dose per portion (beef 787 mg = 16%, chicken 668 mg = 13%, herring 650-1,000 mg = 13-20%). Beta-alanine's per-portion contribution sits at the TOP of the creatine range yet got the opposite label. Worse, the submission's own form_caveat concedes the dietary route is biologically equivalent: isomolar oral L-carnosine raised muscle carnosine 65.8% versus 64.2% for 6.4 g/day of free beta-alanine (Harris 2006). If the food-borne precursor is present at hundreds of mg per 100 g and is biologically equivalent, TRACE is the wrong word. The 'free beta-alanine is absent from food' point is a form argument, not an availability argument, and the submission itself resolves the form question in food's favour. Correct label: RICH (dose-limited), on identical reasoning to creatine.

BETA-ALANINE's TRACE label is further undercut by the very paper cited for its headline number. Ali 2019 exists to show that native strains far exceed broilers: strain HH breast holds 511.04 mg carnosine plus 1,525.80 mg anserine per 100 g = 767 mg beta-alanine equivalent, i.e. 1,304 mg in a 170 g breast, 41% of a 3.2 g dose. The submission cited the paper and used only its lowest strain, then generalised to 'chicken breast is the richest ordinary food' - a claim it never tested against pork, turkey or tuna.

QUERCETIN AND TAURINE bundled into one item with one RICH verdict is a category error. The two compounds have different gap sizes (quercetin 25-50x habitual intake; taurine within one order of magnitude via shellfish), opposite dietary distributions (plant-only vs animal-only, so the vegan implications are inverted), and opposite form problems (supplement aglycone differs from food glycosides for quercetin; chemically identical for taurine). No single availability label can be correct for both. They should be scored separately.

QUERCETIN classified RICH is inconsistent in the opposite direction from beta-alanine. Its best realistic portion contribution is 7.0% of a 500 mg dose (one 15 g tablespoon of capers, a salt-cured condiment), and its everyday sources give 2-5%. That is materially WEAKER per portion than beta-alanine's 18%, yet quercetin got RICH and beta-alanine got TRACE. The two labels are precisely backwards relative to each other. The submission's own text concedes habitual intake is 'tens of milligrams' against a 500 mg dose.

HMB classified TRACE contradicts its own evidence and should be SYNTHETIC. The item lists zero foods (foods: []), states that no composition database carries an HMB value, states the catfish/grapefruit/alfalfa claim has no quantified backing, and concludes 'food contributes no measurable preformed HMB at all'. All of that checked out under independent verification. TRACE implies detectable-but-tiny dietary presence; the evidence presented supports no dietary presence at all. Endogenous production of 0.3-0.4 g/day is not a dietary source. Note this cuts against the submission's interest, so it is an error of over-generosity, not of salesmanship.

CREATINE, PROTEIN, CAFFEINE and NITRATE classifications are correct and I could not break them. Nitrate is rightly the one item where a normal portion meets the trial dose (80 g of rocket = 6.19 mmol = 103% of 6 mmol), and protein is rightly the one where food beats the supplement outright.
missing_foods: NITRATE - RHUBARB, median 2,808 mg/kg (EFSA Table 9, n=58), 2.5x beetroot. At 280.8 mg/100 g, just 132 g reaches 6 mmol - a normal portion, and better than the butterhead lettuce (188 g) the submission does list. This directly refutes its claim that 'rocket is the only food where the trial dose fits inside a portion a person would actually eat'. EFSA's own text flags it: 'Rhubarb showed particularly high values.'

NITRATE - ten further vegetables in the cited EFSA tables have medians ABOVE beetroot's 1,100 mg/kg and were all omitted: amaranth 2,660 (140 g = 6 mmol), lamb's lettuce 2,130 (175 g), mixed lettuce 1,878, beet leaves 1,770, curled lettuce 1,628, oak-leaf lettuce 1,553, silverbeet/chard 1,510, Belgian endive 1,475, white radish 1,256, black radish 1,245. Cos lettuce (1,097) and fennel (783) also beat the spinach entry that was included. The submission mined one row of Table 7 and the beetroot row of Table 10 and left the richer neighbours on the page.

QUERCETIN - richer sources sitting in the very database cited (Release 3.3) were omitted: lovage leaves 170.00 mg/100 g, elderberry juice concentrate 108.16, dock (Rumex) 86.20, radish leaves 70.37, chokeberry juice concentrate 68.17, wild rocket (Diplotaxis) 66.19, juniper berries 46.61.

QUERCETIN - more damaging, five ordinary kitchen foods beat the submission's nominated 'everyday source' (red onion, 39.21): dill weed fresh 55.15, coriander/cilantro leaves 52.90, yellow wax hot peppers 50.63, fennel leaves 48.80, wild rocket 66.19. Also omitted: radicchio 31.51, watercress 29.99, elderberries 26.77, pan-fried white onion 26.90. Naming capers (a condiment) as the only rich source while missing herbs at 50-55 mg/100 g overstates how narrow the food route is.

PROTEIN - two foods richer per 100 g than anything on the list, both in CoFID 2021: turkey breast fillet, grilled, meat only (18-356) at 35.0 g, and Parmesan, fresh (12-526) at 36.2 g. The submission's ceiling was chicken breast at 32.0 g.

PROTEIN - also omitted from CoFID: sardines grilled 25.4 g and canned in brine drained 22.1 g, tuna canned in sunflower oil drained 25.4 g, pumpkin seeds 24.4 g, king prawns grilled 23.5 g, mackerel grilled 20.3 g, tempeh 20.7 g (2.6x the tofu figure used, and the obvious plant-source omission alongside seitan), dried prawns 83.1 g. Separately, using CoFID's traditional 'Yogurt, Greek style, plain' at 5.7 g understates modern strained/high-protein pots and skyr at roughly 10-12 g per 100 g, making dairy look weaker than a shopper would find it.

BETA-ALANINE - pork loin was omitted entirely despite pork appearing in the creatine item; pork loin carries carnosine in the low hundreds of mg per 100 g, comparable to or above the beef figure used. Turkey breast (carnosine-rich glycolytic white muscle) and tuna/skipjack and other pelagic fish (among the richest anserine sources known) are also absent, as is rabbit. The item's own claim that glycolytic white muscle far exceeds red oxidative muscle predicts these are rich, and none was checked.

CREATINE - rabbit muscle is named in the submission's own availability_note as measured at ~30 mmol/kg by Harris 1997 but given no food row, so the reader never sees it. Lamb, venison and other game muscle sit in the same range and are absent. Kangaroo is reported above the beef figure in the wider literature.

CAFFEINE - guarana is missing, and it is the single richest natural caffeine source (seed/powder roughly 2-6 g per 100 g, i.e. 25-75x brewed coffee per gram); it is also the ingredient that makes many energy products potent. Instant coffee powder on a dry basis (roughly 3-4 g per 100 g) and yerba mate are likewise absent. A list whose stated purpose is to show that ordinary items reach the dose omitted the items that overshoot it most easily.

TAURINE - scallops, mussels, octopus and squid are the classic wet-weight-rich taurine foods and none appears. This is a self-inflicted gap: the submission cites Laidlaw 1990 (PMID 2352336), which analysed 29 meats on an as-eaten basis, but uses it only for the negative 'no plant taurine' point, while sourcing its shellfish food rows from an umami/taste study's dry-weight figures and converting them with an admitted self-supplied moisture assumption. A wet-weight primary source was already in the citation list and went unused for exactly the rows that needed it. Dark turkey meat and tuna dark muscle are also omitted.
dose_gap_errors: NITRATE, the recommended food target is wrong: 'roughly 8 mmol (about 130 g of rocket or 130 mL of concentrate) is the better food target'. At the EFSA median of 4,800 mg/kg (480 mg/100 g), 8 mmol = 496 mg of nitrate requires 103 g of rocket, not 130 g. Conversely 130 g of rocket delivers 624 mg = 10.06 mmol, a 26% overshoot of the stated target. CORRECTED FIGURE: about 103 g of rocket. (The companion 130 mL of concentrate is right: 8/8.4 x 140 = 133 mL.)

TAURINE, the oyster dose percentages are wrong because the source value is wrong. The submission used 2,046 mg/100 g dry weight for Kumamoto oyster; the paper reports 1,845.33. On its own 80-83% moisture assumption the corrected chain is: 314-369 mg/100 g as eaten (claimed 350-410), 235-277 mg per 75 g of meat (claimed 260-310), and 7.8-9.2% of a 3 g dose (claimed 9-10%). CORRECTED FIGURES: 1,845 mg/100 g dry, 314-369 mg/100 g wet, 235-277 mg per portion, 7.8-9.2% of dose.

BETA-ALANINE, the beef carnosine range low end is wrong by roughly 90-fold: 'carnosine in beef ranged from 0.003 to 418.7 mg/100 g across 21 muscles' (repeated in the food row and the dose_gap). The paper reports 0.012-18.508 umol/g wet tissue = 0.27-418.7 mg/100 g. CORRECTED FIGURE: 0.27-418.7 mg/100 g. The stated 0.003 mg/100 g is 30 ng/g, which no skeletal muscle can contain; it appears to be an unconverted umol/g-scale number left inside a mg/100 g range. The 418.7 high end is correct, and the taurine range in the same paragraph is converted correctly.

EVERYTHING ELSE CHECKS OUT. I re-derived roughly 90 further dose-gap and per-portion figures and found no other arithmetic fault. Confirmed correct: creatine 3 g = 763 g and 5 g = 1,272 g of raw beef at 393 mg/100 g; 667 g and 1,111 g on Balsom's 4.5 g/kg; 500-770 g of herring; all nine creatine per-portion and per-cent-of-dose values; the protein worked day (14.1+9.7+41.6+16.2+9.0+7.6 = 98.2 g, plus 24.9 g tuna = 123.1 g, over the 112 g target) and all twelve protein percentages; beta-alanine 923 g of broiler breast for 3.2 g, 3.15 kg counting carnosine alone, 3.8 kg of beef, over 20 kg of thigh, and the 39.4%/37.1% mass fractions; HMB 60 g of leucine at 5% conversion = 2.6 kg of cooked breast carrying about 800 g of protein, and 30 g/1.3 kg/400 g at 10%; quercetin 214-428 g of capers, 1.28-2.55 kg of red onion, 12.5-25 kg (70-140) of apples, and the 74% peeling loss; taurine 4.9 kg of beef, 6.3 kg of thigh, about 670 g of clam meat; all seven nitrate per-portion conversions at 62 mg/mmol and all six whole-vegetable gram requirements (rocket 78 g, butterhead 188 g, beetroot 338 g, iceberg 441 g, spinach 474 g, celery 537 g); the 100 mL beetroot-shot equivalence for 6 mmol; and the 47 g rocket ADI cross-check (3.7 mg/kg x 60 kg / 4.8 mg/g = 46 g).
verdict.net_assessment: This is a strong submission that survived adversarial checking better than expected. I verified 4 of 4 USDA FDC IDs (171890, 171891, 170273, 171477) down to NDB number, food description and nutrient value; all 14 CoFID 2021 food codes and protein values to the decimal, queried against the dataset itself, including the three I specifically suspected of being wrong (cottage cheese 9.4, boiled egg 14.1, red lentils 8.1); all 8 quercetin values with their sample counts and min-max ranges from Flavonoid Release 3.3; roughly 25 EFSA nitrate statistics across three tables plus five contextual claims verbatim; and 13 of 13 PMIDs/DOIs as real papers with correct titles, journals, years and pagination. No invented source, no fabricated PMID, no phantom FDC ID. Harris 1997, Harris 2006, Burke 2003, Wylie 2013, McCusker 2003, Hollman 1995, Laidlaw 1990, Ali 2019, BraCaffT and the Kochman matcha range were all confirmed exactly, several of them figure-for-figure. Three genuine numeric faults. (1) Kumamoto oyster taurine is 1,845.33 mg/100 g dry weight, not 'about 2,046', and the error propagates through three derived per-portion and per-cent-of-dose figures. (2) The beef carnosine range low end, 0.003 mg/100 g, should be 0.27 mg/100 g, a roughly 90-fold slip from leaving a umol/g figure unconverted; it is biologically impossible as printed and is repeated twice. (3) The recommended nitrate food target of 'about 130 g of rocket' for 8 mmol should be about 103 g. Beyond that, roughly 90 further dose-gap computations were re-derived and every one checked out, which is a genuinely unusual hit rate. Citation hygiene has two soft spots: Meat Sci 2004;68(2):201-7 is attributed to 'Purchas RW, Busboom JR' when the authors are Purchas, Rutherfurd, Pearce, Vather and Wilkinson (used twice), and the four-fold creatinine rise at 90 min/70 C is a lamb result applied to meat generally. The bivalve taurine values are cited to 'Table 3' but live in Figure 1B of what is actually an umami study, and five of the nine creatine food rows (herring, pork, salmon, cod, milk) rest entirely on a 1994 narrative review's compiled table with no traceable primary analysis and no database cross-check possible, so those should be marked indicative rather than established. The real weakness is classification, not arithmetic. The availability labels are applied inconsistently in both directions: beta-alanine is called TRACE while delivering 18% of its dose per portion, and quercetin is called RICH while delivering 7% at best, so the two labels are exactly backwards relative to each other and to the RICH label creatine earned at 13-20%. Beta-alanine should be RICH (dose-limited), and the submission's own cited paper contains a native chicken strain at 767 mg beta-alanine equivalent per 100 g (41% of a dose per breast) that it declined to use. HMB should be SYNTHETIC rather than TRACE, since the item lists no foods and its own verified text says food supplies no measurable preformed HMB. Bundling quercetin and taurine under one verdict is a structural error given their opposite dietary distributions and form problems. Food coverage is the other soft area, and notably it is soft in ways that make the food route look worse than it is: rhubarb at an EFSA median of 2,808 mg/kg reaches 6 mmol of nitrate in 132 g, which falsifies the claim that rocket is the only vegetable where the dose fits a normal portion, and ten more vegetables in the cited tables beat beetroot; turkey breast (35.0 g) and Parmesan (36.2 g) beat every protein food listed; dill, coriander, fennel leaves and yellow wax peppers all beat red onion for quercetin in the cited database; guarana is missing from a caffeine list; and scallops, mussels and octopus are missing from taurine even though the paper that would have supplied wet-weight values was already cited for a different point. Overall: the numbers are largely trustworthy and unusually well sourced, the arithmetic is 97% clean, and the substantive corrections needed are two wrong values, one wrong recommended target, two label reversals, one label upgrade to SYNTHETIC, one de-bundling, and a broader sweep of the source tables the authors already had open.

items.availability_note: Psyllium husk is itself a food ingredient (the milled seed coat of Plantago ovata), not an extracted molecule, so the supplement and the food are the same material. Ordinary foods also supply the same class of viscous soluble fibre: oats and oat bran (beta-glucan), pearled barley, and legumes. USDA FDC records for psyllium husk powder give 67 g soluble and 11 g insoluble fibre per 100 g (FDC 1742558).

items.dose_gap: This is the one supplement in the group where the pill and the food are the same thing, so the gap is zero: the 10 g/day husk dose that beat placebo in primary-care IBS (Bijkerk 2009, BMJ 339:b3154, PMID 19713235) is about one heaped tablespoon, and 9 g of husk powder already supplies 6.0 g of soluble fibre (FDC 1742558). Matching that 6-7 g of SOLUBLE fibre from ordinary foods is a different matter: at 0.42 g/100 g you would need roughly 1.6 kg of cooked porridge (about 7 cups), at 0.44 g/100 g about 1.5 kg of cooked lentils, at 0.41 g/100 g about 1.6 kg of chickpeas, or about 500 g (3 cups) of canned kidney beans at 1.36 g/100 g. Cooked split peas are the trap: 10.65 g total fibre per 100 g but only 0.09 g of it soluble (Li 2002), so you would need roughly 7 kg. The separate, easier target of 3 g/day of oat or barley beta-glucan IS reachable by eating: about 40-50 g of dry oats at 6-8% w/w, or 75 g at 4% (Hughes & Grafenauer, DOI 10.3390/nu13082556). Summary: general soluble fibre is achievable from oats and barley; psyllium's specific gel dose is realistically only achievable from psyllium.
items.form_caveat: There is no extract-versus-food problem here because psyllium husk is unprocessed plant material, but there are two real caveats. First, physical: the husk must be taken with a full glass of fluid, because a gel-forming dose swallowed dry can obstruct the oesophagus or bowel. Second, and more often missed, 'soluble fibre' on a label is not one thing. Psyllium's arabinoxylan gel is viscous and poorly fermented; inulin carries the same soluble-fibre label but ferments fast and produces gas, which is the opposite of what an IBS patient wants. Substituting one for the other on gram-for-gram grounds is a mistake. Third, oat beta-glucan's benefit tracks viscosity, which depends on molecular weight; milling, extrusion and prolonged heating degrade it, so a heavily processed oat product with an identical gram figure on the label is not equivalent to whole rolled oats.
items.bioavailability: Nothing here is absorbed, so 'bioavailability' means viscosity, water-holding and fermentability. Psyllium holds water through the whole colon with a low gas yield, which is why it improves both constipation and diarrhoea; legume soluble fibre and inulin are largely fermented in the proximal colon and behave quite differently at the same gram intake. Analytical method is a real source of confusion: the AOAC 991.43 gravimetric soluble-fibre values used by Li et al. run systematically higher than the enzymatic-chemical (Englyst/NSP) values used in UK tables, and the authors say so explicitly, so soluble-fibre numbers from different tables should not be mixed. Head-to-head evidence backs the distinction: at the same 10 g dose, psyllium beat placebo at one and two months while wheat bran did not (PMID 19713235).

items.supplement: Wheat bran and insoluble fibre supplements for IBS
items.availability_note: Wheat bran is a food, sold as a plain milled cereal fraction, and it is one of the most fibre-dense foods in any composition table: 42.8 g total dietary fibre per 100 g (USDA FDC 169722), of which 35.0-48.4 g is insoluble and only 1.5-4.0 g soluble (Stevenson et al., Int J Food Sci Nutr 2012;63:1001-1013, DOI 10.3109/09637486.2012.687366). Arabinoxylan makes up about 70% of the non-starch polysaccharide, cellulose 24% and beta-glucan 6%. The problem with this supplement is not availability; it is that the indication is wrong.

items.dose_gap: There is no dose gap at all, and that is the point worth making. The 10 g/day of bran tested against psyllium and placebo in IBS (PMID 19713235) is about 3 heaped tablespoons of plain wheat bran, or roughly 2 servings of bran flakes; a single cup of bran (58 g) is nearly six times the trial dose. Nobody needs a supplement to reach it. What the trial found is that reaching it does not help: bran was no better than placebo in months one and two, its month-three advantage did not survive worst-case analysis, and early dropout was highest in the bran arm specifically because IBS symptoms got worse. A separate review of the wheat bran literature reaches the same conclusion and quotes official guidance that wheat bran should not be recommended to people with IBS (DOI 10.3109/09637486.2012.687366).
items.form_caveat: The food is safe and useful; the supplement indication is the problem. Wheat bran is a genuinely effective faecal bulking agent, with a mean increase of about 5 g of stool per 1 g of bran consumed (DOI 10.3109/09637486.2012.687366), and it is a reasonable food for ordinary constipation and general fibre intake. In IBS it commonly makes bloating, distension and pain worse, and it was the arm patients dropped out of. A second, less obvious caveat: wheat bran carries fructan (white wheat flour measures 0.75 g fructan/100 g, DOI 10.3389/fnut.2024.1446771), so a bran-loading strategy also raises FODMAP intake in exactly the patients least able to tolerate it. Insoluble-fibre supplements sold as 'IBS fibre' are marketing the wrong fibre class; the evidence in IBS favours the viscous, poorly fermented kind (psyllium).
items.bioavailability: Not absorbed. The mechanism is mechanical bulking plus water-holding by arabinoxylan and cellulose, and it works: bran accelerates small bowel transit and increases faecal weight dose-dependently. Particle size matters more than gram total, because coarse bran bulks and irritates while finely milled bran loses much of the effect, so two products with the same fibre label are not interchangeable. Only 1.5-4.0 g per 100 g is soluble, so bran contributes almost nothing to the viscous-gel effects (cholesterol, glycaemia, stool consistency in diarrhoea) that people often assume 'fibre' delivers.

items.availability_note: Inulin and fructo-oligosaccharide (FOS) are genuinely abundant in ordinary plants: chicory root and Jerusalem artichoke at 12-20 g per 100 g fresh weight, garlic at 15.6-16.7 g per 100 g, onion at about 2 g per 100 g, with much smaller amounts in leek, asparagus, banana and wheat. GOS is the exception and should not be lumped in with them: the beta-galacto-oligosaccharide used in trials is manufactured enzymatically from lactose and has no meaningful presence in ordinary food, while the galacto-oligosaccharides that DO occur in legumes are alpha-galactosides (raffinose, stachyose, verbascose), a chemically different family. Habitual intake is low: measured mean fructan intake is 1.6-1.7 g/day in Slovenia (DOI 10.3389/fnut.2024.1446771) and median inulin intake 1.3 g/day in UK schoolchildren (PMID 40808333).

items.dose_gap: Supplement doses are typically 5-10 g/day, against a habitual dietary intake of only 1.3-1.7 g/day. Adding 5 g of fructan by eating means roughly 250 g of raw onion (two to three medium onions), or about 30 cloves of garlic, or about 40 g of Jerusalem artichoke, or roughly 4.5 kg of banana, or about 5 kg of raw asparagus. So the answer splits: for onion, garlic, chicory root and Jerusalem artichoke the dose is reachable; for banana, leek and asparagus it is not, by two orders of magnitude. The tolerance ceiling is the more useful number. In a randomised crossover trial, up to 10 g/day of native inulin and up to 5 g/day of oligofructose were well tolerated, while 10 g of oligofructose substantially increased symptoms, chiefly flatulence then bloating (Bonnema et al., J Am Diet Assoc 2010;110:865-868, PMID 20497775). With FOS, excess flatus began above 30 g/day, borborygmi and bloating above 40 g/day, and cramps and diarrhoea at 50 g/day, and chronic dosing did not build tolerance (Briet et al., Eur J Clin Nutr 1995;49:501-507, PMID 7588500). One cup of Jerusalem artichoke therefore delivers roughly twice the tolerated daily ceiling in a single sitting. GOS is a hard no: the beta-GOS doses used in trials (a few grams a day) are made industrially by transgalactosylation of lactose, and no ordinary food supplies them.
items.form_caveat: Chicory root is the classic textbook answer and a bad recommendation: it is the industrial source of inulin but it is not eaten as a vegetable in normal diets (it is roasted as a coffee substitute), so its 20 g/100 g headline is not a dietary route. It also illustrates why fibre tables and fructan assays disagree, since USDA lists chicory root at only 1.5 g total dietary fibre per 100 g (FDC 169993) because the method used for that record does not capture inulin. Purified inulin and oligofructose are safe as food ingredients, but concentration is exactly what causes the symptoms: the same molecule that is unremarkable spread across a day's vegetables provokes flatulence and bloating as a single 10 g bolus (PMID 20497775). The reverse caveat matters clinically: the 'eat more prebiotic vegetables' list (onion, garlic, leek, Jerusalem artichoke, wheat) is precisely the list a low-FODMAP diet removes, so in IBS the food route and the supplement route can both make things worse. Finally, do not treat legume alpha-GOS as a food form of supplemental beta-GOS; in Phaseolus vulgaris the measured content is raffinose 0.8-7.4 mg/g, stachyose 20.0-30.9 mg/g and verbascose 0.3-1.3 mg/g (DOI 10.3390/foods15020391), different molecules with different bacterial targets and a well-known flatulence profile of their own.
items.bioavailability: Fructans are not absorbed at all, so the variable is where and how fast they ferment, and chain length decides that. Oligofructose (DP 2-8) ferments proximally and quickly, which is why its tolerated dose was half that of long-chain native inulin in the same trial (5 g versus 10 g, PMID 20497775). Assay and plant part also drive the numbers: onion measured 1.97 g/100 g and leek 0.24 g/100 g by AOAC 999.03 in one national survey (DOI 10.3389/fnut.2024.1446771), while an Australian survey using the Megazyme assay reported 1.2-17.4 g/100 g across high-fructan alliums including leek bulb (PMID 17625872). Storage matters too, since fructan is depolymerised during onion storage. Single figures should be read as indicative, not exact.

items.availability_note: A named probiotic strain is a single clonal isolate held in a culture bank, grown in industrial fermenters, freeze-dried and encapsulated. No food contains it. Fermented foods do carry large numbers of live lactic acid bacteria, but the species and strains present are whichever organisms grow in that food and its starter, never the deposited trial strain. Because probiotic efficacy is demonstrated strain by strain, a food supplying a different strain of the same species is a different product, not a substitute. Numbers for the live-organism load of fermented foods are given under the generic multi-strain entry.
items.dose_gap: The gap is categorical, not quantitative, and no quantity of food closes it. Named-strain doses in trials run from about 1x10^8 to 1x10^10 CFU/day; for example Bifidobacterium longum (formerly infantis) 35624 was effective at 1x10^8 CFU/day (PMID 16863564). A single cup of kefir at 2.5x10^8 CFU/mL supplies roughly 6x10^10 live lactic acid bacteria (DOI 10.3390/foods15101616), so the raw CFU total is easily exceeded by food. The fraction of those cells belonging to the trialled strain is zero, so the CFU comparison is meaningless for a strain-specific claim.
items.form_caveat: This is the single most important form caveat in the assignment. Clinical evidence for probiotics is strain-specific, and often formulation-specific and indication-specific on top of that. Yoghurt, kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, miso, natto and tempeh do not contain the strains tested in the trials, so evidence generated with a named strain does not transfer to any fermented food, and does not transfer to a different strain of the same species either. Eating fermented food is a reasonable dietary habit with its own emerging evidence base, and it is not a substitute for a named strain at a defined dose when a specific clinical effect is the goal. Two further practical caveats: heat kills the organisms, so a pasteurised or cooked ferment (canned sauerkraut, miso stirred into boiling soup, baked tempeh) delivers no live cells at all; and species-level labelling on a supplement ('contains Lactobacillus acidophilus') without a strain designation carries no more transferable evidence than a food does.
items.bioavailability: Survival of gastric acid and bile is strain-dependent, and the delivery matrix changes it: the fat and buffering capacity of a dairy food improves survival relative to a bare capsule, while enteric coating or microencapsulation is used to achieve the same in supplements. Dose is not monotonic, which is the clearest evidence that formulation matters as much as CFU count. In a 362-patient dose-ranging trial, B. infantis 35624 at 1x10^8 CFU/day was significantly superior to placebo and to the other doses, while 1x10^6 and 1x10^10 CFU/day were not, with the highest dose failing because the capsule formulation gelled (Whorwell et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101:1581-1590, PMID 16863564). A higher label CFU is therefore not better, and label CFU at manufacture is not the same as viable CFU at end of shelf life.

items.availability_note: Classified RICH strictly in terms of live-organism load, not in terms of any specific strain. If the deliverable is 'a large number of live lactic acid bacteria of common genera', several ordinary fermented foods supply it at or above supplement label doses: yoghurt has been surveyed at up to 10^9 CFU/g, kefir at 2.5x10^8 CFU/mL, unpasteurised sauerkraut at about 2x10^8 CFU/g, and kimchi at 10^7.14 to 10^9.23 CFU/g. If the deliverable is a defined blend of characterised strains at a stated dose, no food supplies it. One gap in the sourcing: I could not find a peer-reviewed viable count for natto, which is fermented with Bacillus subtilis var. natto and sold unpasteurised, so no CFU figure is given for it here rather than an estimate; tempeh is included instead as a sourced soy ferment.

items.dose_gap: For total live cells there is no gap. The source review calculates that about 10^10 cells is the intake likely needed to affect the microbiota, and that this is met by 100 g of a food carrying 10^8 cells/g (PMID 30197628). One cup of kefir, one cup of yoghurt, about 120 g of raw sauerkraut or a cup of kimchi each clear that bar, and kimchi at the top of its measured range delivers more live organisms in one serving than most 50-billion-CFU capsules. The gap is entirely qualitative: identity, characterisation and consistency. Fermented food counts vary across four to six orders of magnitude between products and batches (yoghurt below 10^4 to 10^9 CFU/g), the organisms are usually not identified to strain, and none of them are the strains in the blend on the label.
items.form_caveat: Fermented food is a reasonable dietary habit; it is not a substitute for a named strain at a defined dose. Even a generic blend at least tells you which species you are getting and roughly how many; a jar of sauerkraut tells you neither, and a pasteurised jar tells you nothing because it contains no live cells. The practical points that decide whether a food delivers anything: it must be labelled raw, unpasteurised or 'live cultures' and kept refrigerated; heat destroys the organisms, so miso added to boiling soup, cooked kimchi and baked tempeh contribute essentially nothing; and long-aged cheeses can be several orders of magnitude lower than young ones. Conversely, a supplement claim of 50 billion CFU means little if the strains are unnamed, because probiotic effects are demonstrated strain by strain, and CFU counts on labels refer to manufacture, not to end of shelf life.
items.bioavailability: Gastric and bile survival is strain-dependent and matrix-dependent. Fermented dairy foods buffer stomach acid and their fat content improves transit survival, which is a genuine advantage of the food route over an uncoated capsule; supplements compensate with enteric coating or microencapsulation. Almost none of these organisms colonise permanently, so the effect is dose-dependent and ceases when intake stops, which applies equally to food and to capsules. The source review notes that many fermentation microbes are closely related to probiotic organisms and can share mechanisms, which is the honest basis for recommending fermented food, but relatedness is not equivalence, and it does not license transferring a strain-specific trial result onto a jar of kimchi.

items.availability_note: This strain was isolated from the ileal mucosa of a healthy human donor, not from any food, and has since been reclassified from Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis to B. longum subsp. longum 35624 (genome and exopolysaccharide characterisation: PLOS One 2016;11:e0162983, PMC5033381). It is propagated industrially from a proprietary strain bank and freeze-dried. It is present in no food, no fermented food and no other supplement brand. Comparative genome analysis identified a 35624-specific gene cluster encoding the biosynthesis of its exopolysaccharide EPS624, which is the kind of strain-level distinction that makes substitution unsound.
items.dose_gap: Infinite: there is no quantity of any food that supplies this strain. The trial dose is small in absolute terms, 1x10^8 CFU/day, which is roughly the number of live bacteria in half a gram of unpasteurised sauerkraut, so the dose is not the obstacle; the identity is. Fermented foods can supply a thousand times more live cells than the effective dose of 35624 while supplying none of it.
items.form_caveat: The dose-response data make the point better than any argument about food. In the 362-patient dose-ranging trial, 1x10^8 CFU/day of B. infantis 35624 was significantly superior to placebo for abdominal pain, the composite score, bloating, bowel dysfunction and incomplete evacuation, while 1x10^6 and 1x10^10 CFU/day were not, the highest dose having formed a gel in the capsule (Whorwell et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101:1581-1590, PMID 16863564). If a tenfold change in dose of the same strain in the same capsule abolishes the effect, then swapping the strain for a different Bifidobacterium in a yoghurt cannot be assumed to preserve it. Anyone advised to take 35624 should be told plainly that no diet reproduces it, and that a generic bifidobacterium supplement is not the same product.
items.bioavailability: The strain was selected partly for surviving gastrointestinal transit, and its documented actions are immunoregulatory and barrier-related rather than nutritional: enhanced gut barrier function, accelerated intestinal transit and reduced visceral hypersensitivity. It does not permanently colonise, so the effect depends on continued daily intake. Formulation dominates delivery: the failure of the 1x10^10 CFU arm was a formulation failure, not evidence against high cell numbers, and it is the clearest illustration that CFU on a label is not the active variable on its own.

items.availability_note: Glutamine is one of the most abundant amino acids in ordinary dietary protein, so any protein-containing meal supplies it. The important caveat about the numbers: USDA composition tables report 'glutamic acid', which after the acid hydrolysis used in amino acid analysis is the sum of glutamate and glutamine, because glutamine is converted to glutamate during hydrolysis. The figures below are therefore the combined Glu plus Gln pool, and the glutamine share of that pool is roughly half in most animal proteins. Treat the values as an upper bound on glutamine content.

items.dose_gap: Small, and this is the one entry where the food route is genuinely competitive. The trial dose is 5 g three times daily, 15 g/day for 8 weeks, in post-infectious diarrhoea-predominant IBS with increased intestinal permeability (Zhou et al., Gut 2019;68:996-1002, PMID 30108163). On the combined Glu plus Gln figures, 15 g comes from about 323 g of cooked chicken breast, 440 g of cod (about 2.5 fillets), 183 g of parmesan, 865 g of natto or roughly 1.1 kg of cooked lentils. Correcting for the fact that only about half that pool is glutamine, matching 15 g of glutamine specifically needs roughly double those amounts, so about 600-700 g of cooked chicken breast a day: a large amount of meat, but not an impossible one, and an ordinary diet supplying 80-100 g of protein already delivers on the order of 8-12 g of glutamine. So the supplement roughly doubles habitual glutamine intake rather than supplying something the diet lacks. It is not a case like creatine or NMN where food cannot get close.
items.form_caveat: The difference is not the amount, it is the delivery. The trial gave 5 g of free crystalline L-glutamine three times a day on an empty-stomach schedule, producing a sharp luminal and plasma bolus; dietary glutamine arrives protein-bound, released slowly by digestion, and a large fraction is consumed by the enterocytes themselves on first pass. Whether the clinical effect depends on that bolus pattern has not been tested against a food-protein comparator, so 'just eat more protein' is a plausible but unproven substitution. Two practical points: free glutamine is heat-labile and degrades in aqueous solution, so cooking and storage reduce the free glutamine in food while leaving protein-bound glutamine intact; and glutamine supplementation is not risk-free in everyone, since it is a nitrogen donor and high doses warrant caution in hepatic or renal impairment, whereas the same amount arriving as ordinary food protein raises no comparable concern.
items.bioavailability: Absorbed as free amino acid and as di- and tripeptides, then extensively extracted by the small intestinal mucosa on first pass, which is the mechanistic argument for a gut-directed effect and also the reason plasma appearance underestimates delivery to the target tissue. Because USDA reports Glu and Gln as one pooled value, no composition table can tell you the true glutamine content of a food, and any per-food glutamine figure quoted to two decimal places should be treated with suspicion. In the trial, the measured mechanism was normalisation of an elevated urinary lactulose/mannitol ratio, so the endpoint was permeability, not amino acid status; a food equivalent would have to reproduce the permeability effect, which has not been shown.

items.availability_note: Both are manufactured, by different routes, and neither has a dietary source. Lactase supplements are microbial beta-galactosidase produced by fermentation of Aspergillus oryzae, A. niger or the yeast Kluyveromyces lactis and then purified; the mammalian brush-border lactase that the supplement substitutes for is a membrane enzyme of the small intestinal epithelium and is not present in any food. Pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancreatin, pancrelipase) is an extract of porcine pancreas glands: the source review states plainly that the preparations with demonstrated efficacy are derived from porcine sources (de la Iglesia et al., eClinicalMedicine 2026;94:103880, DOI 10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103880). The nearest thing to a food source is pancreas eaten as offal (sweetbread), which is not a realistic route for the reasons in the dose gap.
items.dose_gap: For pancreatic enzymes the gap is absolute. Recommended dosing is a minimum of 40,000-50,000 units of lipase with main meals and 20,000-25,000 units with snacks, taken with every meal for life (DOI 10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103880). No food supplies active lipase in those quantities. Raw pancreas is the only tissue that contains the enzymes at all, it is not eaten raw in any normal diet, cooking denatures them, the delivered activity would be unmeasurable and uncontrolled, and there is no enteric protection so gastric acid would destroy most of what survived. For lactase, the gap is more interesting. There is one genuine partial food route: live yoghurt and kefir cultures carry microbial beta-galactosidase into the gut, which is why fermented dairy is better tolerated than milk by lactase-non-persistent people. But that only handles the lactose in the fermented product itself; it does not give you dose-adjustable enzyme to take with an arbitrary lactose-containing meal, which is the whole point of a lactase capsule. I did not find a peer-reviewed per-100-g beta-galactosidase activity figure for retail yoghurt, so no number is given rather than an estimate.
items.form_caveat: For pancreatin, the caveats are pharmaceutical, not dietary. Dose must be titrated to steatorrhoea, meal fat content and disease severity; the enzymes must be enteric-coated to survive gastric acid; the capsules are taken during the meal, not before or after; and the porcine origin is a real issue for vegetarian, vegan, Muslim and Jewish patients and should be disclosed. Nothing sold as a plant-based or 'vegan pancreatic enzyme' has demonstrated equivalence for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, and treating a diagnosed insufficiency with a supermarket digestive enzyme blend risks continued fat malabsorption, weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. For lactase, the honest framing is that this is a targeted, cheap, low-risk aid rather than a nutrient: the alternative food strategy (hard cheese, live yoghurt, small lactose doses spread through the day) works for many people, and lactase capsules only matter when the meal is unavoidable and the dose is large.
items.bioavailability: Both are enzymes, so 'bioavailability' means surviving intact and active to the site of action rather than being absorbed. Lactase works in the lumen of the upper small intestine and is itself digested, so the timing relative to the lactose load determines the effect. Pancreatic lipase is irreversibly denatured below about pH 4, which is why uncoated pancreatin is largely wasted and why the field has moved to pH-sensitive enteric microspheres, and why an emerging approach is adding bicarbonate to raise local pH around the pancreatin. Coadministered acid suppression is sometimes needed to make the enzymes work at all. None of this can be replicated by eating anything.

items.availability_note: The active ingredients come either from plant parts nobody eats or from industrial fermentation. Commercial bromelain is extracted from pineapple stem and basal stem, not from the flesh: measured activity is 2,909 GDU/g in basal stems, 1,179 GDU/g in peels and 694 GDU/g in cores, while crowns had activity below the detection limit (Foods 2024;13(4):589, DOI 10.3390/foods13040589). Papain is a cysteine endopeptidase complex obtained from the latex of unripe Carica papaya, again not the ripe flesh that is eaten; multiple EFSA food-enzyme opinions describe exactly this source and note that dietary exposure from its use as a processing aid is of the same order as, or up to one order of magnitude above, the intake of the corresponding fraction from unripe papaya latex (for example EFSA Journal 2026, DOI 10.2903/j.efsa.2026.9950). The amylase, protease, lipase and lactase components of these blends are Aspergillus or yeast fermentation products with no dietary presence. USDA does record the edible fruits (pineapple raw, FDC 169124; papaya raw, FDC 169926), but no proteolytic activity value for the eaten flesh appeared in the sources found, so no figure is given for it.
items.dose_gap: Bromelain supplements are dosed by activity, typically 500-2,000 mg of a preparation standardised to around 2,400 GDU/g, giving roughly 1,200-4,800 GDU per dose. At the measured activities above, that is equivalent to about 0.4-1.7 g of basal stem extract or about 1-4 g of peel extract, and neither the basal stem nor the peel is eaten. Expressed against food you would actually put in your mouth, the answer is that it cannot be done: the crown has no detectable activity, the core (694 GDU/g) is usually discarded, and no sourced activity figure exists for the ripe flesh, which is the only part normally eaten. For papain the same logic applies with an added twist, since the source material is the latex of the unripe fruit, which is irritant and is not food. For the fungal amylase, protease and lipase components there is no food source at all. Any expectation that eating fresh pineapple or papaya delivers a supplement-equivalent enzyme dose is unsupported.
items.form_caveat: The whole food is safe and the concentrate is not always. Fresh pineapple and papaya are ordinary fruit; concentrated bromelain has anticoagulant and antiplatelet activity and interacts with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs, and papain and chymopapain are recognised respiratory and contact allergens, which EFSA flags in its allergenicity assessments of the food enzyme. The matrix also destroys the premise: these are proteins, so heat and gastric acid inactivate them. Canned and cooked pineapple has no meaningful proteolytic activity left, which is why canned pineapple does not stop gelatin setting while fresh pineapple does, and any orally swallowed enzyme without enteric protection is exposed to pepsin and pH 2 before reaching the small intestine. The most important caveat is scope: these blends are not equivalent to pancreatic enzyme replacement and must not be substituted for it in diagnosed pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, where the requirement is 40,000-50,000 lipase units per meal in an enteric-coated porcine preparation (DOI 10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103880). Nor is the plant-derived lactase in a blend interchangeable with a dose-standardised lactase product.
items.bioavailability: Enzymes are not absorbed and do not need to be; they act in the lumen, so what matters is surviving to the right pH and place. Stem bromelain and fruit bromelain differ even in isoelectric point (pI 9.5 versus 4.6, DOI 10.3390/foods13040589), which is why extraction pH determines which enzyme you actually get and why 'bromelain' on a label does not identify a single molecule. Activity, not milligrams, is the meaningful unit, and GDU, CDU, FIP and USP units are not interconvertible, so a milligram figure on a bottle says almost nothing about what it will do. Both bromelain and papain are irreversibly denatured by cooking and largely by gastric acid unless enterically protected, so an uncoated capsule and a bowl of fresh pineapple share the same fundamental delivery problem.
