misclassifications: 'Lactase and pancreatic enzymes' is classified SYNTHETIC but bundles two products with different availability, and the SYNTHETIC label contradicts the entry's own text. Its dose_gap concedes a real dietary route for lactase activity: live yoghurt and kefir carry microbial beta-galactosidase into the gut, which is why lactase-non-persistent people tolerate fermented dairy. Pancreatin is correctly SYNTHETIC (porcine gland extract, no realistic food route). Lactase should be split into its own entry at PARTIAL or TRACE, with the fermented-dairy route stated in the availability field rather than buried in the gap narrative.

'Prebiotics: inulin, FOS, GOS' is classified RICH as a single item while its own availability_note says the beta-GOS used in trials 'has no meaningful presence in ordinary food'. A compound the entry itself identifies as manufactured by transgalactosylation of lactose is being carried under a RICH heading by association with inulin. GOS needs a separate SYNTHETIC entry; inulin and FOS can stay RICH.

'Generic multi-strain probiotic blends' RICH and 'Probiotics, named strain only' SYNTHETIC take opposite positions on what the deliverable is, inside the same group. The named-strain entry states that a CFU comparison 'is meaningless for a strain-specific claim'; the blends entry then grades RICH on exactly that CFU comparison. The RICH grade only survives by redefining the deliverable as 'any live lactic acid bacteria'. Label it explicitly as a redefined endpoint, or grade it PARTIAL, because a reader scanning availability fields will read RICH as 'food replaces this'.

'Over-the-counter digestive enzyme blends' NOT_FOOD is too strong for the plant proteases, and the entry's own form_caveat relies on the opposite fact. Fruit bromelain is present in edible pineapple flesh and juice with real proteolytic activity, which is precisely why fresh pineapple stops gelatin setting and canned does not. Papain also occurs in unripe papaya flesh, not only in latex. The fungal amylase, protease, lipase and lactase components are genuinely NOT_FOOD. This item is a bundle of two different availabilities and the plant-protease half should be TRACE or PARTIAL. Separately, the statement that no proteolytic activity figure exists for the eaten flesh is a sourcing gap in this submission, not an absence in the literature.

Psyllium is correctly RICH, but the availability_note's claim that oats, barley and legumes supply 'the same class of viscous soluble fibre' is contradicted twice by the entry's own content. Its data show legume soluble fibre at 0.41-1.36 g/100 g, and its bioavailability field says legume soluble fibre is largely fermented proximally and 'behave[s] quite differently at the same gram intake'. Beta-glucan is also not psyllium's arabinoxylan. Narrow the claim to oat and barley beta-glucan for viscosity, and drop legumes from the same-class list.

'Wheat bran and insoluble fibre supplements for IBS' is graded RICH on wheat products alone, yet the title covers insoluble-fibre supplements generally. The other common insoluble-fibre supplement bases (powdered cellulose, corn bran, rice bran) get no food comparators, so the RICH grade is only demonstrated for the wheat-bran case.

B. infantis 35624 is graded SYNTHETIC, which is right for availability, but the availability_note calls it 'propagated industrially from a proprietary strain bank' while also correctly stating it was isolated from human ileal mucosa. A reader may take SYNTHETIC to mean chemically synthesised. Worth a one-line note that SYNTHETIC here means 'no dietary source', not 'artificial molecule', since the same code is applied to lactase and pancreatin, which are genuinely manufactured.
missing_foods: Ground flaxseed/linseed and chia seed. Both are ordinary foods with roughly 27-34 g total dietary fibre per 100 g and a large viscous mucilage fraction. They are the closest dietary analogues to psyllium's gel and are the glaring omission from a viscous-soluble-fibre entry that instead fills its food list with legumes whose soluble fibre is under 1.4 g/100 g.

Konjac glucomannan (shirataki noodles, konjac flour), the highest-viscosity food fibre available, and guar/partially hydrolysed guar gum. Both are sold as foods and both are viscous and poorly fermented, which is the property the psyllium entry says matters.

Pectin-rich fruit and vegetables for soluble fibre: passion fruit, avocado, Brussels sprouts, oranges, pears. Omitting these leaves the impression that only oats, barley and legumes supply soluble fibre.

Corn bran, crude, at 79 g dietary fibre per 100 g, the top-ranked fibre food in USDA and nearly double wheat bran. Its omission is what allows the false claim that wheat bran is 'one of the most fibre-dense foods in any composition table'. Rice bran (about 21 g/100 g) and rye bran are also absent.

Extruded all-bran type cereals (about 29-30 g fibre/100 g) and rye crispbread, both far more fibre-dense per serving than the bran flakes at 16.9 g/100 g that were chosen as the ready-to-eat comparator.

Globe artichoke (Cynara scolymus) and shallots, both in the top fructan group of Muir et al. 2007 (the paper the submission itself cites for the 1.2-17.4 g/100 g range), and salsify, which the cited Nutrition Bulletin paper names as inulin-rich in the very sentence the garlic figure was taken from. All three were omitted while asparagus and banana, at trace levels, were given full entries.

Dandelion root and greens, burdock root, and yacon: recognised high-inulin foods, and dandelion greens are eaten as a vegetable in a way chicory root is not, which answers the entry's own objection that chicory is not a dietary route.

Rye and rye bran. Rye is a higher-fructan cereal than wheat and a substantial habitual contributor in northern European diets, yet only wheat bread and wheat flour appear. Dried onion and garlic powder are also omitted despite being concentrated fructan sources used in ordinary cooking.

Vital wheat gluten/seitan for glutamine: about 75 g protein per 100 g with glutamate around 35% of gluten protein, so roughly 25-30 g glutamic acid per 100 g. It is the densest ordinary food source of the Glu+Gln pool by a wide margin, three to four times parmesan, and its omission is what produced the incorrect 'parmesan is the densest ordinary food source' claim. Soy protein isolate, whey and casein concentrates, dried spirulina and peanuts are also missing.

Kiwifruit for the digestive-enzyme entry. Actinidin is a cysteine protease present in ordinary edible ripe green kiwifruit, with human data: a crossover study in healthy older adults compared green kiwifruit (actinidin-containing) against gold kiwifruit (actinidin-free) with beef meals to test gastric protein digestion, and in vitro work shows enhanced breakdown of multiple food proteins at gastric pH. This is the one genuine food route for a swallowed protease and it directly undercuts the NOT_FOOD grade.

Other dietary enzyme sources omitted: ginger (zingibain), fig latex (ficin), malted barley (diastatic amylase), and raw honey (diastase). None replace pancreatin, but they are real dietary enzyme sources and belong in a NOT_FOOD justification.

Natto for the fermented-food entry. The submission flags its own gap, which is honest, but Bacillus subtilis var. natto viable counts of roughly 10^8-10^9 CFU/g are documented in the natto literature. Also missing: water kefir, kombucha, brine-fermented (non-pasteurised) pickles, kvass, skyr, traditional buttermilk, and young raw-milk cheeses.
dose_gap_errors: Garlic, prebiotics entry: 'about 30 cloves of garlic' to reach 5 g of fructan. Wrong by 3x, and internally contradictory. The entry's own food row states 1 clove (3 g) supplies about 0.5 g inulin and is '10% of a 5 g/day supplement dose', which gives 10 cloves. Recomputed on the entry's own 15.6-16.7 g/100 g: 5/0.167 to 5/0.156 = 29.9-32.1 g of garlic, i.e. 10.0-10.7 cloves. Corrected figure: about 10 cloves. Using the correct garlic value of 9-16 g/100 g, it is roughly 10-19 cloves, still not 30.

Natto, glutamine entry: '865 g of natto' for 15 g of Glu+Gln. Wrong by 1.9x. At 3.337 g/100 g, 15/0.03337 = 449.5 g. Corrected figure: about 450 g. (865 g would only be right if natto were 1.73 g/100 g.) This error is one-directional in the argument's favour, since it makes the food route look harder than it is.

Bran flakes, wheat bran entry: the 10 g/day trial dose of bran is 'about 3 heaped tablespoons of plain wheat bran, or roughly 2 servings of bran flakes'. The two halves are matched to different targets. 10 g of crude bran contains 4.28 g of fibre; one 29 g serving of bran flakes contains 4.90 g. So the fibre-matched answer is 4.28/4.90 = 0.87, i.e. roughly 1 serving, not 2. Two servings supply 9.8 g of fibre, which is more than double the fibre in the trial dose. Corrected figure: about 1 serving of bran flakes.

Oats for beta-glucan, psyllium entry: '3 g/day of oat or barley beta-glucan ... about 40-50 g of dry oats at 6-8% w/w'. The arithmetic is internally right (3/0.08 to 3/0.06 = 38-50 g) but the 6-8% input is oat-bran-level, not whole-oat-level, and the cited source contains no grain beta-glucan percentages at all. At the typical 4-4.5% for rolled oats, 3/0.045 to 3/0.04 = 67-75 g. Corrected figure: about 67-75 g of dry oats, or 40-55 g of oat bran. The barley half (75 g at 4%) checks out.

Asparagus, prebiotics entry: 'about 5 kg of raw asparagus' for 5 g of fructan. Arithmetically correct at the 0.1 g/100 g fresh figure used (5/0.001 = 5,000 g), but that figure is a dry-matter conversion at odds with datasets giving up to about 0.5 g/100 g fresh, where the answer becomes 1,000 g. Corrected figure: roughly 1-5 kg, stated as a range. The 'two orders of magnitude' claim for asparagus does not survive the upper end.

Whole-wheat bread, wheat bran entry: 3.8 g of fibre per 2 slices and 13% of the reference intake, both resting on an unconfirmed 32 g slice. At the 28 g slice USDA legacy commonly gives for this record, 2 slices = 56 g = 3.36 g of fibre and 11% of the 30 g reference intake. Corrected figures: 3.4 g and 11%, pending confirmation of the slice weight.

Habitual glutamine baseline, glutamine entry: 'an ordinary diet supplying 80-100 g of protein already delivers on the order of 8-12 g of glutamine. So the supplement roughly doubles habitual glutamine intake'. At glutamine's 4-8% share of food protein, 90 g of protein gives 3.6-7.2 g, and habitual intake is conventionally 3-6 g/day. Corrected figure: about 4-7 g/day, so a 15 g/day supplement is a three- to four-fold increase, not a doubling. This changes the entry's conclusion from 'small gap' to 'moderate gap'.

Kidney beans, psyllium entry: 'about 500 g (3 cups) of canned kidney beans'. The gram figure is right (6.7/0.0136 = 493 g) but 3 cups at the entry's own 177 g/cup is 531 g. Corrected figure: about 2.8 cups. Minor, but the parenthetical overshoots the gram target it is meant to restate.

Tempeh, generic-blend entry: 'up to 10^11 at the top of the range' per 100 g portion and 'roughly 0.1-100x a typical 1-10 billion CFU/day label dose'. The arithmetic follows from a 9 log CFU/g ceiling that could not be found in the cited review, which supports 7.01 log for laboratory-made tempeh and 81% of retail samples above 10^7 CFU/g. Until the 9 log figure is sourced, the defensible per-100 g figure is about 1x10^9 CFU, i.e. roughly 0.1-1x a label dose.
verdict.net_assessment: This is a strong, unusually well-sourced submission. Every one of the 17 citations I could test resolved to a real paper on the right subject: all nine PMIDs (19713235, 16863564, 30108163, 20497775, 7588500, 17625872, 30197628, 40808333, 8777017) verified with matching journal, year, volume and pages, and all eight tested DOIs resolved, including the two 2026 papers that looked like the most likely fabrications (10.3390/foods15101616 is a real kefir fermentation study, PMID 42195820; 10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103880 is a real pancreatic exocrine insufficiency review, PMID 42011215). Nothing was invented. The verbatim transcription is also good: the Ferjancic fructan values, the Rezac fermented-food counts including the kimchi 7.14-9.23 log range and the tempeh 81%-above-10^7 figure, the kefir 8.40/8.00 log counts, the Stevenson 70/24/6 NSP split, the Bijkerk doses and dropout narrative, and the Bonnema tolerance thresholds all check out word for word. The USDA per-100 g values I could reach (wheat bran 42.8, oat bran 15.4, barley 3.8, whole-wheat bread 6.0, chicory root 1.5, cod 3.4, natto 3.3) were all correct, and the chicory-root point (20 g inulin against a USDA record of 1.5 g total fibre) is a genuinely good catch that holds up. The per-portion arithmetic is almost entirely clean: of roughly 40 per-portion and percentage calculations I re-ran, all but one were correct to the stated precision. The failures cluster in two places. First, three source misreadings, two of them consequential: the garlic figure of 15.6-16.7 g/100 g is a range the cited paper gives across four foods (Jerusalem artichoke, chicory root, salsify, garlic), not garlic's own value of about 9-16 g/100 g; the claim that bread and flour were the largest habitual fructan contributor is contradicted by the cited survey, where onion led at 0.72 g/day against white flour's 0.41 g/day; and the 6-8% oat beta-glucan figure is attributed to a paper that is a packaged-product label audit and contains no grain composition data at all. Second, four dose-gap numbers that do not survive recomputation: garlic 30 cloves should be 10 (and contradicts the submission's own food row), natto 865 g should be 450 g, bran flakes 2 servings should be 1, and 40-50 g of dry oats for 3 g beta-glucan should be 67-75 g. Two superlatives are false in a way that also reveals the omissions: wheat bran is not among the most fibre-dense foods (corn bran is 79 g/100 g) and parmesan is not the densest ordinary source of the Glu+Gln pool (vital wheat gluten is roughly 25-30 g/100 g). The habitual glutamine baseline of 8-12 g/day is roughly double the accepted 3-6 g/day, which is load-bearing because it converts a three- to four-fold supplement increase into a claimed doubling and drives the entry's headline conclusion. On classification, the substantive problem is bundling: three items each pair two things with different availability under one grade (lactase with pancreatin, GOS with inulin and FOS, plant proteases with fungal enzymes), and in the lactase case the SYNTHETIC grade is contradicted by the entry's own concession that live yoghurt and kefir carry microbial beta-galactosidase. The RICH grade on generic probiotic blends is defensible only under a redefined endpoint that the named-strain entry in the same group explicitly calls meaningless. The most notable food omissions are flaxseed and chia from a viscous-fibre entry, corn bran from an insoluble-fibre entry, globe artichoke and salsify from a fructan entry, vital wheat gluten from a glutamine entry, and kiwifruit actinidin from an entry arguing that no ordinary food supplies a digestive protease. The psyllium provenance claim also needs softening: FDC 1742558 is a branded manufacturer-label record for NOW Psyllium Husk Powder whose own total-fibre field reads 0 g, so the 78 g total is the submitter's arithmetic, not a USDA analysed value. On balance: the reasoning and the qualitative form and bioavailability caveats are the best part of this submission and mostly survive scrutiny; the corrections needed are four arithmetic fixes, three re-citations, two deleted superlatives, one baseline revision, and the splitting of three bundled availability grades.

items.availability_note: Turmeric is a genuine culinary food (the dried, ground rhizome of Curcuma longa, USDA FoodData Central FDC 172231), so the compound is present in ordinary diets. It is classified TRACE rather than RICH because the curcuminoid concentration is about 3% of the powder by weight, so realistic culinary portions deliver roughly 3 to 10 percent of a standard 1,000 mg curcuminoid supplement dose. Turmeric is also the only meaningful food source; curry powder is 5 to 60 times weaker again.

items.dose_gap: A 1,000 mg curcuminoid capsule equals about 21 to 32 g of turmeric powder every day: 32 g if you count curcumin only at 3.14% w/w, about 21 g if you count all three curcuminoids at roughly 4.7%. That is 7 to 11 level teaspoons, close to a third of a standard supermarket spice jar per day, and inedible in food. For scale, a generous curry portion carries 1 to 2 g of turmeric, or 30 to 60 mg of curcumin, and a South Asian diet at the commonly quoted 2 to 2.5 g turmeric per day yields only 63 to 79 mg of curcumin (arithmetic from the 3.14% figure). So the supplement dose is roughly 15 to 30 times a heavy dietary intake and cannot be reached by eating.
items.form_caveat: This is the single most important form gap in the whole list. Culinary turmeric has no liver-injury signal; 95% curcuminoid extracts, especially those boosted with piperine or reformulated as phytosomes, micelles or nanoparticles, are now a leading identified botanical cause of drug-induced liver injury in US and Australian case series, with a reported HLA-B*35:01 association. The EFSA/JECFA acceptable daily intake for curcumin (E 100) is 3 mg/kg body weight per day, i.e. 210 mg for a 70 kg adult: one teaspoon of turmeric in food (94 mg curcumin) sits below it, while a single 1,000 mg curcuminoid capsule is about five times over it. Concentrated extracts also inhibit CYP3A4 and UGT enzymes and interact with anticoagulants, which food-level turmeric does not. Second caveat cutting the other way: scaling up culinary turmeric is not a safe workaround either, because turmeric powder in some supply chains has been adulterated with lead chromate for colour (well documented in Bangladeshi turmeric), and gram-level daily dosing of spice-grade powder magnifies that exposure.
items.bioavailability: Curcumin is close to a worst case for oral absorption: poor solubility, extensive intestinal and hepatic glucuronidation and sulfation, and rapid biliary excretion leave systemic exposure at or below detection limits after dietary amounts. Co-administered piperine 20 mg raised curcumin bioavailability roughly 20-fold in humans (Shoba et al. 1998, PMID 9619120), and modern phytosome, micellar and nanoparticle formulations claim 10 to 185-fold increases over unformulated powder. The practical consequence is that milligram equivalence between spice and supplement is misleading in both directions: a formulated 500 mg extract can deliver more systemic curcumin than 30 g of raw powder, and the traditional practice of blooming turmeric in hot oil with black pepper is a crude version of the same trick.

items.availability_note: Green tea, matcha, white tea and oolong all deliver EGCG in tens to hundreds of milligrams per cup. This is the one group in this set where an ordinary beverage genuinely reaches the doses used in trials: EFSA's own exposure assessment puts the 95th percentile adult intake from green tea infusions at 866 mg EGCG/day, above the 800 mg threshold at which supplements raise transaminases.

items.dose_gap: 800 mg EGCG, the dose at which supplements produce measurable liver enzyme rises, is about 4 to 5 cups of green tea at EFSA's mean brewed concentration of 70.2 mg/100 mL, or 10 to 16 cups of more typically brewed retail tea, or roughly 24 to 53 bowls of matcha at 2 g each. Unlike every other entry here, the gap is genuinely closable: EFSA's own 95th percentile adult tea drinker already takes in 866 mg EGCG/day from infusions, and mean adult intake is 90 to 300 mg/day. The difference that matters is not the milligrams but the vehicle: the tea drinker's 800 mg arrives spread over a day in two to three litres of water, usually with food, while the supplement delivers it as one fasted bolus.
items.form_caveat: State this plainly: the beverage carries no meaningful liver signal, the extract does. EFSA concluded that intake at or above 800 mg EGCG/day taken as a food supplement causes a statistically significant increase in serum transaminases, while catechins from green tea infusion prepared in the traditional way, and reconstituted drinks of equivalent composition, are in general considered safe. Same molecule, different product. Risk concentrates in high-dose, single-bolus, fasted dosing of concentrated extracts, and Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/2340 now prohibits supplements delivering 800 mg or more EGCG per day in the EU. Green tea extract is also the ingredient behind a large share of liver injury cases attributed to weight-loss and fat-burner blends, which is a warning about the extract and not about tea.
items.bioavailability: Systemic bioavailability of EGCG is low, on the order of 0.1 to 1% of an oral dose as the unchanged compound, with heavy glucuronidation, sulfation and methylation plus colonic degradation. The critical modifier is food: fasted dosing raises EGCG Cmax severalfold compared with the same dose taken with a meal, and fasted administration is both the way extracts are typically taken and the condition associated with hepatotoxicity. Milk and food proteins bind catechins and blunt peak levels, so tea with milk is pharmacologically not tea on an empty stomach. Brewing extracts only part of the leaf's EGCG whereas matcha delivers the whole leaf, but note that per gram of leaf, shade-grown matcha is not richer in EGCG than a good sencha, so the popular claim that matcha is a many-fold EGCG upgrade does not hold up in the measured data.

Red wine averages 1.9 mg trans-resveratrol per litre, so the entire classic dietary source contains less resveratrol per litre than a single capsule. Supplement resveratrol is not extracted from grapes at all: it is made synthetically or extracted from Japanese knotweed root (Polygonum cuspidatum), which is not a food.

items.dose_gap: This is the textbook illustration and the numbers are brutal. A 150 mg resveratrol dose equals 79 litres of average red wine (150 mg ÷ 1.9 mg/L), which is about 105 standard 750 mL bottles, or roughly 450 glasses, every day. Even at the highest concentration ever reported in a red wine (14.3 mg/L) it is still 10.5 litres per day. From grapes: 30 kg of table grapes daily. From peanuts: 29 kg of boiled peanuts, or 2.7 tonnes of roasted peanuts. Trials commonly use 150 to 1,000 mg/day and the SRT501 cancer studies used up to 5 g/day, all of it manufactured. There is no dietary route to these doses, and no plausible diet gets past about 5 mg/day.
items.form_caveat: Three separate mismatches. First, the supplement is not a food extract: commercial resveratrol is synthetic or comes from Polygonum cuspidatum root, a non-food plant, so the grape imagery on the label is marketing rather than sourcing. Second, wine's stilbenes are mostly the glucoside trans-piceid, at about three times the aglycone concentration, arriving inside a large mixed polyphenol and ethanol matrix, so wine is not a dilute resveratrol capsule. Third, and decisive: recommending wine as a resveratrol source is a bad recommendation regardless of dose, because ethanol is a Group 1 carcinogen and the alcohol harm arrives at one glass while the resveratrol dose would require a hundred bottles. Separately, high-dose resveratrol (2.5 to 5 g/day) causes diarrhoea and nausea and inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and sulfotransferases, giving it real interaction potential (warfarin, for example) that a glass of wine does not have.
items.bioavailability: Oral resveratrol is well absorbed (about 70% of the dose crosses the enterocyte) but systemic bioavailability of the unchanged aglycone is under 1 to 2% because of near-immediate intestinal and hepatic glucuronidation and sulfation; plasma peaks from dietary quantities sit in the low nanomolar range, while in vitro activity is generally demonstrated at micromolar concentrations. Piceid, the form dominant in grapes and much of wine, must be deglycosylated before absorption, adding another step. Gram doses are needed to reach micromolar plasma levels, which is precisely why the food route is closed.

items.availability_note: Genuinely present at milligram levels in ordinary seafood. Wild sockeye salmon carries 26 to 38 mg per kg of flesh, so a single fillet supplies several milligrams, which is the same order of magnitude as a supplement capsule. This is the strongest food case in this set, although matching a 12 mg daily dose from fish alone still means eating a large salmon portion every single day.

items.dose_gap: A 12 mg daily dose, the most common dose in the clinical literature, equals 315 to 460 g of wild sockeye salmon every day at 26 to 38 mg/kg, or about 550 g using the review's own dietary anchor of 3.6 mg per 165 g portion. From farmed Atlantic salmon it is 1.5 to 2.0 kg per day. From shrimp, 170 g to 1.4 kg depending on preparation. From krill meal, about 320 g. So a single 140 g sockeye fillet already covers roughly a third of a 12 mg dose, and this is the only entry in this set where a normal portion and a capsule are the same order of magnitude. Sustaining 12 mg/day from fish is still unrealistic, and eating 350 to 500 g of oily fish daily would push past standard advice on methylmercury and persistent organic pollutants.
items.form_caveat: Chemical form differs by source. Salmon astaxanthin is largely free or protein-bound; krill and Haematococcus astaxanthin is esterified with fatty acids; and much supplement and feed astaxanthin is synthetic astaxanthin dimethyldisuccinate, a different stereoisomer mixture from the natural 3S,3'S form. This matters for the safety arithmetic: EFSA's acceptable daily intake of 0.2 mg/kg body weight per day (14 mg for a 70 kg adult, replacing the earlier 0.034 mg/kg) was derived from a rat carcinogenicity study on the synthetic material and then applied to the algal form, so a 12 to 24 mg capsule sits at or above the ADI while a salmon fillet does not. A safety review of 87 human studies, including 35 at 12 mg/day or more, found no safety concerns with natural astaxanthin and argues the synthetic-derived ADI should not govern it (Brendler & Williamson, Phytother Res 2019, PMID 31788888, DOI 10.1002/ptr.6514). One honest twist: the astaxanthin in farmed salmon is itself an added feed pigment, so eating farmed salmon for astaxanthin means eating a supplemented animal.
items.bioavailability: Astaxanthin is a lipophilic xanthophyll and absorption depends on fat and micelle formation: uptake from a lipid-based formulation or a fatty meal is severalfold higher than from a dry powder taken fasted, and esterified forms must first be hydrolysed by pancreatic lipase. Overall human bioavailability is low and highly variable (single-digit percentages), which cuts in favour of the food: salmon arrives pre-packaged with its own lipid and a food matrix, so the plasma difference between a 4 mg fillet and a 12 mg dry capsule is smaller than the milligram gap implies.

items.supplement: Saffron, SAMe and other mood botanicals
items.availability_note: This is a deliberately mixed group and the honest answer splits three ways. Saffron is the one true culinary member and is listed under foods below despite the NOT_FOOD label on the group, because its clinical dose is literally a cooking quantity and omitting it would hide the most useful finding here. SAMe is not a dietary component at all: it is synthesised continuously in the body from methionine and ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase, mostly in the liver, there is no meaningful preformed SAMe in food, and commercial SAMe is manufactured by Saccharomyces cerevisiae fermentation and then stabilised as the tosylate disulfate or 1,4-butanedisulfonate salt (so for SAMe alone the correct classification is SYNTHETIC). St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum aerial parts), rhodiola root, ashwagandha root and Griffonia simplicifolia seed, the source of 5-HTP, are plants nobody eats as food in any normal diet; they have no composition-table entry and no portion size because they are not eaten.

foods.per_100g: 100 g of saffron is 3,333 clinical doses of 30 mg. The active apocarotenoids (crocins, picrocrocin, safranal, crocetin) make up as much as 8% of the dry weight; standardised extracts used in trials deliver roughly 3.4 mg of crocins per 30 mg dose
foods.per_portion: 700 mg of saffron, i.e. 23 times the 30 mg dose used in depression RCTs
foods.source: USDA FoodData Central FDC 170934 (Spices, saffron; 1 tbsp = 2.1 g, so 1 tsp = 0.7 g). Trial dose: Akhondzadeh S et al., Crocus sativus L. in the treatment of mild to moderate depression, PMID 15852492 (30 mg/day for 6 weeks, comparable to fluoxetine 20 mg/day on HAM-D)

foods.food: Saffron, culinary pinch as used to season a dish
foods.portion: a generous pinch, about 0.1 g (roughly 20 to 30 threads), seasoning a dish for four. For reference the FDA reference amount customarily consumed for saffron is 0.125 g
foods.per_portion: about 25 mg of saffron per person from a dish for four; 125 mg for a single reference serving
foods.pct_rda_or_dose: 83% of the 30 mg trial dose per serving of the dish; over 400% for one 0.125 g reference serving
foods.source: USDA FoodData Central FDC 170934 (spice entry and reference serving); trial dose PMID 15852492

items.dose_gap: For saffron the gap is essentially zero, which is the finding worth reporting: the 30 mg/day used in the depression RCTs is about 8 to 15 threads, less than a generous culinary pinch, and one teaspoon of saffron in a paella is over twenty doses. Saffron is the rare supplement whose trial dose is sub-culinary; the barrier is cost, not physiology. For SAMe there is no gap to compute because there is no food source: trials use 400 to 1,600 mg/day of a manufactured molecule, while the body's own SAMe turnover (on the order of grams per day) is fed by roughly 1 g/day of dietary methionine from protein foods, which is a different intervention from swallowing SAMe. For the remaining botanicals (St John's wort typically 300 mg three times daily of a 0.3% hypericin extract, rhodiola 200 to 600 mg, ashwagandha 300 to 600 mg root extract, 5-HTP 100 to 300 mg) the food gap is undefined because the source plants are not foods at any quantity.
items.form_caveat: Saffron is the mildest food-versus-extract case in this whole set, since trials use either powdered stigma or a hydroalcoholic extract standardised to crocins and safranal, so kitchen saffron is close to the trial material. The caveat is at the top end: saffron is toxic at gram doses, with roughly 5 g reported as a toxic dose and 12 to 20 g as potentially lethal, and it is a traditional abortifacient, so scaling from a pinch to a spoonful is genuinely hazardous. Standardised extracts also concentrate crocins, so milligram-for-milligram an extract is not the spice. For the rest of the group the form gap is total: St John's wort is a potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inducer that has caused transplant rejection, contraceptive failure and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; ashwagandha root extracts have accumulated a documented cluster of hepatotoxicity case reports, including in regulatory reviews, while traditional use was of small amounts of root powder in milk as medicine and never as a food; purified 5-HTP bypasses the rate-limiting tryptophan hydroxylase step that normally regulates serotonin synthesis, which is exactly why it carries serotonin syndrome risk with serotonergic drugs and why no food behaves like it.
items.bioavailability: Saffron's crocins are poorly absorbed intact and are hydrolysed in the gut to crocetin, which is what appears in plasma; safranal is volatile and is partly lost in long simmering, so a slow-cooked dish delivers a different apocarotenoid profile than a capsule taken cold, and blooming saffron in warm liquid before adding it is the culinary analogue of extraction. SAMe is chemically unstable and is degraded in gastric acid unless enterically coated, and oral bioavailability is only about 1% because of extensive first-pass metabolism, which is why oral doses are 400 to 1,600 mg while parenteral doses are far smaller. The classic bad recommendation in this space is 'eat turkey or eggs for 5-HTP': food supplies tryptophan, not 5-HTP, and dietary tryptophan competes with the other large neutral amino acids in the same protein meal for LAT1 transport across the blood-brain barrier, so a high-protein meal can lower rather than raise brain tryptophan availability. Food is a poor delivery route for this entire group.

items.availability_note: Mixed category, classified TRACE because that is the dominant pattern, with important exceptions in both directions. Caffeine is the one component with a genuinely RICH food source (coffee, tea) and the only one with a consistent thermogenic effect. Raspberry ketone is present in raspberries at 0.001 to 4.3 mg/kg, thousands of times below the 100 to 1,400 mg/day sold, the archetypal TRACE case. Garcinia gummi-gutta rind (Malabar tamarind, kodampuli or kudam puli) is a real culinary souring agent in Kerala and parts of Southeast Asia, used in fish curry and asam laksa in place of tamarind or lime, so it does have a food identity, and at about 30% hydroxycitric acid it is the one fat-burner botanical whose culinary use actually delivers supplement-scale amounts of its active compound. Green coffee extract's chlorogenic acids come from unroasted beans, which nobody eats. Bitter orange peel (p-synephrine), yohimbe bark and Coleus forskohlii root are NOT_FOOD, and pure synthetic components such as higenamine or DMAA appear in these blends with no food origin at all.

items.dose_gap: Component by component. Raspberry ketone: 100 mg, the smallest common dose, is about 23 kg of fresh raspberries at the highest natural concentration of 4.3 mg/kg, and the 1,400 mg top dose is roughly 326 kg; the authors of the safety review note that even the lowest recommended supplement dose is about 56 times the threshold of toxicological concern for its structural class. Not reachable by eating, by three orders of magnitude. Green coffee: extracts standardised to 45 to 50% chlorogenic acids at 400 to 1,600 mg/day supply roughly 200 to 800 mg CGA, while roasted coffee holds only 0.9 to 1.9 g CGA per 100 g of grounds, so a few cups reach the low end and the concentrated dose exists only because green beans are inedible. Caffeine is the exception that is easy to reach: 200 mg is four to five cups of filter coffee or two espressos. Garcinia is the striking case: at 30% HCA, 3 g of dried rind carries about 900 mg HCA, equal to the top of the supplement range, so the culinary plant genuinely delivers the active compound.
items.form_caveat: The governing pattern in this category is that the food is safe and the concentrate is not, and Garcinia is the cleanest illustration. Centuries of culinary use of the dried rind as a souring agent in South and Southeast Asian cooking carries no liver-injury signal, while concentrated HCA supplements have produced 34 published hepatotoxicity case reports including nine liver transplants and one death, plus more than 200 adverse events of liver injury and 93 international case reports reviewed by Health Canada. The injury looks idiosyncratic rather than dose-dependent, with a proposed HLA-B*35:01 association, so the traditional culinary use carrying none of the extract harm is not a claim that the dose is lower; it is that the concentrated extract product behaves differently from the pot of curry. The same shape repeats across the category: green tea extract in fat-burner blends versus drinking tea (see that entry), bitter orange p-synephrine stacked with caffeine and linked to cardiovascular events versus orange peel in marmalade, yohimbe bark extract versus nothing edible at all, and raspberry ketone at food flavouring levels of milligrams per kilogram versus 100 to 1,400 mg/day capsules with essentially no human toxicology. Add the labelling problem: proprietary blends routinely under-declare caffeine and stack multiple stimulants, so the food comparison is the only reliable one available, which is to count your caffeine in cups and treat the rest of the label as unquantified.
items.bioavailability: Caffeine is the outlier and the reason these blends do anything: it is almost completely absorbed, peaks in 30 to 60 minutes, and behaves much the same from coffee as from a tablet, with coffee's chlorogenic acids only modestly slowing absorption. Chlorogenic acids themselves are poorly bioavailable, with roughly a third absorbed in the small intestine and the remainder extensively metabolised by colonic microbiota into hydroxycinnamic acid derivatives, so the milligrams of CGA printed on a green coffee label map badly onto systemic exposure. Raspberry ketone is rapidly conjugated and cleared, which is one reason the human evidence for it is close to non-existent. Hydroxycitric acid absorption from Garcinia is incomplete and depends on the salt form (calcium, potassium or magnesium salts differ in solubility), which helps explain why the pooled human weight-loss effect is at best around 0.9 kg over placebo despite doses that a bowl of Kerala fish curry could match.

misclassifications: SAFFRON GROUP LABELLED NOT_FOOD - the clearest error in the submission. Saffron is a supermarket spice with USDA composition and portion entries, and the submission's own text concedes the clinical dose is "literally a cooking quantity" and lists it under foods anyway. A 0.1 g culinary pinch serving four delivers about 25 mg per person against a 30 mg trial dose, and one teaspoon is 23 doses. This is the only entry in the whole set with a dose gap at or below zero, and it is filed under the label that means the compound cannot be obtained from food. Correct classification for saffron is RICH. The group should be split: saffron RICH, SAMe SYNTHETIC, St John's wort / rhodiola root / ashwagandha / Griffonia NOT_FOOD.

BITTER ORANGE p-SYNEPHRINE CLASSIFIED NOT_FOOD - wrong, and it is the sharpest miss because the food source reaches the supplement dose. Citrus juices naturally carry "up to 25-40 mg p-synephrine per quarter liter", and Seville orange juice was measured at ~57 mcg/mL, about 13 mg per 8 oz serving. Supplement studies used 5.5-80 mg per dose, with 10-53 mg/day in the pooled overweight/obese subjects. So a single glass of citrus juice sits squarely inside the supplement dose range. The submission's own framing ("bitter orange p-synephrine ... versus orange peel in marmalade") treats the food source as trivial when it is dose-equivalent. Reclassify as RICH, or at minimum give it a food entry with numbers. Source: Stohs SJ et al., A review of the human clinical studies involving Citrus aurantium and p-synephrine, Int J Med Sci 2012, PMC3444973.

CURCUMIN CLASSIFIED TRACE - inconsistent with the submission's own numbers and with regulatory benchmarks. TRACE should mean the compound is barely present. A level teaspoon of turmeric carries 94 mg of curcumin, which is 45% of the JECFA/EFSA ADI of 210 mg for a 70 kg adult. A food that delivers nearly half a regulatory ADI in one teaspoon is not a trace source; it is a rich source measured against a supplement dose that itself sits about five times over the ADI. The submission has silently redefined TRACE as "low relative to a 1,000 mg capsule", which is a different axis from every other entry. Recommend RICH with the dose gap stated separately, or add an explicit intermediate tier.

WEIGHT-LOSS BLENDS CLASSIFIED TRACE - self-contradicted within the same record. The submission simultaneously states that caffeine has "a genuinely RICH food source", that Garcinia rind "does have a food identity" and "genuinely delivers the active compound" at supplement scale, and that other components are NOT_FOOD or purely synthetic. Four different availability classes are being flattened into one label chosen because TRACE is "the dominant pattern". Split the entry per component, or use a MIXED label; the current label makes caffeine, the one thing in the category that reliably works and is trivially available from food, invisible.

ANTARCTIC KRILL LISTED AS A FOOD ENTRY - krill meal is a dried feed and aquaculture ingredient, not a 100 g human portion, and the entry conflates it with "frozen whole krill" to reach 3.7 mg per 100 g. Either drop it or restate it on a wet-weight basis (roughly 0.8-1.0 mg/100 g) with a realistic food vehicle such as krill oil capsules or the whole-krill products actually sold for consumption.

JAPANESE KNOTWEED DESCRIBED AS "NOT A FOOD" - overstated. Polygonum cuspidatum young shoots are eaten as a spring vegetable in Japan (itadori) and are a commonly foraged edible in the UK and North America, and itadori tea is a traditional beverage made from the same plant. The submission's argument (that supplement resveratrol is not grape-derived) survives without this claim, so soften it to "not a food in Western diets and not a composition-table food" rather than "not a food".

SAMe CLASSIFIED SYNTHETIC - broadly correct and I would keep it, with one wording fix. There is no meaningful preformed dietary SAMe, no composition-table entry, and the submission is right that the body makes it from methionine and ATP. But commercial SAMe is produced by Saccharomyces cerevisiae fermentation, which the submission itself states, so it is biosynthetic rather than chemically synthetic. If SYNTHETIC in this schema means "no dietary source", the label holds; if it means "chemically manufactured", it does not fit a fermentation product.
missing_foods: Peanut skins (redskin peanut testa) - the richest resveratrol fraction of the peanut by a wide margin and genuinely eaten on redskin, boiled and Spanish peanuts. The submission lists three peanut forms and omits the one part that concentrates the stilbene, which weakens the peanut dose-gap numbers: the roasted-kernel figure of 0.055 ug/g is explicitly for peanuts without seed coats.

Red and purple grape juice - the obvious non-alcoholic member of the resveratrol group. Its omission is conspicuous given the submission's (correct) argument that recommending wine as a resveratrol source is a bad recommendation because ethanol is a Group 1 carcinogen. Grape juice is the alternative that argument implies, and it is left out.

Muscadine grapes, bilberries, blueberries, cranberries, pistachios and cocoa - all documented dietary stilbene sources. The resveratrol entry mentions "a few berries" in the availability note but gives no berry a food row, so the "about 5 mg/day" dietary ceiling is asserted rather than built from entries.

Salmon roe (ikura/sujiko) - a well-known astaxanthin-dense food eaten in normal portions, absent from an entry list that otherwise covers six seafoods. Also missing: wild chinook/king, pink and chum salmon, Arctic char, and red sea bream (tai), all standard astaxanthin food sources in the same literature the entry already cites.

Shell-on crustaceans eaten whole - crayfish, small crab, and head-on/shell-on prawns. The entry notes that astaxanthin concentrates in shell and head and then prices the portion on peeled meat, without ever listing the preparation where the pigment actually is.

Fresh turmeric rhizome - the whole-food form of the only meaningful curcumin source, and increasingly sold in UK/US supermarkets. Given that the entry hinges on turmeric being "a genuine culinary food", omitting the unprocessed rhizome (and prepared mustard and turmeric-coloured pickles, where turmeric is the colourant) leaves the food case thinner than it needs to be.

Oolong tea and gunpowder green tea - the availability note explicitly claims oolong delivers EGCG "in tens to hundreds of milligrams per cup" but no oolong row exists. Gunpowder green tea was the highest-EGCG product measured in the independent commercial survey at 70.22 mg/g, above both matcha grades, and is missing. Bottled/RTD green tea is also absent, which matters because it is the commercially dominant form and is far weaker than any entry listed.

Seville orange juice and bitter orange marmalade - the food sources of p-synephrine, named dismissively in the form_caveat but given no entry or number, which is what allowed the NOT_FOOD classification to stand.

Guarana, yerba mate, cocoa and dark chocolate, and energy drinks - the caffeine dose-gap paragraph rests on coffee and green tea only, while guarana powder is itself an ingredient in the very blends under discussion and is in the same cited caffeine table.
dose_gap_errors: CURCUMIN, supplement-to-diet multiple: "the supplement dose is roughly 15 to 30 times a heavy dietary intake" does not follow from the submission's own figures. A heavy South Asian intake is given as 2 to 2.5 g turmeric = 63 to 79 mg curcumin. 1,000/79 = 12.7 and 1,000/63 = 15.9. CORRECTED: about 13 to 16 times, not 15 to 30. The top of the claimed range is roughly double the truth. On a total-curcuminoid basis (2-2.5 g at ~4.7% = 94-118 mg) the multiple falls further, to about 8.5 to 11 times.

MATCHA, per-bowl EGCG and bowls-per-dose: both figures are wrong because the underlying concentration is 3 to 7 times too low. CORRECTED: a 2 g bowl supplies about 101 to 113 mg EGCG (at 50.53-56.57 mg/g measured by HPLC in 15 commercial products), which is 13 to 14% of an 800 mg dose, not 2 to 7%. And 800 mg is about 7 to 8 bowls of matcha, not "roughly 24 to 53 bowls". The qualitative conclusion in the bioavailability field (that matcha is not a many-fold EGCG upgrade on a good sencha) is actually supported by the corrected data, which found no statistically significant EGCG difference across tea types, so fixing the numbers strengthens rather than weakens the argument.

MATCHA, internal percentage mismatch: the stated 15 to 34 mg per bowl is 1.9 to 4.2% of 800 mg, but the pct field says "2 to 7%". The 7% is silently borrowed from the unverified higher NMR figure that appears only in a parenthesis. Even on its own numbers the row does not reconcile.

ASTAXANTHIN, ADI threshold: "a 12 to 24 mg capsule sits at or above the ADI" is arithmetically false at the low end. The EFSA ADI of 0.2 mg/kg bw/day gives 14 mg for a 70 kg adult. 12 mg is 86% of the ADI, i.e. below it. CORRECTED: only doses of about 14 mg and above exceed the ADI, so the 12 mg dose used in most of the clinical literature sits just under it while a 24 mg dose is about 1.7 times over. This matters because the 12 mg figure is the anchor for the entire entry.

ASTAXANTHIN, krill portion and dose gap: 3.7 mg per 100 g, "31% of a 12 mg dose" and "from krill meal, about 320 g" all apply a dried-meal dry-weight concentration (37.41 mg/kg) to a wet food portion. CORRECTED on a wet-weight basis (krill is roughly 78-80% water): about 0.8 to 1.0 mg per 100 g of whole krill, i.e. 7 to 8% of a 12 mg dose, with roughly 1.2 to 1.5 kg/day needed. The 320 g figure is arithmetically consistent with 37.4 mg/kg but describes 320 g of dried animal feed, not food.

GARCINIA, per-person HCA: "about 900 mg HCA in the pot" is then scored as matching "the top of the 72 to 900 mg HCA range delivered by supplements", comparing a whole-pot figure against a per-person dose. On the submission's own dish-for-four convention used in the saffron entry, CORRECTED: about 225 mg HCA per serving, the middle of the supplement range rather than the top. Two further reductions are ignored: HCA transfers only partially from rind into broth, and the rind is fished out and discarded rather than eaten. Using 30% (the maximum of the 10-30% literature range) compounds the overstatement. The claim that "the culinary plant genuinely delivers the active compound" is defensible in order of magnitude, but not at the top of the supplement range.

GREEN COFFEE, roasting loss: "a roughly six-fold loss on roasting" is only true at one corner of the stated numbers. 5.4 g/100 g green against 0.9-1.9 g/100 g roasted is a 2.8-fold to 6-fold loss. CORRECTED: about 3 to 6-fold. Both endpoints also rest on the misattributed Awwad figures, which report mg/L in solution rather than g/100 g of bean.

SAFFRON, thread count: "the 30 mg/day used in the depression RCTs is about 8 to 15 threads" implies 2 to 3.75 mg per thread, while the next entry's "about 0.1 g (roughly 20 to 30 threads)" implies 3.3 to 5 mg per thread. The two rows cannot both be right. CORRECTED on the submission's own 0.1 g / 20-30 thread basis: 30 mg is about 6 to 9 threads. (Published saffron thread weights of roughly 2 mg would instead give about 15 threads and imply 0.1 g is nearer 50 threads, so the 20-30 thread figure is the likelier error.)

SAFFRON, apocarotenoid fraction: "as much as 8% of the dry weight" and "roughly 3.4 mg of crocins per 30 mg dose" are mutually exclusive in the same sentence, since 3.4/30 = 11.3% crocins alone, above the stated 8% ceiling for all apocarotenoids combined. One figure must be corrected; neither could be verified against a source.

GREEN TEA, EFSA intake anchors: the dose-gap paragraph states mean adult intake as "90 to 300 mg/day" against EFSA's actual 85.98 to 321.21 mg/day, and treats 866 mg/day as the P95 when EFSA's P95 spans 308 to 866.25 mg/day across surveys. CORRECTED: mean 86 to 321 mg/day; P95 308 to 866 mg/day. The claim that "EFSA's own 95th percentile adult tea drinker already takes in 866 mg/day" is the strongest sentence in the entry and it uses the single highest survey value as if it were the general case.

TURMERIC, pseudo-range: the dose gap and the food row both lean on "0.58 to 3.14%", but 3.14% is a mean, not a maximum, so no range with 3.14% as its ceiling can be constructed from the cited paper. The 21-32 g/day and 7-11 teaspoon figures themselves recompute correctly from 3.14% and 4.7%, so the arithmetic survives; the range framing does not.
verdict.net_assessment: Above average for this kind of submission, and unusually honest in prose, but it fails in a specific and repeated way: the qualitative arguments are mostly right while the numbers propping them up are sometimes borrowed from citations that do not contain them. Verification held up well in three places. Every EFSA green tea figure matched exactly (70.2 mg/100 mL from 100 samples in 12 references, 7,116 mg/100 g dry leaf, the 800 mg transaminase conclusion), every Ambati astaxanthin figure matched exactly (sockeye 26-38 mg/kg, Atlantic 6-8, trout 6 and 25, the 165 g/3.6 mg anchor), and the resveratrol entry is the strongest in the set, with the 1.9 +/- 1.7 mg/L wine mean independently corroborated and roughly a dozen unit conversions and dose-gap divisions all recomputing correctly. Tayyem's 3.14%, Bredsdorff's 4.3 mg/kg and 56x TTC, van Breemen's 34 cases and 9 transplants, Shoba's 20-fold, Brendler's 87 studies, the BraCaffT caffeine table and both USDA spice portion weights all check out to the digit. Three findings are serious. First, the matcha row is wrong by 3 to 7-fold and its citation does not contain an EGCG figure at all: Kolackova 2022 reports chlorogenic acid 2,090-2,460 ug/g and catechin 10.2-23.1 ug/g, and independent HPLC of 15 commercial products gives matcha 50.53-56.57 mg EGCG/g, so a bowl is about 101-113 mg and 800 mg is 7-8 bowls, not 24-53. Second, the chlorogenic acid comparison misattributes bean percentages to a paper that reports mg/L in solution, and the green coffee dose gap rests entirely on it. Third, the saffron trial citation is wrong about its own design: PMID 15852492 is placebo-controlled, and the fluoxetine comparison belongs to a different trial. On classification, two labels should not survive review. The saffron group is filed NOT_FOOD while the entry itself demonstrates a dose gap of zero, which is the single most useful finding in the submission and is contradicted by its own label. And bitter orange is called NOT_FOOD when citrus juice carries up to 25-40 mg p-synephrine per quarter litre against supplement doses of 10-53 mg/day, making it dose-equivalent to the capsule. Curcumin at 94 mg per teaspoon, 45% of the JECFA ADI, is also not a trace source on any normal reading, and the krill row applies a dried-feed dry weight to a wet food portion. Nine dose-gap calculations need correcting, most consequentially the curcumin supplement-to-diet multiple (13-16x, not 15-30x) and the astaxanthin ADI threshold (12 mg is below the 14 mg ADI, not at or above it). One framing point worth raising with the author: four of the six entries are not polyphenols. Astaxanthin is a carotenoid, saffron's crocins are apocarotenoids, SAMe is an activated amino acid derivative, and caffeine is an alkaloid, so the group label describes only curcumin, EGCG and resveratrol plus the phenolic raspberry ketone. Recommendation: reject and return for correction of the matcha row, the chlorogenic acid attribution, the saffron trial citation, the two classification errors, and the nine arithmetic items, with page-level citations required for the eleven figures marked UNVERIFIABLE. The structure, the form-versus-food caveats and the bioavailability sections are genuinely good and should be kept.

items.availability_note: NMN is genuinely present in plant and animal foods, but at sub-milligram-per-100 g levels, roughly 100 to 1,000 times below a single capsule. The reference dataset (Mills et al. 2016, Cell Metab, PMID 28068222 / DOI 10.1016/j.cmet.2016.09.013) puts every food it measured between 0 and 1.88 mg/100 g. A 2025 HPLC-DAD/LC-MS-MS survey of plant foods (Alegre & Pastore, CyTA J Food, DOI 10.1080/19476337.2025.2458753) found NMN spanning 40 to 13,000 ug/100 g, richest in broccoli and green beans, which is the same order of magnitude. Cow milk is not a meaningful NMN source: its NAD+ precursor content is dominated by nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside, not NMN (Trammell et al. 2016, PMID 27052539). Supplement NMN is not extracted from food, it is made by microbial fermentation or enzymatic/chemical synthesis.

items.dose_gap: Unbridgeable. Taking the richest food at its richest measured value (edamame, 1.88 mg/100 g), a 250 mg dose needs 13.3 kg of edamame a day, and at the low end of the same food's range (0.47 mg/100 g) it needs 53 kg. A 1,000 mg dose needs 53-213 kg. Broccoli: 250 mg requires 22-100 kg, about 245 to 1,100 cups. Avocado: 250 mg requires 104-463 whole avocados a day. Cucumber peel is the most quoted 'NMN food' and the least useful: you would have to pare the skin off roughly 1,250 cucumbers to reach 250 mg. There is no eating pattern that reaches a supplement dose, and no reason to think the trace dietary amounts do anything a supplement dose is claimed to do.
items.form_caveat: Substantial. NMN is a phosphorylated nucleotide and is not absorbed intact in any large quantity: it is dephosphorylated in the gut to nicotinamide riboside and then to nicotinamide before or during absorption, so an oral NMN capsule is partly a nicotinamide delivery system. Food NMN arrives as a minor component of a mixed NAD+ vitamer pool (nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, NR, NAD+ itself) inside intact cells and is measured after extraction, not necessarily released by chewing and digestion. Supplement material is manufactured by fermentation or enzymatic synthesis, never extracted from broccoli or edamame despite the marketing imagery. Regulatory status also differs: the FDA has taken the position that NMN is precluded from being marketed as a US dietary supplement, while it is sold freely elsewhere, so 'food-derived' framing on a label carries no compositional meaning.
items.bioavailability: Food NMN quantities are too small for bioavailability to matter. For the supplement form, human and mouse tracer work shows the oral route delivers NAD+ precursors largely after conversion to nicotinamide riboside and nicotinamide rather than as intact NMN (Trammell et al. 2016, Nat Commun 7:12948, DOI 10.1038/ncomms12948, for the NR side of the same pathway). Separately, ordinary diets already supply 15-20 mg/day of niacin equivalents feeding the same NAD+ pathway, which is thousands of times more molar precursor than the NMN in any vegetable portion, so the scarcity premise behind NMN supplementation is not a dietary-shortfall argument.

items.availability_note: NR is a real dietary vitamer, best characterised in cow milk, where it is present at single-digit micromolar. Trammell et al. 2016 (J Nutr 146(5):957-963, PMID 27052539, DOI 10.3945/jn.116.230078) found cow milk carries about 12 umol/L of NAD+ precursor vitamins, 60% nicotinamide and 40% NR, and an enzyme-coupled milk assay measured NR at 4.3 +/- 2.6 uM (Ummarino et al. 2017, Food Chem 221:161-168, DOI 10.1016/j.foodchem.2016.10.032). That is about 1.1 mg per litre. Plant foods carry 62 to 1,600 ug per 100 g, highest in wild chicory, banana and orange (Alegre & Pastore 2025, CyTA J Food, DOI 10.1080/19476337.2025.2458753). Every one of these is three orders of magnitude below a 250-1,000 mg capsule. Commercial NR chloride is synthesised, not extracted from milk.

items.dose_gap: Not reachable. At 1.1 mg NR per litre of milk, a 300 mg dose is about 273 litres of milk a day, roughly 1,150 cups; a 1,000 mg dose is about 910 litres. From the richest plant food measured (1.6 mg/100 g) a 300 mg dose is about 19 kg a day. Put the other way, one 250 mg NR capsule contains as much NR as roughly 230 litres of milk. Milk is genuinely the best dietary source of NR and it is still useless as a route to a trial dose.
items.form_caveat: Important. Commercial NR is nicotinamide riboside chloride, a synthesised salt; the free NR in milk is a fragile glycosidic nucleoside that degrades on storage and is reduced in milk from mastitic (S. aureus positive) cows, and Trammell et al. also found conventional milk carried more NR than organic. So even the food number is a moving target. More significant: the whole diet already supplies plenty of the pathway's dominant precursor, nicotinamide, at 15-20 mg/day of niacin equivalents, so NR supplementation is not correcting a dietary gap in NAD+ precursors; it is a pharmacological attempt at a different pharmacokinetic profile. Also note that high-dose nicotinamide-family precursors carry methyl-group and flushing/hepatic considerations at gram level that a glass of milk obviously does not.
items.bioavailability: NR is absorbed orally and raises blood NAD+ in humans, which was the point of the original demonstration (Trammell et al. 2016, Nat Commun 7:12948, DOI 10.1038/ncomms12948). Absorption is not the constraint; the constraint is that food quantities are microgram-scale. There is also a route difference: much oral NR is cleaved to nicotinamide in the gut and liver, so a fraction of any dose acts as plain vitamin B3, which is abundant in food. In milk, NR is free in solution and not bound to milk proteins (NMR testing in Trammell et al. found no binding), so what little is there is available, it is simply trivial in amount.

items.availability_note: This is the one entry on the list where ordinary food beats the supplement outright. Wheat germ, dried soybeans, mushrooms, green peas, fermented soy and some aged cheeses carry milligram-per-portion quantities. Measured mean dietary spermidine intake is 54.7 to 87 umol/day depending on population, that is 7.9 to 12.6 mg/day (Munoz-Esparza et al. 2019, Front Nutr 6:108, PMID 31355206, DOI 10.3389/fnut.2019.00108), and the Bruneck cohort recorded 9 to 11.5 mg/day (Kiechl et al. 2018, Am J Clin Nutr 108(2):371-380, PMID 29955838, DOI 10.1093/ajcn/nqy102). Trial capsules delivered 0.9 mg/day in the SmartAge trial and 1.2 mg/day in the earlier pilot. The diet supplies roughly ten times the capsule.

items.dose_gap: The gap runs backwards, which undercuts the supplement premise. Two tablespoons of wheat germ (14 g) supply 3.1-5.0 mg of spermidine, three to five times the 0.9 mg/day dose used in the 12-month SmartAge trial and still above the 3.3 mg/day used in its follow-up. A quarter-cup of dried soybeans or a cup of sliced mushrooms supplies about 9 mg, close to an entire ordinary day's intake. Measured habitual intakes are 7.9-12.6 mg/day, so a typical 1 mg capsule adds roughly 8-13% on top of what the person is already eating, which is well inside the day-to-day variation of a normal diet. To match a day's dietary spermidine from capsules you would need about ten of them. Anyone who wants more spermidine should buy wheat germ, which costs a fraction of the capsules and delivers several times the dose.
items.form_caveat: Real, in both directions. Most 'spermidine' products are wheat germ extracts standardised to about 1 mg, not purified spermidine, so the label compound is the same molecule as in the food and there is no extraction advantage. Against that, aged cheese and natto also carry biogenic amines (histamine, tyramine, putrescine) which matter for people on MAO inhibitors or with histamine intolerance, so the richest fermented sources are not risk-free foods even though they are ordinary ones. Polyamines are also proliferative signalling molecules and concentrated long-term supplementation lacks the observational safety record that food-level intake has; the epidemiology (Bruneck) supports dietary intake, not high-dose extracts, and cannot be transferred to a capsule. Wheat germ also goes rancid quickly, so buy small and refrigerate.
items.bioavailability: Dietary polyamines are absorbed readily in the upper small intestine, and gut bacteria synthesise more, so intake is not the only input and circulating levels are homeostatically buffered. An exploratory double-blind RCT giving older men 40 mg/day of spermidine, roughly forty times a typical capsule and four times a rich day's diet, reported minimal change in circulating polyamines, which suggests the pharmacokinetic ceiling is reached long before supplement dosing adds anything. Germination changes the picture too: commercially germinated wheat grain measured 19-24 mg/kg spermidine against 221-337 mg/kg for industrially separated wheat germ, an 85% drop, so the processing of the food matters more than any supplement choice.

items.availability_note: Organ meats and oily fish are genuine, substantial sources. Beef heart contains 113 mg/kg, chicken heart 116-132 mg/kg, mackerel dark flesh 43-67 mg/kg (Pravst et al. 2010, Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr 50(4):269-280, DOI 10.1080/10408390902773037, table reproduced in Vaghari et al. 2016, Am J Biochem Biotechnol 12(4):214-219, DOI 10.3844/ajbbsp.2016.214.219). Total habitual dietary intake is 3.8-5.4 mg/day, higher in men than women (Mattila & Kumpulainen 2001, J Food Compost Anal 14:409-417, DOI 10.1006/jfca.2000.0983). So the food is real, and one portion of heart is two to three days of ordinary intake. The problem is that supplement doses are 100-300 mg, which is a different universe. Supplement CoQ10 is produced by microbial fermentation or chemical synthesis, not extracted from beef.

items.dose_gap: Not reachable, though the food is respectable. A 300 mg/day dose requires about 2.7 kg of beef heart, 2.3-2.6 kg of chicken hearts, or 4.7 kg of the very richest sardines, which is about 51 tins a day, rising to over 60 kg if your tins sit at the low end of the measured range. The whole day's ordinary dietary CoQ10 is 3.8-5.4 mg, so a 300 mg capsule is roughly 55 to 80 days of eating compressed into one dose, and even a modest 100 mg capsule is about 20 to 26 days' worth. Anyone whose reason for taking CoQ10 is a claimed pharmacological effect at 100-300 mg cannot get there by eating. Anyone whose reason is simply 'my diet is low in CoQ10' can move the needle meaningfully with a weekly portion of heart, liver or oily fish.
items.form_caveat: Significant. CoQ10 is a large lipophilic quinone (MW 863) and crystalline ubiquinone powder in a dry tablet absorbs very poorly; commercial products use oil suspensions, solubilisates or reduced-form ubiquinol precisely because the raw molecule does not dissolve. Absorption is saturable, so a 300 mg dose does not deliver proportionally more than a 100 mg dose. Food has one genuine advantage here: CoQ10 in meat and fish comes packaged with fat, and taking supplemental CoQ10 with a fatty meal materially improves absorption, so a capsule swallowed on an empty stomach may deliver less than the label implies. Cooking costs some of the food content, with reported losses of roughly 15-32% frying pork cutlets and about 15% grilling beef. Finally, most body CoQ10 is made endogenously and the biosynthetic pathway shares its early steps with cholesterol synthesis, which is the basis of the statin argument; neither food nor supplement changes that pathway.
items.bioavailability: Low and formulation-dependent for the supplement, which is the honest headline. Ubiquinol (reduced) and solubilised formulations achieve higher plasma levels than plain crystalline ubiquinone, and all forms depend on dietary fat and bile for uptake. In the food matrix, CoQ10 sits in mitochondrial membranes and is co-ingested with fat, so uptake per milligram is probably as good or better than a dry capsule, but the milligram totals are 20 to 80 times too small. Note also that the reduced/oxidised split differs between foods: a Japanese survey of 70 food items found ubiquinol-10 above 20 ug/g in pork shoulder, bovine liver, chicken heart, horse mackerel, young yellowtail and soybean oil (Kubo et al. 2008, J Food Compost Anal 21:216-222, DOI 10.1016/j.jfca.2007.09.003), so 'ubiquinol' is not an exclusively supplemental form.

items.availability_note: Alpha-lipoic acid exists in food only as lipoyllysine, covalently attached to lysine residues in the E2 subunits of mitochondrial keto-acid dehydrogenases. Direct LC measurement of meats found 2.11-3.99 ug/g fresh weight in hearts, 0.71-1.40 ug/g in kidney and 0.56-1.17 ug/g in liver (Kaminska & Chwatko 2020, J Agric Food Chem, PMID 32886880, DOI 10.1021/acs.jafc.0c03778), i.e. 0.06-0.40 mg per 100 g. The classic vegetable figures, spinach 3.15 and broccoli 0.94 ug lipoyllysine per gram of DRY weight, work out to about 0.03 and 0.01 mg per 100 g of fresh vegetable. A 600 mg capsule is four to five orders of magnitude above any of these, and the food form is not free lipoic acid at all.

items.dose_gap: Absurd, and worse than the arithmetic suggests. Using the richest food at its richest value (turkey heart, 0.40 mg/100 g), a 600 mg dose is 150 kg of heart per day. Using spinach, the textbook answer, it is about 2,100 kg of raw leaves, roughly 71,000 cups, per day. Broccoli is similar. But the real point is qualitative: what food contains is not alpha-lipoic acid, it is lipoyllysine, lipoic acid amide-bonded to protein-bound lysine. Human lipoamidase activity releases very little free lipoic acid from that bond, so the free-ALA yield from eating spinach is not merely small, it is close to unmeasurable. A 600 mg fasting capsule produces micromolar plasma peaks of free racemic lipoic acid; no quantity of food produces a detectable free-ALA peak at all. This is the clearest food/supplement discontinuity on the list.
items.form_caveat: Large, and it cuts against the supplement. Supplemental ALA is chemically synthesised as a 50:50 racemate of R- and S-lipoic acid; nature makes only the R enantiomer and only protein-bound. So the capsule contains a molecule (S-lipoic acid) that does not exist in food. Absorption also differs by design: capsules are dosed fasting because food reduces ALA absorption by roughly 20-30%, whereas the trace food form is unavoidably taken with food. On safety, the whole food is unremarkable and the concentrated free acid is not: high-dose free ALA has been linked to insulin autoimmune syndrome with severe hypoglycaemia in genetically susceptible people, and there is a paediatric accidental-overdose literature with seizures and death. Spinach has done none of that. If you want the 'antioxidant vegetables' benefit, eat the vegetables; if you want the 600 mg neuropathy dose from the ALADIN/SYDNEY trials, understand you are taking a synthetic drug-dose racemate with its own risk profile, not a vegetable extract.
items.bioavailability: Free supplemental ALA is absorbed reasonably well but cleared very fast, with a plasma half-life on the order of half an hour, and the R enantiomer reaches higher plasma levels than S. Food lipoyllysine is a different question: it is not a bioavailable source of free lipoic acid, because the lipoyl group stays bound to the enzyme protein and is largely digested along with it rather than released as the free dithiol. The measurement literature reflects this, noting that free lipoic acid in tissues is low if present at all and that essentially all of it is protein-bound. Spinach also carries the usual oxalate caveat for other purposes, but oxalate is not the reason spinach fails as a lipoic acid source; the reason is that there is almost none there and what is there is chemically locked up.

items.availability_note: MSM (dimethyl sulfone) really does occur in food, and the numbers are tiny: cow's milk 3.30 mg/kg, coffee 1.60, tomato up to 0.86, alfalfa 0.77, tea 0.30, beer 0.18, Swiss chard up to 0.18, corn up to 0.11 mg/kg (Pearson, Dawson & Lackey 1981, J Agric Food Chem 29(5):1089-1091, DOI 10.1021/jf00107a049; values tabulated in the 2026 MSM review, PMC13071705). Milk, the richest of them, is 0.33 mg per 100 g. Supplement doses are 1.5-6 g/day. The bulk MSM sold as a supplement is not extracted from milk or vegetables: it is manufactured by oxidising dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) with hydrogen peroxide or nitrogen dioxide and then purified by distillation or crystallisation. Functionally this is a synthetic bulk chemical with a token natural presence.

items.dose_gap: One of the widest gaps here. A 3 g/day dose from milk, the richest listed food at 3.30 mg/kg, needs about 909 kg of milk a day, roughly 880 litres or 3,700 cups. From coffee it is about 1,875 litres, some 7,800 mugs. Even the low end of the osteoarthritis trial range, 1.5 g/day, needs 450 kg of milk. Adding up a plausible whole day of milk, coffee, tea, tomatoes and vegetables gives well under 1 milligram of MSM, so a single 3,000 mg dose is thousands of days of dietary MSM at once. There is no food-based route to a supplemental MSM dose, and it should be described as a synthetic sulfur compound taken at pharmacological dose, not as a nutrient you might be short of.
items.form_caveat: Yes, and it is mostly about honesty in marketing. Commercial MSM is made by oxidising DMSO, so it is chemically identical to the trace natural molecule but industrially produced; purity grades differ (distilled versus crystallised) and residual DMSO or solvent is a real quality variable between brands. The common marketing move of pointing at garlic, onions and brassicas as 'natural MSM foods' is wrong: those foods are rich in allicin, thiosulfinates and glucosinolates, which are different sulfur chemistries and not MSM, and eating them does not deliver MSM. Sulfur adequacy in the diet comes from methionine and cysteine in protein, which is a separate question from MSM entirely. There is no case in which a whole food substitutes for an MSM capsule, and equally no evidence that anyone is MSM-deficient.
items.bioavailability: Absorption is not the limiting factor. MSM is a small (94 Da), highly water-soluble, uncharged molecule and is absorbed close to completely after oral dosing, distributing widely including across the blood-brain barrier, which is why it is detectable in cerebrospinal fluid. Circulating MSM in people who take no supplements comes partly from these trace food amounts and partly from bacterial and endogenous metabolism of other sulfur compounds. Because uptake is near-complete for both, the food-versus-supplement comparison reduces entirely to the dose, and the dose ratio is roughly 1:4,000 per cup of milk.

items.availability_note: This is the one supplement on the list whose trial dose is genuinely reachable by eating, because the supplement is simply hydrolysed collagen and several ordinary foods are almost pure collagen. Gelatine is thermally hydrolysed collagen: 85.7 g protein per 100 g with tryptophan recorded as 0.000 g (USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy, Gelatins, dry powder, unsweetened). Plain pork crackling is 61.3 g protein per 100 g with a collagen amino-acid signature (glycine 11.9 g, proline 7.3 g per 100 g). Trial doses are 2.5-15 g/day over 3-18 months (Paul, Leser & Oesser 2019, Nutrients 11(5):1079, PMID 31096622, DOI 10.3390/nu11051079). Bone broth, the popular food answer, is the unreliable one.
